AT sr. STEPHEN'S GATE. How few are born to live in ha Is of fame, To revel in the splendour of a name: Yet many fear ob;curity as a sin, - Who toil half madly some renown to win.. A being of this kind his brain disturbed With strangely latN, •,- • ,00ughts, nor curbed His appetite for that forbidden fruit, -thhich could not such a mortal sit. He was no King in intellect or mien; In fact, though city barn, precisely green. A simple man, and old, whose very looks suggested ignorance of men and books. NoYr this uncouth designer—such he seemed— Had never worked, nor idled, sitoply dreamed. His days were spent in picturing toe age, When he shim d pose the sagest of the sage. What freaks have lifted people on to stilts, Teo 11t1e hitherto except for public jilts ! Our dreamer made th:s tempting truth his text, And patience kept his soul from gAting vext. Though time no honours to him nearer brought, The self-same confidence its spirit wrought; Resolving into dreaws his wish to be The leader or a potent Ministry. "For Parliament" he mused (alas, how ofa An indication of a brain gone soft) "Must one day own the majesty of might, And see in me its centre and its light:" "Pis said attraction rqles the bqinan bireefa cur irtians to planes we would fill; No doubt some wish.es govern what we do, And lead us into funny habits, too. At any rate specific tea-one moved (Grotesquely, as the sequel pls.:city pawed), This silly man. whose footfalls strilck no ear As prefixing the advent of a peer ! For day by day at proud St Stephen's gate He stood—a Lazarous of the State— Or loitered, ralr,r—snmewhat of a lout To those who marvelled why ha was about! His wistful looks but feelaiy told desires That "Paled their ineffectual fr " Before necessity's cold law, which crushed And finally his mohstrous cravings hushed. As INTERESTING DOG Ateectoree—An invalid gentleman from London, always accompanied by his dog, a beautiful Skye terrier, was in the habit of visiting the" Wells" every morning to drink the waters. After his death, ten months -since, the dog was given to a lady residing in Tunbridge Wells, bat the little creature appeared at the " Wells" regu- larly every morning, and spends nearly the whole of the day watching for his beloved master, and when he sees any one approaching who appears at all feeble he reins to meet him, and then comes back with a sad disappointed look in his lovely eyes. The ladies who visit the " Wells" notice and feed him; he accepts their attentions gratefully, but will never follow one of them. The servant of his present owner generally fetches him home at night. —City Press BOBBIE AND 'THE Pia.—Robert Forsyth, gravedigger, bellman, and minister's man, at Biggar, was asked by his master, who was knowing in pigs, to take one of a very fine litter to his friend, the then minister of Dolphieton. Bob was told to be sure and inform the receiver of everything about its " blood and culture"—not only who its father and mother, but who its forebears generally were. "And ye see, Rib, be sure ye tell this afore ye let it oot, for he'll never head a word after that for glowerin' at its perfections" So off Rob trudged with his pock and his high-bred burden. When bee ime to Candy Burn, a little way out of Biggar, wbere a dram was then so'd, he met Richie Robb, a hamoorist and wag, who seeing the bedral, says, "Whaur are ye gatin ?" " 00, "I'm genii to Dowfintonti, post the wannerfust pig ever was pigget ; its for the minister." "Ay man! Come yer ways in and tale a dram, and let's see the pig." The pig was seen and admired, and then the drain and a crack. Meanwhile Richie takes oat the pig and pate in a young puppy-dog about the same weight, and Robbie trudeee off, arriving in the afternoon at the manse of Dolphinton. The minister was out looking about him, and knew Roh. "What's this in the pock, Robbie, my man?" "Ay. ye may well speir, Mr. Meek. Its joust the maist extraordinar pig ever was. My maister has set it a parteekler present to you, wi' his compliments." "Let us see'c, Robbie." "Na,na, sir, I mann first put yet up to its generation, sae to speak." He then detailed its ante- cedents, and let it solemnly escape at the corner. Out edam the puppy, winking and lively. "That's a dowg, Robbie!" says the minister. "A dowg ! a dowgi as share's daith it is a dowg ; it was as sure, Mr. Meek—as fac's daith—it was a pig when it gaeci in I" "Wee!, Rob- bie, it's a elovvg noo, so you may tak' it back. But come in and has yer four °ore." Robbie took a fearful look at the beast, returned it with much subdued blasphemy, astonish- ment, and cruelty to the pock, and, making a hearty meal, started again, giving a sceptical keek into his pock every now and then on his way when he thought nobody saw him, to see what further change was going on. He arrived once more, disgusted, bewildered, and weary' at Candy Barn, where, of course. Richie was waiting for him. " Ye've been ling, Robbie, and what for are yo carrvin' the pock ower yer shouther ?" Robbie gave a grunt of disgust and told his story. " That's awfa', Robbie, petfectly fearsome;' ye mann dap in and hae a dram. 00, mann tell Tibbie." Rob flung down his pock with its portentous contents—which gave an unmistakable yowl—and took his dram and told his woes. Of course Richie transposed the pig once more, and )n went Rob, hearted by drink a little, but full of alarm as to his master, who met him at the deor eager to knew what his friend:thought of the pig. Robbie flung down his pock with a desperate air, took his stand, and, rubbing his forehead, poured out the prodigious story—". A whaulp, an atoolute whaulp, as ye may see, sir, wi' yer atni een." Open- ing the pock and giving it, a vindictive kick, eat came the pig.of the morning! "As fac's daith, Mr. Watson, it was whanlp at Dowfintoun, and I look it in noose and thans to see if it was turnin' into onything else; and IS was a whaulp at Candy Burn, and that Richie Bob can aver and swear." "Nay dolt, Rabbis, Ricbie ken 3 a' about it," said tl.e more knowing minieter.—Dr. John Brown. TILE SPEAKING CONDENSER.—In a former note we an- nounced that M. Dunand had succeeded in making the "singing condensor " of Varley act as a telephonic receiver of speech. Since his first experiment he has brought the apparatus into a more practical form. It consists of a trans- mitting circuit consisting of a micropbone,a battery of four Leclanche cells, and the primary of a small induction coil, haying about 0•5 ohms resistance. The receiving circuit is composed of the line wire, a receiving condenser or conden- sere, and a battery of from six to twenty •Leclanche cells, according to the number of receiving condensers employed. The microphone is of a peculiar construction. Two metal plates enclosed in a ring of wood and forming a box, are connected in the circuit. Each plate has attached to its inner centre a small button of carbon, and between these two buttons is a little spindle of carbon held there by a bra's wire crossing the interior of the box between the two plates, and capable (by the degree of torsion given to it) of in- creasing or lessening the pressure of the microphonic con- tact between the two ends of the spindle and the buttons. All condensers will serve as receivers provided a battery be employed in the receiving circuit to keep them charged ; but M. Danand prefers those having thickness not over six centimetres, and made of thirty or thirty-six sheets of tin- foil separated by sheets of ordinary or of paraffined paper. A thin ring of wood or ebonite placed round each surface gives solidity to the pole. One side is fitted with a gutta- percha earpiece, or two conden=ers hung from a headpiece may be fixed upon each ear of the observer. When loud speaking is required, twelve condensers are placed in an open trough about three inches apart, and by this arrange- ment speech may be heard over a radius of five or six yards when a battery of thirty cells is used in the receiving cir- cuit. —Engineering.

He would impress on all the farmers through the country the advantages held out to them in the school. As regarded the male agricultural students, they were not at first so success- ful; but he was happy to say that in the last term they had made a great advance. Daring the last two terms only 12 male pupils passed through the school, whereas during the present term just closed eleven pupils, with another, an ex- tern pupil, had received instruction there. The mere fact of the pupils having doubled -though they had not yet had anything like the number which they ought to have, and which the committee expected ere long to have—was a very favourable augury for the success of the school. This school was certainly aided by the Government with a large subvention but very justly, and as far as he could judge very properly, the Government had determined that their aid should to a certain extent depend on local exertions; al, if they found that the people of the county Cork and of the province of Munster did not come forward and contri- bate in some manner towards the support of the school, they would not feel themselves juqified in continuing the large subvention. In every country in the world it had now been found that technical,education for the young was the only means by which success could be insured in any branch of industry. It was not the slightest use to give a person a book unless he was first taught how to read, and there was no use in giving a man a farm who had not been taught the elementary and the true principles of farming. The Irish farmers were face to face with competition from all parts of the world. In every country in Europe there were institu- tions whose object was to teach agriculture in its best form, and though this institution was but a new one, he believed that it had done a considerable amount of good. He earnestly hoped that those young gentlemen whom he ad- dressed would, when they went home, benefit by the lessons they had received in that institution. It could be said of all cf them that while they had been there their conduct had been most exemplary, and he hoped that when they went out into the world to pursue their avocations they would show by their knowledge and by their conduct that the time they had spent in that institution had not been spent in vain.

The truth only came to light but slowly, and then the sole punishment the younger Dalrymple received was dismissal from office. That was his sole punishment then; but he will ever remain gibbeted in history with Guise and Alva, with Kirk and Claverhouse, with So2jah Dowlah and Shefket Pasha, as a pitiless man of blood, who spared neither age nor sex, slaying not as a soldier,-but as an assassin. One feels some little satisfac- tion in recording that the posterity of the author of the Glencoe Massacre has died out, and that the title and estates are now held by the descendants of one of his younger brothers.

Society for the Encouragement of Agriculture, has sub- scribed £2OO, and the agricultural societies of Melnn, Meaux, and other places have completed the amount needed, which will be mainly expended in the purchase of cows for the continuation of the experiments. SHEEP WORRYING IN DERBYSHIRE.—SeveraI farmers in the neighbourhood of Brough and Bradwell, Derbyshire, have sustained serious losses by the depredations of two dogs amongst their sheep. On Tuesday morning the dogs were surprised worrying a sheep in a brook, and they were driven off. They returned later in the day, and Mr. Brown, farmer, of Shatton, succeeded in knocking both over, but was not near enough to kill, and they are still at large. Up to Thursday morning the dogs had killed two lambs and severely bitten six ewes and four lambs belonging to Mr. Unwin, of Brough. Mr. Brown had lost two sheep, and many more had been bitten. Mr. Sidebottom had found four sheep dead and several others badly mutilated. CURIOSITIES OF GRILFTING.—M. CaHier!) records in a rel• cent number of the Revue Horticole a case wherein he grafted a Jerusalem artichoke on to the stein of the sun- flower. The method of procedure is not stated, but a curl- ous result followed, namely, the formation of tubers on the stem of the sunflower, no tubers being found below ground, although several were found on the stem just above ground. We trust M. Corriere will give us farther particulars as to , this interesting experiment. The figure does not show how I the graft was effected, nor whether the tubers were formed I on the stock both above and below the graft. M. Carriers also figures a graft of the tomato on the stems of Solarium dalcamara. Our readers will remember the analogous ex- periments of Mr. Mauls and Mr. Alexander Dean some years since. LECTURES ON THE PRINCIPLES Or AGRICULTURE.— Professor Tanner asks us to inform the teachers in elemen- tary schools that, with a view of facilitating instruction upon the principles of agriculture in these echools, he is prepared to make arrangements to deliver a series of short courses of lectures on this subject in various parts of Eng- land and Wales. These courses will each consist of four lectures, and they will be given in each selected town upon two succeeding Saturdays, two lectures being given on each of those days. These courses of lectures will be commenced early in September, but in the selection of the towns for their delivery the convenience of the greatest number of teachers will be specially considered. Applications should state :—First, the names of the district teachers' associa- tions which could conveniently make use of the coarse of lectures at the town proposed; second, whether suitable ac- commodation can be obtained in that town for the delivery of these lectures, and the conditions on which such lecture. room can be obtained. It has been suggested that the sec- rotaries of the local associations would probably be willing to assist in making the necessary local arrangements. Com- munications should be addressed to Professor Tanner, Science and Art Department, South Kensington, London, S.W —The Schoolmaster. THREAD-WORMS IN THE AIR PASSLGES OF LAMES.—The Strongylus Filaria which are found in irritating numbers on the air passages of young cattle and sheep in the form of ova and immature worms, are picked up in the herbage, and escaping destructive maceration in the gastric fluids, are Carried by the blood into the lung textures, there undergo further changes, and shortly pass outwards into the bronchial tubes,-eausing much irritation, producing tho loud spasmo- dic cough, interfering with eating and thriving, and killing some weekly subjects. From the widening distribution of the ova of the Strongylns, the "lung complaint of lambs," as it is sometimes called, has during the last few years be- cams more wide-spread and serious. How are the tormentors to be got rid of? inquires our correspondent. Good feeding alone enables some vigorous patients to cope with an get rid of their tormentors; but their riddanca is greatly has- tened by administering in a little milk a drachm of oil of torpentine, repeatnd for two or three consecutive mornings'

_ _ was supposed . Bee pat work, except during the brief intervals ..owed for meals and exercise. A convict able to Fet t..''..rough his task of picking three pounds of oakum early .n the afternoon could read or walk about his cell as he pleased, but there was no such relaxition for Devitt. The bucket was placed in the middle of the cell, and must not be put near the wall, leaning against the wall not being allowed. If a convict attempted to lean against the wall he was liable to punishment. Mr. Davitt found that the constant stooping posture to which he had to submit caused him severe pain in the chest, and caused a stoop in his back. But in order that my readers may rightly understand what prison life in Millbank is really like, let me briefly describe a convict's day. Rising at six, the first hour is spent in cleaning the cell and the corridor in front of thE cell doors. Unlike Pentonville, the corridors at Millbank contain cells on one side only, a wall, relieved by high- placed windows, being opposite the cell doors. The cons vim! to be allowed to clean thQ , windows, for they can thus obtain a glimpse of outside life. I Soon after seven the breakfast is served, consisting of three- quarters of a pint of cocoa,and as much bread as the convict cares to eat of the 20 ounce loaf, which is given to him in the morning and must last him all day. Breakfast over, the convicts are marched to chapel, and it is while they are passing through the corridors that opportunities are afforded of trafficking for tobacco. The man who has well-to-do friends outside will soon find ways and means of obtaining not only tobacco, but other luxuries, such as butter, pies, fruit, tkc. Of course the warders are implicated, and it has been said there are few warders who will not do it, pro- vided they are sure of their man—that he will not " split" on them. The man who has "snout"—tobacco—can pro- cure as much meat, bread, cheese, des., from other prisoners las he can consume, and the chief warders are accustomed to suspect convicts who seem to get fat of having tobacco in their possession. But it is seldom found, only very small quantities being served out to the convict at a time. It is very dear to the convict: if he gets two pounds of the weed in exchange for a £5 note, sent to the peeeant warder by the convict's friends, he does well. The punishment awarded to a convict found with tobacco in his possession is very severe, three days' bread and water at least, sometimes seven and even foerteen, the loss of all privileges, including letter writing and receiving, visits from friends, and a loss of probably three months' remission of sentence. The daily prayers at the prison chapel are little better than a farce. The time-20 minutes—allowed is so short that the prayers have to be gabbled over in an irreverent manner by the chaplain or his assistant—in a way that cer- tainly does not give one the idea of worship. Once or twice a week the convicts remain in chapel for a further period of 10 or 15 minutes to practice singing—the only part of the chapel performance liked by the men. On returning to the cells labour is resumed till dinner time, unless the exercise hour intervene. Exercise is taken in single file round a large yard, walking in summer, and partly at "the double" in cold weather. Several warders are stationed round the yard to stop talking, but "old lags" contrive to elude the vigilance at the corners, and sometimes the warder actually falls asleep whilst standing, of which of course the men take advantage. Dinner in a convict prison, if the convict gets his full allowance • and it is well cooked, and clean, is, in reality, a far better meal than most country labourers can procure. On Sunday, dinner consists of 4 ounces of cheese and 12 ounces of bread; on Monday and Saturday, a pound of potatoes, four ounces of meat (boiled) with about half a pint of the broth, and four ounces of bread; Tuesday and Friday, the same, except that mutton is served instead of beef; and on Thursday a pound of suet pudding is substituted for the meat and broth. For a small man, this quantity, in separate con- finement, is usually sufficient, but for a man of Davitt's physique, it is not enough, so Devitt complained to the governor that he had not sufficient food, and was referred to the doctor, who refused to allow him any more. The only thing in the shape of a knife allowed in convict prisons is a piece of tin, which the convicts sharpen on the stone floors. Mr. Devitt could not use this with one hand, and com- plained that he was compelled to bite his moat, or rather to tear it with his teeth. Devitt, admitted, what is often found to be the case, that the natural vexation which any man experiences, being imprisoned for the first time, had an effect upon his health which lie attributed to insufficient food.

At first, Dayitt was told he would have to pick a certain quantity of oakum per day, but it was impossible for him to pick even half as much as a man with two hands, and his inability to perform the task assigned to him, did not entail any punishment. Convicts under sentence for treason-felony, were not treated a whit differently to those convicted of ordinary crimes. For instance, Davitt had to wash and scrub his cell floor, although he had but one hand to do it with. He was under "special surveillance" as a dangerous prisoner, and was therefore not allowed to work out of his cell.

To a well-educated man like Davitt, the prison library books were a great boon, but he was wont to complain bit- terly of the difference between the Homan Catholic and the Protestant convicts, so far as their library books were con- cerned. The Protestant prison library contained many entertaining books that were prohibited by the prison priest. As a Catholic prisoner, Davitt was allowed four small religious books, two school books—an arithmetic and a geography, and one library book changed every fortnight. The books most coveted by Prcitestant prisoners are such serials a. the "Leisure Hour,"" Sunday at Home," "Good Words," &c. Chamber's Journal was stopped in 1867, in consequence of its containing some articles on Convict Life. _Devitt often complained of the childish character of the books sup- plied to him, but obtained no redress. To be continued.

div.head: "OUR OLD NOBILITY.' [Published by 2lfr. E. J. Kibblewhite, 31, Tavistock-steeet, London, WC., and reprinted by permission.] THE DALRYMPLES.
div.p: "OUR OLD NOBILITY.' [Published by 2lfr. E. J. Kibblewhite, 31, Tavistock-steeet, London, WC., and reprinted by permission.] THE DALRYMPLES.

I presume that the narrow Protestants who used to accuse ' me of hostility to the Reformation because I did not shrink from exposing the deeds of the time-serving Protestants in the reigns of Henry and Edward have long since found out their mistake. It may be that because I have endeavoured to do justice to such great Whig houses as the Cavendishes, Fitz- williams, and Fitzinautices, some may yet be disposed to think that I am actuated by party prejudice in favour of the Whigs. Perhaps, in dealing with the Dalrymples, I may be able to remove such an impression. I know that men are sometimes actuated by an unconscious bias ; but because I am aware of that fact, I believe I have spoken favourably of the great Whig houses only in so far as they have really aided the popular cause by honest and disinterested service.

So far as the landed possessions of the Dalrymples are concerned, they are exclusively a Scottish family. In the new Domesday Book, the Earl of Stair is credited with the possession of 83,872 acres, with a rent-roll of £44,640. The Countess of Stair has also 19,266 acres, with a rent-roll of £13,616; and the trustees of the eighth Earl have 13,201 acres, with a rent-roll of £10,701. In all, the Dalrymple family have, in Wigtonshire alone, 82,666 acres, the total acreage of which county is but 288,960; so that they hold two-sevenths of the whole county. he origin of the Dalrymples is somewhat obscure. According to Burke, a certain William de Dalrymple acquired the lands of Stair Montgomery, in Ayrshire, by his marriage with an heiress of the Kennedys. These Dal- rymples were among the first families of importance in Scotland who accepted the Protestant faith, for we find that as early as 1494 the wife of the son of this William de Dal- rymple. was accused before the Council of James IV. of holding heretical doctrines. The charge was, however, dis- missed. The great-grandson of this lady was one of the first who, about 1544, openly professed the doctrines of the Reformation.

The Dalrymples still hold considerable property in Ayrshire, at Stair, from which place they take their title, and elsewhere. Forty years ago, the estate of Bargany, which derived additional value from its coalpits and ironworks, was the property of Henrietta Dalrymple Hamilton, Duchess of Coigny, but the present Earl married the daughter of that lady, and thus has consolidated the property. The real founder of the family was James Dalrymple, a lawyer, who was a Lord of Session under Cromwell. He retained the office under Charles 11., ultimately. becoming President of the Court. Burnet describes him as "a man of very mild deportment, but a false and cunning man; a great perverter of justice, in which he had a very particular dexterity of giving some plausible colours to the greatest injustice." It was this Dalrymple who was first seated in Wigtonshire. Early in life he married a lady by whom he became possessed of certain lands in the parish of Old Luce in that county. A much larger portion of his acquisitions in Wigtonshire, however, was purely ecclesiastical property, which for a time was in the possession of the Earl of Casailis. Mr. Burton's account of the way in which Gilbert, Earl of Cassilis, became possessed of the lands of Glenluce Abbey is worth quoting. According to the family historian, Gilbert was "ane particular man and ane greedy man, and cared not how he gat land so that he could come by the same." He had his eye on a few of the estates of the Abbey of Glenluce, and had dealings with the Abbot about them. That Abbot, however, died before the writs were signed, "and then he dealt with ane monk of the same abbacy, wha could counterfeit the Abbot's hand writ and all the haill convent, and gat him to counterfeit their subscriptions. When this was done, fearing that the monk rnight make unpleasant revelations, he got a certain carl to 'stick' (stab, him, and then he got ane to accuse the earl of theft and hung him in Cronsgate, and so the lands of Glenluce were conquest." A pretty story of forgery and murder, is it not? I dare say not a few such tales woad have been told

div.head: PRISON LIFE OF MICHAEL DAVITT. BY THE AUTHOR OF "SKETCHES or CONVICT LIFE," ETC.
div.p: THE PRISON LIFE OF MICHAEL DAVITT. BY THE AUTHOR OF "SKETCHES or CONVICT LIFE," ETC.
CHAPTER I. HIS EARLY LIFE: MILLBANK.

Mr. Michael Davitt was born at Straid, near Castlebar, in county Mayo, in 1846. His father was a tenant farmer, and, being evicted in 1851, the family removed to England,. and settled in Lincashire. Michael, at the early age of nine, was sent to work in a cotton mill, and was but a year at that employment when he had the misfortune to have his right arm so badly 'crushed in the mill machinery as to necessitate its amputation at the shoulder. For the next five years he attended the Wesleyan school at Haslingden, and at the age of fifteen got employment as assistant letter-carrier and book-keeper in the printing office in con- nection with the post-office in that town. For six years he followed this occupation, carrying the mail bags to the station twice a day, and occasionally taking the place of the regular postman. The postal circuit at Haslingden was a very extensive one, and he had sometimes long distances to travel to deliver letters. In 1803 Mr. Davitt became a commercial traveller, dealing extensively in firearms, an occupation which eventually got him into trouble. On the 14th of May, 1870, be was arrested in London with a gun- smith, named John Wilson, from Birmingham. He was tried at Newgate on a charge of Fenianism, or" treason- felony, and on the 17th July, 1870, was sentenced by Lord Chief Justice Cockburn to 15 years' penal servitude, Wilson being sentenced to seven years. A man named Corydon was the informer on the occasion, and Davitt declared solemnly that he had never seen Corydon before in his life till he confronted him in the dock.

As my object in these articles is to chronicle the life of Davitt in the convict prisons in which he was confined, I will pass briefly over his detention in Newgate. Prisoners who have been often "in trouble," or old gaol birds, liked Newgate. The food was good and plentiful, the officers humane, the work not hard, and not exacted with that amount of rigour shown at other metroplitan prisons. The cells in Newgate are large and comfortable, and instead of the plank bed so common in gaols, there was a comfortab'e hammock. Convicts who are novices generally wish to be removed from Newgate to one or other of the convict pri- sons, the tales told by old lags regarding the latter places being tinged with couleur de rose so highly as to lead the novice to believe that when he once sets his foot in a convict prison his sense of punishment will almost be at an end. But a few weeks of convict prison life soon serves to dispel the illusion, and the wretched convict looks back to his few weeks' detenticn at Newgate with regret, and despite the solitary confinement, would gladly go back again to serve out his sentence. The teirible experiences of Mr. Davitt in the various convict prisons in which he was confined will prove this. On leaving Newgate he was taken to Millbank.

Milbank convict prison consists of six separate blocks of buildings, called pentagons, which are so constructed as to be in reality so many separate prisons. This mode of con- struction is so derogatory to the discipline deemed neces- sary, that its abandonment has for some years past been contemplated, the new prison at Wormwood ~crubs being substituted therefor. The cells at Millbank are about ten feet by seven. They are closed by an iron-barred gate, the bars of which are about one-and-a-half inch square, and by an inner door, the space between being about 18 inches, the thickness of the wall. Opposite to the door, and on the floor, is a sloping wooden plank-bed, raised at the head about flinches, and at the foot about four inches above the stone floor. A wooden bolster raised about four inches higher than the rest of the bedstead is anything but con- ducive to easy rest. A mattrass, filled with straw or cocoa nut fibre, three blankets in winter and two in summer, a rug. and two coarse linen sheets form the bedding, no pillow beyond the wooden one being provided. A wooden platter and spoon, a wooden salt box, two tin pint mugs, a bright pewter or zinc chamber utensil, an ordinary school slate, a large wooden bucket, about a foot in height, with a closely-fitting lid, which forms the only seat for the occu- pant of the cell; a short-handled hair broom or brush, a stiff millboard, having printed on it an abstract of the printed rules and regulations' and a small gas jet, without tap, protruding from the wall about four feet from the ground, complete the cell inventory. The cell windows are much larger than in other convict prisons, and there is more ventifation. The work done at Millbank consists of oakum-picking, tailoring, shoe- making, carpentering, coopering, ticsmithing, and several other handicrafts. When a convict enters Milbank he is asked his trade, and if it be one that ha can follow in the prison he is usually allowed to do so, unless he is down on his "caption sheet "—a record of his antecedents—as a dangerous character, or a prison breaker, in which case he must pick oakum. This is rightly regarded as a downright punishment, the oakum picker being compelled to sit all day on the low wooden bucket described above. Mr. Davitt used to complain bitterly of this part of his prison career. Being a one-armed man, he could do nothing in the way of work but pick oakum, and it was his principal complaint in reference to the cells at Millbank that he was thus compelled to sit on the bucket, no stool being allowed, and no table. For ten hours a day be bad to sit on the bucket, for though he bad no specific task of oakum picking to perform, yet he

div.head: LITERATURE.
div.p: LITERATURE.

TRAIZSFER OF LAND By REGISTRATION.—This is the title of an essay by Sir Robert Torrens, K.C.M.G., published in pamphlet, form for the Cobden Club by Messrs. Cassell, Petter, Gal pin, and Co. In the pamphlet the author advo- cates registration under the duplicate method operative in British colonies, and he claims that the success which has attended that method in the nine colonies in which it is in operation warrants the belief that the like result will follow its adoption in this country. In an appendix specimens are given of the various forms of /Ise registration, which on the whole appears simple, and, we should think, would not be difficult of application in this country. LAND NATIONALISATION, ITS NECESSITY, AND ITS AIMS, I by Alfred Russel Wallace, author of "The Malay Archi- pelago," "Island Life," 4c. (London: Trubner and Co., Ludgate Hill).—ln this volume, which will be found of much value at the present juncture, is given a comparison of the system of landlord and tenant with that of occupying ownership in their influence on the well-being of the people. As a complete solution of the land problem the writer argues (1) that landlordism mast be replaced by occupying owner- ship—no less radical reform will get ride of the wide-spread evils of our present system; (2) erraneernents must be made by which the tenure of the holder oeland must be secure and permanent, and nothing must be permitted to interfere with his free use of the land, or his certainty of reaping all the fruits of any labour or outlay he may bestow upon it; (3) arrangerhents must be made by which every British subject may secure a portion of land for personal occupation at its fair agricultural value; (4) all suitable tracts of enclosed or waste lands must (under certain limita- tions) be open to cultivation by occupying owners; (5) the freest sale and transfer of every holders interest in his land must be secured; and (6) in order that these conditions be rendered permanent sub-letting must be absolutely prohi- bited, and mortgages strictly limited. These, the writer urges, are necessary requirements. Occupying and virtual owneiship must go together. The State must be the real owner or ground landlord, and every other individual holder must hold its land from the State, subject to what- ever general laws and regulations might be made for all land t,O held. The scheme, it will be seen from the above, is a sweeping one, but it must be admitted that the writer adduces many facts and figures in support of it which are deserving of very careful consideration. MYSTERIES OF LONDON and WONDERFUL DREAMS OF REMLREABLE MEN AND WOMEN (London: Messrs. Dip- rose and Bateman, Sheffield-street, Lincolns' Inn Fields).— The former volume contains some very amusing sketches of London life, and a very pleasant hour or two may be spent in their perusal. They are written by "One of the Crowd," and whoever he may be he is remarkably clever at depicting the various traits of human character. In the latter volume, which is the work of Mr. J. Redding Ware, is given, as the title implies, the dreams of remarkable men and women brought down to the present time, and we need scarcely say that within its pages some very remarkable things are related alike difficult to understand or to believe. The last item in the book is one relating to sleeping on the side, and may be worth reproducing for husbands of an inquisitive turn of mind. It is as follows :—" Dr. Delaney (United States) says if you sleep on your right side your dreams will be old and faint remembrances; the dreams are apt to be childish and illogical ; sleepers on the right side also compose verses of no great value. Sleepers on the left side dream intelligent dreams about recent events. So if a man wants to dream what his wife used to say to him and about him before they were married he must sleep on his right side; if he wants to dream of what she says to him now, he must sleep on his left side." REVIVAL AND REVIVAL WORK (London: Messrs. Morgan ' and Scott, office of the Christian,l2, Paternoster Buildings). —This volume contains a record of the labours of Messrs. Moody and Sankey, the American revivalists, and it ha-s been compiled by the Rev. John Macpherson, whose in- terest in this particular walk of literature is well known. The author has fully exhausted his subject, which is treated in a pleasant and attractive vein, and the publication of the volume at a time when there is so much infidelity abroad is calculated to be productive of much good to those who may be awakened by its influence. THE ALPHABET OF GARDENING is the title of a sixpenny volume issued from the office of The Gardeners Magazine. The work is by Shirley Ilibberd, F.R.H.S., it is profusely illustrated, and its pages contain a mass of information, care- fully compiled, for all interested in gardening operations. Many practical hints are thrown out, asd with these gar- deners will doubtless profit. We are favoured with the usual parcel of periodicals from Messrs. Cassell, Petter, Galpin, and Co. Both The Family Magazine and The Quiver are excellent parte for this month ; and the same remark applies to Little Folks, with which is given an extra sheet of eight pages, containing the names of between 4,000 and 5,000 officers and members of the " Little Folks Humane Society.' "Old and New Edinburgh" and the "Popular Educator" have each reached the 20th part, and their standard of excellence is maintained. In "Familiar Garden Flowers," the two illustrations of an orange lily and the rhododendron, are faithfully executed. We have to acknowledge from Messrs. S. W. Partridge and Co., 9, Paternoster-row, receipt of " The British Work-

man," "The Band of Mercy Advocate," and "The Wel- come," each of which contains wholesome reading. In the latter is this month a memoir of John Livesey, one of the seven men of Preston, who were the fathers of the tem- perance movement.

Myra's Jrurnal of Dress and Fashion, Myra's Three- penny Journal, and Le Ilioniteur de la Mode (Messrs. Gou- band and Son, 39 and 40, Bedford-street, Covent Garden), and Weldon's Ltdies' Journal and Weldon's Illustrated Dressmaker are to hand. It is almost unnecessary to ssy that amongst the ladies these publications are grelt favourit3s, containing as they do all the most recent informa- tion as to dress and fashion in London, and Paris as well. We continue to receive copies of the "School Board Chronicle," "The Liberator," and "The Women's Suffrage Journal," each publication doing a good work in its particu- lar sphere.
new tale by Wilkie Collins, entitled "Heart and science:" A story of the pr6t, time? begins in the Liverpool Weekly Post to-day (Saturday).

div.head: TIIE STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: TIIE STATE OF IRELAND.

Mrs. Oonnell, a:poor woman who was shot on Friday at Coolagh, near Clarernorris, died on Saturday. She was suspected of intending to take an " evicted " farm which has been lying waste for years, hence the murder. Colonel Brackenhury, the director of the Royal Irish Criminal Investigation department and Assistant Under Secretary, left Duolin on Wednesday for London, with the intention, it is understood, of resigning his appointment. Near Dublin Castle, on Tuesday morning, it was seen that several of the "proclamations" under the new Crimes Act had been tampered with by placing over the final words "God save the Queen" a green printed slip inscribed "God save Ireland." The authorities, of course, soon tcok measures to deface the obnoxious sentiment. It is announced that Mr. Michael Davitt, hearing just before he left New York of the Eastern crisis, expressed much delight thereat, and the hope that Mr. Gladstone's Government would be overthrown. Mr. Davitt is on his way to Paris, where he will have interviews with Mr. Egan, the treasurer of the Land League. A Limerick correspondent telegraphs :—The driver of the mailcar between Tulla and Limerick was attacked and nearly murdered on Tuesday morning by some men. He was kicked in a brutal manner, several of his ribs being broken, and he now lies in a dangerous condition. The motive is supposed to be that he had taken the place of a driver who had been dismissed.

The first motion under the Prevention of Crime Bill was made in Dublin, on Tuesday, by Mr. Murphy, Q.C., on behalf of the Crown. The Vice-Chancellor granted orders upon the certificate of the Attorney-General to remove from Galway prison for trial in Dublin Michael Walsh, charged with the murder of Constable Kavanagh, and Patrick Walsh, also charged with murder. _

A Daily News special correspondent, who is describing the state of Ireland, teleg: aphs that the continued wet Weather is giving rise to serious apprehensions. The excessive rains of the last fortnight have done much harm to all the crops. The corn is being injured, the hay destroyed, and the potatoes blighted. But for the excessive rain there was the prospect of a splendid harvest—its cessation can only miti- gate the disaster, and cannot prevent great loss. The first arrest under the new Act took place on Satur- day. It was that of a man named Sullivan, charged with having threatened a farmer. A police patrol on Saturday morning discovered a number of dogs worrying a flock of sheep belonging to Lord Donraile, near Butterant. Several of the sheep were killed. During the last twelve months a number of sheep have been destroyed in the district, and it now seems probable that the ravages have been made by dogs. At the opening of the Donegal Assiz2s Lord Justice Fitz- gibbon was able to congratulate the county on the insignifi- cant list of crimes for investigation. The list of the county inspector, his Lordship said, was a remarkable and gratify- ing document. At the opening of the county Antrim Assizes it was found that there were only 16 cases for trial, and Mr. Justice Harrison remarked with pleasure that in that populous county law and order and the authority of the Queen were observed and respected. At Carrickfergus there were no prisoners for trial.

Judge BArry, addressing the grand jury af the opening of the Cork Assizes, said his repugnance at having to speak in despondency of his county induced him that time 12 months ago to travel too far and too quickly into the region of hope for the country's future. Though there was still existing in the county much to be regretted and deplored, there was a decided appreciable improvement. There were 220 offences committed since last assizes, as compared with 250 in the preceding term, 17 of which were brought to trial. Some of the outrages on cattle were sickening in their details. An Ennis telegram states :—An official report has been received here by County Inspector Smith of a most daring outrage perpetrated on Monlay night in the neighbourhood of Newmarket-on-Fergus. It appears that as a police patrol were going their rounds at Rathfriland, within half a mile of the village, and adjoining Lord Inchiquin's demesne, they heard shots fired near the house of Mr. Denis, and saw two men running away. The police called on them to stand, but they continued to run, and the three police fired on them. The fugitives then stood and returned fire, after which they got away. No casualties are reported on either side.

Mr. O'Donnell, the member for Dungarvan, is determined that there shall be no mistake as to the deliberate intention in which he nsEd the word " infamy " in regard to the action of the Chairman of Committees. In a letter to his constituents, the hon. gentleman says he adopted the epithet in order to characterise the "vile proceedings " of the " Government conspiracy ;" and adds that he was in no hurry or excitement when he chose that word, " having deliberately selected the most dishonouring word that occurred to his memory in order to brand with a suitatle term the most false, the most treacherous, the most tyranni- cal, and the most mean abuse of public trust and authority ever recorded."

A Parliamentary return was issued on Tuesday morning of the number of evictions in the first six months of the present year, distinguishing the number for non-payment of rent, and the number of cases of hardship. The total number of evictions during that period was 3,049, of which 908 were from causes otherwise than the non-payment of rent. In the remaining 2,051 cases, the constabulary reports stated that in 176 cases hardship was ciused to the tenant by his inability to pay rent due from poverty, caused by bad seasons, &T. In 132 cases the constabulary reports did not state the nature of the hardship admitted to exist, and in 346 cases the reports stated that the non-payment of rent was due to unwillingness cr fear of inquiry on the part of the tenant by so doing. The constabulary reports did not state the reasons for the non-payment of rent in the remaining 1,397 cases, or in the cases where a reason was given, it was one which did not come under the head of those already enumerated.

STRONG LANGUAGE.—The Press clauses of the Preventien of Crime Bill have no terrors for the L.ishman. The attack by a mob at Tredegar on some Irishmen—an attack violent and unprovoked, and which will be punished by the law, but which is insignificant by the side of the daily recurring crimes in Ireland—inspires the Irisliman to write in this fashion:--" It is futile to think of getting fair play from the British people. Their thirst for Irish blood is insatiable. At this moment the question of self-defence is a serious one for Irish men and women living among the Thugs of England and Wales. They must consider the peril of their position. There is no law in England to prevent Irish people from having arms in their houses. They cannot tell when or where they may be set upon. Let•them look to their defence, and at once. It is not an hour too soon for them to be ready for an attempt upon their lives. If they are not disposed to let themselves be murdered in cold blood they must put their houses in order, and be prepared to defend their wives and children from the hands of bloody-minded men. • While on their guard they should not give offence, nor be the first to strike a blow."

div.head: DUNECHT MYSTERY.
div.p: THE DUNECHT MYSTERY.
DISCOVERY OF THE BODY.

The Dunecht mystery was on Tuesday partially solved by the discovery of the missing body of the late Earl of Crawford and Balcarres. On Sunday last certain informa- tion was conveyed to Mr. James Cran, deputy chief constable of Aberdeenshire which led to an interview with a man well known to the police—a professional ratcateher and a notorious poacher. This man was examined, and from the information elicited, a police search party, comprising two inspectors, two sergeants, and 22 constables, proceeeded to Dunecht on Monday night, and, assisted by the game- keepers and watchers on the estate, a thorough search com- menced. In the course of a few hours the missing body was found. The actual spot of concealment had been correctly described by the man now in custody. The Castle is air- rounded by woods extending to about three square miles. The body was discovered two feet below the surface in a thicket in the woods a considerable distance from the Castle. At the time the outrage was discovered it was found that mthing in the tomb had been stolen with the exception of the body. When recovered on Tuesday the body was thickly wrapped in blankets. It is quite apparent that it has not been removed from its hiding place since the end of May of last year, so that it has been exposed in damp ground for at least fourteen months. The real perpetrators of this bar- batons act of desecration have not yet been detected, though there is reason to hope that this wished-for consummation may yet be attained. The man now in custody states that shortly after midnight on the date of the crime, in May, 1881, he was poaching on the wooded " policies" of Dunecht, and that during his peregrinations in the semi-darkness he came upon a party of four men whose .suspicious movements had a short time previously attracted his attention. When he came close upon them they were engaged in burying the body, and upon their observine• the intruder the men set upon him, threw him down, and presented a revolver close to his head. At this moment his assailants, by the nets and other gear which he carried, discovered the nature of the intruder's occupation. He was accordingly sworn to keep the matter of the desecration secret, with the alternative of certain dreadful penalties, and on so prorni:sing was allowed to go his way. The man who has made this statement, and who is in custody, is named Charles Sutor. He is about 41 years of age. His declaration was made volun- tarily; and he is not believed to have been one of the actual perpetrators of the crime, and has only now revealed the secret because of the weight with which, as he says, it continued to pleas on his mind. It is proved beyond doubt that he is the " Nabob" so often mysteriously mentioned in the course of the investigations. The police are still at Dunecht pursuing their inquiries.
