THE ARREARS BILL.—At the evening sitting the Arrears Bill was again proceeded with and passed through commit- tee, after which Mr. Gladstone's new clause affecting tenants of holdings of from £3O to £5O rental was proposed and accepted. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. AFFAIRS IN EGYPT.—Several notices of questions as to the Convention with France for the protection of the Suez Canal were put, and Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN, while declining to enter into particulars, assured the House that everything had been done that was necessary.—Sir W. LAWSON next wished to know if the Khedive hesitated to tell the Egyptian people that Arabi is a rebel; and Mr. A. ARNOLD asked if the Porte had yet replied to the Identie, Note, but on neither of these matters was Sir Charles Dilke in a position to give any information. ABANDONMENT OE LEGISLATION ON THE LAND ACT.— During the Committee proceedings on the Arrears of Rent Bill, the PRIME MINISTER stated that he did not think it would be desirable to hold out any expectation of legis- lation on the Irish Land Act, which would disturb the public mind in a manner which was likely to retard the action that was now going on to the great benefit of the country. The Government could . give no pledge whatever as to the legislation of next year until Parliament had dealt with the question of procedure. THE ARREARS OF RENT BILL.—The Arrears of Rent Bill as amended was ordered to be reported to the House, Mr. GLADSTONE remarking that steps would be taken to have it recommitted after report for the purpose of enabling every member who desired to make a motion in Committee to state his opinion. A preliminary step would also be taken be the Chief Secretary for a proposal of the Government to strengthen the Land Commission for a time by the appoint- ment of a fourth Commissioner, as it was desirable that the administration of this bill should not hamper the Com- missioners in the discharge of their present duties. It was stated that the third reading of the Arrears Bill will be Laken on Friday. THE CONTAGIOUS ACTS: THE SUNDAY CLOSING BILL.— The motion for the second reading of the Contagious Dis- eases Acts Repeal Bill was disposed of by the adoption of "the previous question" without a division. The second reading of the Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday Bill was moved by Mr. STEVENSON, and Mr. CALLAN was speaking at a quarter to six o'clock, when the debate under the standing orders of the House stood adjourned. HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tanatney.

PROPOSED ARMED OCCUPATION OF EGYPT.—The Marquis of SALISBURY asked Earl Granville to give an indication of the policy Her Majesty's Government proposed to pur- sue with respect to the armed occupation of any portion of Egypt, in view of the statement that the French Govern- ment had resolved upon armed intervention.—The FOREIGN SECRETARY promised to make a full statement on Monday of the policy of the Government. OXFORD UNIVERSITY. The Marquis Of SALISBURY moved an address praying Her Majesty to withhold her assent from the proposed statute for the University of Oxford, framed by the University of Oxford Commissioners, con- cerning the nomination of examiners.—The Earl of CAM- PERDOWN defended the statute, and urged that in rejectingit their Lordships would be perpetuating a system which had been condemned by every public body that had investigated the subject.—Lord CRANBROOK, the Marquis Of LANSDOWNE, the Earl of DERBY, and the Lord CHANCELLOR took part in the debate, and upon a division the motion was defeated by 70 to 57.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.- THETSDAY.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.- THETSDAY.

PROPOSED VOTE OF CREDIT.—TERMS OF THE IDENTIC NOTE.—The Pn.tmE Mults-rEn gave notice that on Monday be shall ask for a vekte of credit to enable Her Majesty to strengthen her forces in the Mediterranean. The precise amount of the vote will be stated on Saturday. After the vote the House will be asked to proceed with the tax bill of the year, and Mr. Gladstone will propose a modification, intended to make provision for meeting the charge of the vote of credit. The right hon. gentleman made a strong appeal to members not to ask the multitude of questions put down on the paper relating to Egyptian affairs, on the ground that asking questions of the kind caused inferences to be drawn and impressions created which tended to weaken the action of public authority in regard to this important subject, and which was undoubtedly injurious to public in- terests. He excepted from this appeal any question that might he put in regard to any account which appeared in the newspapers of some new fact of great public interest or importance.—Mr. GLADSTONE subsequently mentioned that during the day a despatch had been received by the Government, from which it appeared that the Sultan had agreed to join the Conference. The terms of the despatch did not contain any-direct reference to the question of the Sultan sending troops to Egypt.—ln reply to Mr. Bourke, Sir C. DILKE stated the precise nature of the measures taken by the Government for the protection of the Suez Canal, and also read the terms of the joint note presented to the Porte with respect to the Turkish intervention. The note shows that the Sultan was aked to send troops, under certain clearly-defined conditions, to restore order in Ezypt The bon. Baronet also read to the House the despatches. which have passed between our Government and that of Austria on our action at Alexandria, the snbstance of which was that Court Kalnoky has stated that the Austrian Gov- ernment were disposed to consider the bombardment as an act of self-defence, caused by the provocative and menacing attitude of the Egyptian authorities, and as an incident which might be without any detrimental influence on the diplomatic situation, provided England limited her action to the disarmament of the forts at Alexandria.

ANSWERS TO QuEsrioNs.—Questions on various matters of general interest were put to ministers.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in reply to Mr. Talbot, hoped that the " block " would be removed from the Imprisonment for Contumacy Bill, and Mr. HUSSEY VIVIAN, who had the "block ' on, said he would remove it if he could feel assured that the bill would be debated.—The PREMIER also stated that the Government did not intend to propose the creation of a ministry of agri- culture and commerce this session ; and it was not intended to give Government employment to Irish labourers in the coming autumn and winter. As to the number of cases that might arise under the Arrears Bill, he thought there might be 200,000, but it did not follow that they would all be proved.—Mr. TREVELTAN explained that Colonel Bracken- bury trid resigned the Assistant Under Secretaryship for Ireland for private reasons; and Mr. GLADSTONE, in answer to Mr. Fowler, said the Government intended to appropriate Tuesday evenings. ARREARS BlLL.—Coming to the Arrears Bill once again, much cariosity was manifested as to the name of the intended fourth Commissioner, and, after several questions had been asked, Mr. Gladstone relieved members by nominating Lord Monck. The bill, as amended, was then considered, and, after several amendments had been disposed of, was recommitted, when Mr. Gladstone proposed a new clause appointing Lord Monck a Commissioner for the limited term of two years.

div.head: LANCASHIRE FACTORY HAND'S CAREER.
div.p: A LANCASHIRE FACTORY HAND'S CAREER.

An extraordinary case (Newhouse 1). Newhouse) came before Vice-Chancellor Bristowe, last week, at the sittings of the Chancery Court of Lancashire. The plaintiff brought the action against his two daughters to set aside a deed executed by him in their favour. The parties reside at Bolton, where, at an early age, the plaintiff worked in a cotton mill. Acquiring a considerable knowledge of the trade, the plaintiff entered into business on his own account some time subsequently. He was not altogether successful, and accordingly obtained an engagement as manager of a mill in Finland. He proceeded thither, accompanied Ly his wife and two daughters, and occupied this position for several years, receiving in salary during that period some £7,000 or £B-,000, and he contrived to save a considerable sum. His family returned to England, and he forwarded money to them. subsequently he also returned to England, but not long afterwards proceded to India in a similar capacity to that in which he was engaged in Finland. He made money there, but, becoming involved in a lawsuit, ex- pended it. Returning home in 1877 he was coldly received by his family, and, according to the evidence, they annoyed and ill-treated him in many ways, the food in the house even being hidden from him. The plaintiff said he had spent some £3,000 on the education of his daughters in order to qualify them for earning their own livelihood should it be necessary for them to do so. His daughters are aged respectively twenty-eight and thirty, and the younger was given an expensive course of instruction in Manchester and London, in order to prepare her for the musical profession. For two years after hi fi return from India, and during part of which time the plaintiff suffered from ill-health, his wife and daughters urged him to settle on them his property, which was worth about £3,000, and be ultimately consented, it being agreed that he should receive in consideration of his executing the deed a sum of £1,538. The deed was executed, but the money the plain- tiff was to receive was either not paid or immediately after- wards got from him by his daughters, and be was left penniless. In these circumstances he came before the court. The defendants contended that the plaintiff executed the deed without undue influence, and when he was in a compe- tent condition. The case was concluded by addresses from counsel. His Honour remarked that the plaintiff's family had appeared all along to consider that the plaintiff was the person to earn the money, and they were the persons to have it. The Vice-Chancellor, in giving judgment said he bad never had to do with a case more painful in its circum- stances or more to be regretted than that before the court. If the two defendants allowed themselves to be parties to this transaction, they, from first to last, mistook the respon- sibilities of that which they had undertaken. They had undertaken to stand between their father and mother, pain- ful under any circumstances, and certainly if, as suggested, it was a trust undertaken by them, it was a most mistaken, erroneous, and unfortunate view for them to take. The two daughters undertook to act as trustees between the father and mother, by which the whole of the father's available property at that moment was taken away from him, leaving him practically dependent upon the bounty of those around him. That that should have been done by two daughters against there own father, whose property it was, and which he had slaved hard in foreign countries to acquire, was to kis mind one s of the most distressing and painful circum- stances which had ever come before him either en the bench or at the bar. His Honour went on to say that there was no evidence of any consideration money having changed hands, and in his opinion the transaction was a sham from begin- ning to end. It was a moral fraud upon the plaintiff. He decided that the deed be given up by defendants in order ' that it might be =yelled. Judgment was stayed for a I men*.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATIMDAY, JULY 2, 111'82.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATIMDAY, JULY 2, 111'82.
M ISOEL LAN EOUS.

The death is announced of Mr. Thomas Teal, of Bolton, perhaps the best known registration agent in Lancashire. Two Yarmouth fishermen, named Causefield and Wolsey, were drowned at North Shields on Saturday by the capsizing of a boat.

The Lancashire and Cheshire Beekeepers' Association will hold a great bee and honey show in connection with the Horticultural Society's show at Preston in September. At Greenwich, on Tuesday, Churchwarden Sanders, of St. JamPs's, Hatcham, was fined 40s. for endeavouring to pre- vent the vicar from:administering the Sacrament to less than three communicants. _ _ _

The London and Brighton coach was upset on Monday evening at Belmont Station' near Sutton, through the horses shieing at a tricycle. Several passengers, including two ladies and the coachmam, sustained severe inkiries,and others were much shaken. _ _ _

The result of the poll recently taken by authority of the Local Government Board on the question of triennial elections of Guardians of the Poor for Manchester was made known on Tuesday night. The majority in favour of the proposed change, of the ratepayers who voted, was 9,131. On Monday afternoon, a little boy named Alfred Sayers, while endeavouring to escape from a room in the Board Schools, Knapp's-road, Bromley-by-Bow, where he had been confined for misconduct, fell from the window to the ground, a distance of sixty feet, and died immediately after- wards. At Durham &ssizA on Saturday Hugh M‘Turk was tried on a charge of murdering a woman named Mary O'Connor, with whom he had lived. He beat her with a stool during a quarrel, and inflicted such injuries as to cause her death. He was found guilty of manslaughter, and was sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude. At Wimbledon on Saturday the silver medal in Hit Queen's Prize was secured by Colour Sergeant Smith, of the Oth Surrey. In the Lords v. Commons contest the Peers proved the victors by 23 points, the totals being Lords 534, Com- mons 511. In the Prince of Wales's Prize competition the b idge and prize of £lOO were carried off by Lieut. Mitchell. of Canada. _ _ . . .

Notwithstanding the alarming rumours which at one time prevailed as to the outdreak of disease among the grouse, it appears there will be a plentiful stock of birds on the Twelfth, the breeding season having been highly favourable to the production of large coveys. The disease was of short duration, and has now apparently entirely disappeared from those moors on which it was observed.

Father Ignatius, who has not been heard of lately, has come in for a windfall, which will bring his monastic build- ings at Llantliony within the range of practical completion. A clergyman who has visited the erratic deacon has given him £6OO to complete the shrine of perpetual adoration, £650 for some oak choir stalls, £5OO for an organ, and £2OO for two Norman windows, and some other friends have found £2,000 to complete the south cloister. In one sense there was remarkable activity in Midlands on Friday and Saturday, for the company bad to defend at Leicester Assizes eigh actions for damages sustained in the serious collision at Desford, which resulted in the death of three persons on the spot and several afterwards a still larger number receiving serious injuries. In all the cases verdicts were given for the plaintiffs, with damages vary- ing in amount from £l5O to £l.OBB. THE MARRIAGE OF THE DUKE OF WESTMINSTER.—An influential public meeting of the citizens of Chester, called by the Mayor (Sir T. G. Frost), was held at tha Chester Town Hall, on Monday, for the purpose of taking into con- sideration the best mode of glowing respect to the Duke of Westminster, on the occasion of his marriage with the Hon. Lady Catherine Cavendish. Sir T. G. Frost presided, and was supported by, amongst others, the sheriff (Mr. Cart- wright), the Very Rev. Dean Howson, the Deputy Mayor (Mr. H. T. Brown) and the Mayoress, and a number of other ladies. On the suggestion of Dean Howson it was decided to present a bracelet to the bride. This suggestion was agreed to, and a committee was appointed to make arrangements for carrying out the proposal. ANOTHER DISCOVERY OF AMMUNITION.—Anetber dis- covery of ammunition has been made in London, close to Clerkenwell ; but in this case it was not the police who came upon the hidden war material. It appears that a Mrs. Booth, who lives off Gray's Inn-road, went into the wash- house to light the copper fire, and shortly afterwards a quantity of ball cartridge, said to number several hundred rounds, which had been hidden in the flue, exploded, and knocked the lady over, rendering her insensible. Of course, the police were immediately communicated with, and a dili- gent search was made in the other houses of the street for further ammunition, but without any being found.

_ MURDEROUS ATTACK ON THE SALVATION ARMY.—AS a regiment of the Salvation Army was passing along Coles- hill-street, Birmingham, on Saturday night, several ruffians joined the procession, when one of the number saatched a watch and chain from Miss Ellen Hickman a member of the army. A gentleman named George Oidershaw, who saw the robbery committed, seized the thief, whereupon the latter violently assaulted his custodian with a heavy iron weapon, fracturing his jaw and removing four of his teeth, this necessitating his removal to the hospital. The des- perate fellow effected his release, but was rearrested by several male and female members of the army. Prisoner was committed to the Warwick Assizes for the robbery and also for doing grievous bodily harm. A BLIND MAN'S EARNINGS.—At the last meeting of the Salford Board of Guardians, one of the relieving officers brought forward the case of a woman who had applied for relief on the ground that her husband, a blind harmoniumist, to whom she had been married only three months, and who plays and sings in the neighbourhood of Shudehill, declined to maintain her. The reason assigned by the husband for the action he had taken was that his wife refused to assist him in his "business " by leading him about, &c. The guardians, finding that the map's plea was not without foundation, declined to interfere in the case. It was stated by the relieving officer that the man, who plays the har - monium with some skill, and is rather a good baritone, was in the habit of earning from to £5 a week at h;s Shude- hill "stand." It is described as "a bad week" when his earnings do not reach .22 103., and as "a bad day" when he does not take 7s. after two or tree o'clock in the afternoon; and he is said to have frequently earned as much as £2 on a Saturday. STABBING AT SEA: A STRANGE STORY.—A strange story of stabbing at sea was told on the arrival of a Glasgow steamer at Dublin, on Saturday. About one o'clock that morning a man named Saunders was walking the deck with another passenger named " Alick," when the latter went forward to where some singing was going on, and presently returned with blood streaming from his forehead. The two men were going to report the occurrence, when someone rushed at Saunders, and, after a struggle, stabbed him in the thigh. A Mrs. Hickey, too, who was sitting in the forecastle along with her husband, was also stabbed, and so quietly was this done that her husband could not believe that she had been stabbed-until she fainted and fell on the deck. One man has been arrested and identified by Saunders, but as yet there is no explanation as to the supposed cause of the outrages. ACTION FOR "HUSH MONEY."—An action to recover " hush money" was tried before Mr. Justice Manisty, at the Carmarthenshire Assizes, on Saturday. David Davies, a brewer' of Llandovery, sought to recover from three farmers named Thomas Walters John Clark, and David Clark, of Llandovery, £3OO, which he alleged was extorted by threats. —The plantiff alleged that on July 6, it year, he was driving near Llandovery, and overtook Willibella Turnbull, the granddaughter of the elder Clark. He gave her a drive. Subsequently the defendants charged him with having seduced her, and, under threats of criminal and civil pro- ceedings, demanded £l,OOO compensation. Eventually £3OO being agreed upon, the plaintiff paid that amount from fear, and to conceal the charge from his wife. He admitted kissing the girl.—The defendants alleged that tge plaintiff paid the money as compensation for the seduction.—The Jury found for the plaintiff against the two Clarks, and agreed that Walters was a go-lietween.—The judge refused to stay execution. THE QUEEN'S PRIZE AT WIMBLEDON.—The great con- test of the Wimbledon rifle meeting was concluded on Tuesday, when Sergeant Laurence, of the Ist Dumbarton Rifles, won the Queen's Prize with a score of 65 points out of a possible 105. This insignificant total, representing as it does the best effort of the most skilful marksman the volunteer force can this year produce, is a long way behind the scores of previous winners of Her Majesty's prize, although it must be added that on Tuesday a high wind and bad light rendered good shooting very difficult. The preliminary practice of the volunteers, carried on from the opening of the season in all conditions of weather, is sup- posed to fit them for every contingency in the actual con- test, but in the present instance the weather has had the best of the struggle. So small a total has never before won the prize except in 1874, when 64 was the highest score, but that year was one in which novel conditions of shooting and targets were introduced. Last July Private Beck (Ist Devon) won with 86 points—an unprecedented score—the next highest recorded being 83, which was sufficient in 1878 to enable a Lancashire man—Taylor, of St. Helens— to carry off the honour and profit. The Prince and Princess of Wales were present at Wimbledon on Tuesday, and wit- nessed the closing scenes of the contest. A BREACH or PROMISE CASE.—When a man has visited a woman ten or a dozen times a day, asked her a hundred times to marry, had the banns called, taken her to live in his house, roused her at midnight by tapping at her win- dow, spent an hour and a half in sweet cony-arse there, and presented her with a brooch, a pair of earrings, and a pair of garters, the lady is fairly entitled to suppose that be means to marry her. But, sad to say, a middle-aged person, named Miss Mary Munn, told this tale of love and courtship in the Court of Passage on Monday, in an action for breach of promise of marriage against Mr. John Scott, a Liverpool carowner, and yet failed to convince the jury that she deserved a solat jun' for her wounded feelings and dis- appointed hopes. Scott was not an inexperienced man; be had had a wife before; and het as was his courtship of middle-aged Miss Munn, he had sense enough to reflect that it would not do for him to marry a woman and her debts too. The lady kept a shop, and, as a preliminary to mar- riage, he urged her to get rid of it and of her creditors, but this she had failed to do, and from July to September he had never seen her. Then, however, she reappeared in an objectionable style, presenting herself at a cabstand where he was, and when he drove off with a " fare " she held on to the cab until several policemen and a crowd of peepla came to the conclusion that he had driven over her. In the following December she called at his house to see "the wife" but he told her sha was too early to seethe wife and too late to be the wife, after which they parted, agreeing to be good friends as they could be nothing more. The lady's chance was gone, and the cruel jury took the man's view of the cpestiou.
A clerical champion' of the Blue Ribbon Army. the Rev. Forbes Winslow, of St. Paul's, St. Leonards, has been entrusted with a thank-offering of £lO,OOO for religious work.

William Hooker, alias Roche, an Irish strolling dog dancer, attending fairs, is in custody at Northampton charged with murdering Ann Shepherd, with whom he cohabited. They stayed at an ins, and the landlady found the woman dead in a corner of the bedroom, with a slight wound in the forehead.

ELOPEMENT FROM BOLTON.—A discreditable elopement has taken place from Bolton. A young woman of attractive appearance, who recently occupied a responsible situation at a public institution in Bolton, has been on visiting terms at the house of a married couple in the vicinity of Moxam Bottoms. The wife suspected nothing wrong until the othlr day, when her husband sold the pianoforte and left home with a trunk of clothing. Inquiries disclosed the fact that the visitor had disappeared, and both are believed to be voyaging to America. The man has left four children. CHARGE OF MURDERING A YOUNG WOMAN.—A young man named George Gallagher was charged at Hammersmith, on Tuesday, with causing the death of a young woman named Grant, by drowning, in the canal at Willesden. The parties, with several other couples, were walking on the canal bank at night, when Gallagher assaulted Grant, and she threatened, if he touched her again, to throw herself into the canal. He did so, and when she jumped in he and his companions made no effort to save her. Gallagher was committed for trial.

ALARMING RAILWAY COLLISION.—ShortIy after nine on Sunday night a passenger train from Wimbledon ran into a couple of trucks which had accidentally become detached from the train preceding it. The rear guard of the Wim- bledon train sustained a severe scalp wound, and a passenger named Smith, living at Denzy-street, Borough, was removed to St. Thomas's Hospital, suffering from the effects of the collision. Several other passengers are reported injured, but not severely.

GREAT FIRE AT KILMARNOCK.—On Monday morning, about half-past one o'clock, a fire was discovered in the wool and yarn store of Messrs. Douglas, Reyburn, and Co., spin- ners and tweed manufacturers, Kilmarnock, Ayrshire. In- formation was at once conveyed to the police, and the fire brigade were speedily on the spot. So rapid was the fire, however, that by the time they reached thebuilding the roof had fallen in, and the whole was enveloped in flames. The patterns and blocks in the calico printing premises were numerous and valuable, and as they have been entirely destroyed, the loss from these alone is estimated at no less than £20,000. A CAT IN A CHURCH OROAN.—Morning prayers at St. Matthews, Sheffield, on Sunday were, a local paper states, marked by an incident of an extraordinary and amusing character. Shortly before the service began, Mr. E. Hobbis, the organist, was greatly puzzled to find some of the keys on the "great organ" firmly fastened down, as though the "trackers" had been cut. Having obtained professional assistance, an examination of the organ was made, when a cat was discovered in the interior of the instrument. All attempts to coax the animal horn its place were unavailing, and it was not until a lighted match had been applied to its tail that the intruder could be persuaded to quit. WASTE OF JUDICIAL STRENGTH.—The waste of judicial strength was again exemplified at Denbigh on Tuesday. Mr. Baron Huddleston, attended by the Sheriff and the usual array, was ready to "deliver the gaol," but fortunately there was not a single prisoner for trial, and the Grand Jury made a presentment protesting against the present custom of holding four assizes per annum in the county, The assizes in Manchester have shown that the present system involves a great waste of the Judges' time. With the exception of the Farnworth murder, there has not been a single case which might not with great advantage have been disposed of at the quarter sessions, whilst on the Nisi Prins side the cases have hardly come up to the county court average. THE SALISBURY SALVAT/CFNIST'S.—On Monday, the Salis- bury magistrates swore in about forty citizens as special con- stables to quell the disturbances which have arisen in con- nection with the processions of the" Salvation Army." In a crowded court, a number of summonses for assaulting the " Army " were heard, and the "captain "of the " Army " appeared in the box in his damaged uniform, and described how his comrades had been peltered with rotten eggs, flour,' and yellow ochre. He himself and his wife were grossly assaulted. For the defence it was urged that the assaults would not have taken place but for the yelling of the "Army," whose proceedings were described as " blatant blasphemy." The magistrates sentenced the defendants to fines varying from 15s. to £2 each. ATTEMPTING TO THROW A DAUGHTER INTO THE CANAL. —At the Manchester Assizes on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Day, Thomas Cox, a boatman, was indicted for having attempted to drown his daughter by throwing her into the canal at Barton-upon-Irwell recently. The man was ac- quitted by direction of the learned Judge, who expressed his surprise that no indictment for a minor offence had been presented. Alexander and Kate Shaw, of Rochdale, were found guilty of having brutally illtreated a young child— niece of the female prisoner—of whom they had the charge. Mr. Justice Day (who is on his first circuit), enlarged upon the barbarity of the offence, and then passed the " severe " sentence of imprisonment with hard labour for twelve months. The case was one of the worst cenceivable, and the wretches in the dock must have received their "severe" sentence with as much surprise as gratitude. THE SEIZURE OF ARMS AT CLERITENWELL.—WaIsh, the manager of the Fenian arsenal in London, was on Monday formally committed to take his trial at the Old Bailey on charge of treason-felony. In the course of Monday's examination it was stated that the number of ball cartridges seized was nearly 9,000, the number of rifles 277, bayonets 276, and pistols 30. The arms were all of private manufac- ture, with imitation Government marks. Less interest, however, attaches to the arms seized than to the various packages sent to Ireland during the last few years, and which have not fallen into the hands of the police. Various cases were followed and intercepted by the police, but the num- bers which reached their intended destination must hate been large, or the game would not have been worth the candle, and Walsh would long ago have ceased to send arms to Ire- land. The point of anxiety is whether with the arrest of Walsh the illicit traffic has ceased. THE SALE OF AN ADVOWSON INTERRUPTED—Mr. Driver offered for sale by auction in Londor, on Tuesday, "The advowson, with the right of next and perpetual presentation to the rectory of Harwood, in the diocese of Oxford." Mr. Charles Webber, on behalf of the Curates' Alliance, proposed to ask a few questions with respect to the " lot " that was being submitted for sale, but the auctioneer refused to enter upon any speculative questions as to how soon or how late the purchaser of the living might realise the benefit of his purchase. He had not attended there to discuss such ques- tions as Mr. Webber had raised. Replying to another remark by Mr. Webber, Mr. Driver said, "I do not come here to bandy words with you. If there are no bids I will with- draw the lot. I would rather have no bit at all than an insufficient bid." Mr. Webber said he had no furthet ques- tion,' to ask. In the result the advowson was not sold. AVITON Fox MALICIOUS PROSECUTION.—The action' brought by a medical man Abrath, residing at Sunderland, against the North-Eastern Railway Company for malicious prosecution and false imprisonment was concluded on Tues- day at Durham Assizes. Dr. Abrath was indicted at a recent assize for conspiring with a person named M‘Mann to obtain heavy damages from the North-Eastern Company in an action in which the jury found for the company. At the trial for conspiracy the defendants were acquitted, and thereupon the present action was brought to recover damages for injury to character. The jury again found for the railway company, hut it would be unfair to assume that they considered Dr. Abrath and M'Mann had been guilty of any fraud. Probably they came to the conclusion that, on the whole case, the company had reasonable grounds for prosecuting—a finding which at once removed the element •of "malice," and is in perfect accord with the direction of the learned Judge (Mr. Justice Gave) who tried the case.

A SHOCKING TRAGEDY.—At the Manchester Assizes, on Tuesday, William Bradburn was indicted for murdering his two children, Phoebe (17) and Peter (9), at Farnworth, on the 3rd May. The prisoner was a steady, respectable man, a widower, and was regarded by his neighbours as a good father, who was very much attached to his children. In April his daughter formed an acquaintance with a young man, and the prisoner immediately developed symptoms of jealousy. He would not allow the young fellow to .visit the house, and on the 2nd of May, when the girl was at home 111, ha declined to accede to her request that he should be sent for. Early next morning he was seen to rush out of the house and to stagger and fall, and it was then found that his throat was cut. He was taken home, and the neigh- bours, on searching the house, found the bodies of the young people in bed with their throats cut. The defence pleaded insanity. The jury found him guilty, with a recommendation to mercy, and sentence of death was passed. PA.TAL BOATING ACCIDENTS: FIVE PERSONS DROWNED. —On Sunday night five men, named David Thompson, married, aged 32, omnibus driver; William Hodgson, single, cab driver; George Woodend, 17, clerk; John M'lCie, 45, potter, married ; and Frank Wright, 42, married, went out with two other men for a sail in. a rowing boat at Whitehaven. The weather was fine. The tide was some distance out when the boat wag being turned round to take on board another man. The boat struck on a bank, and getting broadside on to the sea a large wave struck her and she capsized. Two of the men held on to the boat and succeeded in getting ashore, but all the others were drowned! M‘Kie and Wright belonged to Longton, Staffordshire, were connected with the Potteries and had only been in Whitehaven a very short time. On Monday evening, Mr. Whiteside, coroner, held an inquest on the bodies of the five men, when it was shown they had taken the boat without the sanction of the owner. When they were capsized another boat put off and rescued two of the men. The jury returned a verdict of accidentally drowned.

A LUCKY PAUPER.—The unusual circumstance of a pauper becoming suddenly the possessor of comparative affluence happened in an administration action, in which a petition was on Tuesday (before Mr. Justice Kay) presented for payment out of court of £lo,ono. part of a much larger fund left by an intestate. His next-of-kin were of course entitled to the money, and one of them, a Mrs. Newton, an inmate of a workhouse, was present in court in workhoutte dress, to express directly to the judge, in accordance with the usual practice, her wishes with regard to the disposal of the money she was entitled to. Just kfore her marriage she had received £2,000 of her share, but it had been all spent. Mrs. Newton was given a seat on the bench, and was questioned by his lordship to aseertsin that she under. stood the nature of the proceeding,. His lordship made an order that Mrs. Newton's share of the fund be iovested, so as to produce her an income of £lOO per enure, to he paid to herself qurterly.

They left in the morning Iron: to go to school, but went to bathe instemet hire The colliers employed in the North StafrOM i pits have a received notice of a reduction of 5 per cenf.• coal trade. in consEquence of the continued depression inthie A motion to restrain General Booth, of the Salvagon - • sn' .beir wages, from using the Eagle Tavern and Grecian Theatre, Lona,- was refused by Mr. Justice Kay in the Chancery frnisfort on Thursday, who reserved costs. The shooting for the Elcho International Challer.‘,o Shield at Wimbledon on Thursday, resulted in a victory fo:, England, who scored a total of 1,536 at the three ranges. Ireland came next with 1,505, and Scotland was last with 1,494. Thomas Blower, who was remanded by the Ashton-under- Lvne magistrates on Thursday, was the item of an extra- oidinary adventure. The police went to arrest him at a cotton mill in course of erection. As soon as he saw them he ran to the cross beams on the top floor and there set his would-be capturers at defiance for several hours. He amused himself by running along beams where the policemen dared not follow him. About midnight he was induced to capitulate and was locked up.

The Wrexham and Acton -Colliery, one of the largest col- lieries in North Wales, is on fire, and will probably prevent the men from wotking at least a month, if not longer. The fire broke out in No. IPit, and is believed to have originated in a cabin in which the hookers-on dry their clothes. The flames were first discovered about one o'clock on Thursday morning. Fortunately no one is hurt, but the destruction to property must be serious. _ _

The recent representation of a coroner's jury in favour of the speed of trains being reduced to a lower rate than usual when entering the Blackburn railway-station has been acted upon and trains now enter at a speed of three or four miles an hour. The change has, however, led to a great increase of the practice of passengers leaving the train whilst in motion, and on Thursday Thomas M‘Gibbon, a traveller, was fined five shillings and costs by the Blackburn borough justices for thus offending. The Freeman's Journal announces that Col. Brackenbury has tesigned owing to differences of opinion with Earl Spencer as to the means to be adopted to detect crime in Ireland. This, the Freeman says, is highly creditable to Lord Spencer as a ruler and gentleman. The individual effectiveness of the espionage system would be entirely counterbalanced by the general detestation of its authors and its use.

At one o'clock on Thursday morning, a fire was discovered to be raging in Messrs. Grove and Stark's manufactory, Longton. The brigade were quickly on the spot, but only after nearly three hours' hard work were the flames got under. A range of new buildings containing a large quan- tity of ware was completely destroyed, and the damage, which is covered by insurance, is estimated at £l,OOO. Six hundred hands are idle.

At Bolton, on Thursday, a schoolboy named Thos. Stones was charged with housebreaking. He had broken into two houses near his own home in Holden-street, by taking panes of glass from the kitchen windows. He ransacked drawers, and stole nearly £3 in money, a cigar-holder, watch chain, and other articles. He was arrested next morning at school with some of the articles in his possession. He was sent to an industrial school.

At Middleton, on Thursday, Joseph Hussey was sentenced to three months' hard labour for violently assaulting Ann Pendergrast. The prosecutrix gave evidence against the prisoner's brother at the last Salford sessions, and because of this he set on her on Saturday night, knocking her down and kicking her about the head and body. Her face pre- sented a dreadful appearance. A Kings Lynn correspondent telegraphed on Tuesday afternoon that a fisherman named Parke Thwaites, aged fifty, residing apart from his wife and family in Pilot-street, murdered a woman namen Harriet Fox, with whom he cohabited, by stabbing her to the heart, and afterwards com- mitted suicide by stabbing himself in a similar manner The woman left him a few weeks ago, and was about to marry another man. Jealousy was the cause of the terrible creme. Intelligence received from Lloyds on Thursday morning states that the new iftn ship Hermes, of Glasgow, 1,464 tons register, on her first voyage, bound from the Clyde to San Francisco, has- been totally lost with her crew of forty hands. The vessel sailed from Greenock on the 3rd Decem- ber last and has never been heard of since, and being now several months overdue there is no doubt she has foundered with all on board. Insurance companies will suffer heavily the vessel and cargo being worth £30,000. At Bolton, on Thursday, John Armstrong, his wife, and son were charged with wounding four constables. Rearing a fight in the defendant's house in Newton, an officer en- tered but was pitched out. He obtained the assistance of three other officers and re-entered. The Armstrongs then assaulted them with pokers, pots, and pans, and one con- stable was fearfully cut over the eye, and had to be removed to the infirmary. The other officers were also injured. The prisoners were committed for trial. On Thursday afternoon a young man named Montague Ryle D. Newby, who was articled to a firm of solicitors in Manchester, murdered a younc, woman named Howard in a house in St. Leonard's-street, Chorlton-on-Medlock, and afterwards committed suicide. Newby, who is said to be the son of a clergyman residing in Rutlandshire, has for some time been paying attention to Howard, who led an immoral life. Some disagreement was caused between them owing, it is reported, to her partiality for another of her lovers. Newby want to visit her shortly after four o'clock on Thursday afternoon, and after an angry conversation had taken place between them—latrahot her under the left ear with a revolver, death ensuingdirectly, and then killed him- self in like manner.

POLIGAISEY IN THE UNITED STATES—Polygamy in the United States (says the St. James's Gazette) does not appear to be confined to the Mormons. The Rev. Dr. Leonard Bacon, of Cennecticut, alleges that there is as much poly- gamy in New England as in Utah, and that it is more open and shameless. It originated in the impulses of a large por- tion of the New England people, and is, he asserts, pro- moted through the assistance and connivance of the divorce laws and the judicial tribunals. Even the clergy are in many instances polygamists. A professor in a theological seminary of the dominant orthodox sect of New England, who was a polygamist, long occupied his chair without scandal or objection; and he is still held in high estimation by the clergy of the Congregational churches. These poly- gamy practices are, Dr. Bacon says peculiar to the native population; foreign-born citizens do not share in them. Dr. Bacon's statements have attracted much attention in the United Statee--especially in Utah, where they have awakened "sad surprise." At Manchester Assizes, on Wednesday, five prisoners, charged with complicity in what are known as the next of kin frauds, were indicted before Mr. Justice Day. They were James Stodden Rogers, 8.A., Birmingham, principal; Arthur Mackenzie, William Albert Beeton, and William Evans, Manchester, Birmingham, and London managers; and John Henry Shakespeare, described as solicitor and legal adviser of the Manchester manager. The head office of " business," under cover of which frauds were committed, was at Birm- ingham, and Rogers, who professed to have devoted con- siderable time to the study of pedigrees, advertised that 25 millions of money lay unclaimed, and could be recovered by the respective next of kin, The advertisements attracted many people,. and for some time the office, which had established local agencies and bore the style of the International Law Agency, did a good business. People paid heavy fees, but, receiving no return, at length became importunate, and in April, after a most exciting scene at the offices in Birmingham, the prisoners were arrested in different towns. Eventually it was decided to proceed against them OR the charge of defrauding a Man- chester lady. The trial concluded on Thursday. Rogers, the principal of the international agency, in his address to the Jury, contended that the agency was a bona fide one, that the business was a legitimate one, and that the money received from various persons was for actual work done. Mackenzie's defence was that he, as the manager of the Manchester branch, only acted as Rogers's representative and that he took part in no fraud. For Shakespeare it was contended that he simply acted as solicitor to the agency, and only re- ceived payment for professional services. Beeton urged that he knew nothing whatever of the nature of the business carried on, and acted simply as clerk to the concern. In Evans's case the judge held that there was not sufficient evidence to go to the jury, and he was discharged. The jury found Rogers, Shakespeare, and Mackenzie guilty on the first count of the indictment and Beeton not guilty. The latter, however, was ordered to be detained in custody, and the council for the prosecution said he would consider whether he would proceed against the prisoner on other counts of the indictment. Meanwhile, sentence on the con- victed prisoners was deferred. I BRATE Genre—A very interesting ceremony took place at the Borough Court-house, Stockport, on Wednesday. It consisted of the presentation of two rewards for bravery •displayed by a young woman. On the 15th April a dwel- ling-house in Brown-street, Stockport, was partially destroyed by fire. The inmates, a family named Loftus, and several lodgers, were in bed at the time. They nar- rowly escaped with ther lives, except one girl, whose charred 'body was afterwards found on one of the beds. Annie Loftus. aged 17, machine operative, was one of those who made gocd their escape. Then, discovering that a. sister, aged seven years, had been left behind, she returned, ascended the burning staircase, groped her way through the smoke, and, notwithstanding she was much burned on the face and hands, succeeded in rescuing the little girl from a position of imminent peril. One of the inmates had thrown her child from the window of the second storey, and then jumped through, fracturing one ef her levs, which has since been amputated in the Infirmary. The braze conduct of Annie Loftus excited general admiration. The Mayor (Mr. James Leigh) started a subscription on her behalf, and the magistrates presented to her a sum of money. Raron Albert Grant, of London, also forwarded a handsome donation. The Order of Ste John of Jerusalem in England voted her the silver medal and diploma and the Royal Society for the Protection of Life from firs. awarded her their testimonial. The awards from these societies were publicly presented on Wednesday—the medal and diploma by Mr. John Furley,"a member of the Order of St. John, and thee medal was pinned on the young woman's breast by the Mayoress. The Mayor presided, and made the presentation of the Royal Society's tcertificate. There was a large attendance of magistrates, members of the Town Council, ladies, and the public, the court-room being well filled. This may be easily detected, ter if Cocoa thickens in the cup it proves the addition of starch. THE EGYPTIAN QUESTION
THE BOMBARDMENT OF ALFXANDRIA.
From various newspoper correspondents we cull the fol- lowing details as to the bombardment of Alexandria:
DESCRIPTION OF THE RUINS.

correspondent of the Times thus describes a visit to the Alexandria :—" At last we reached what had been treiW/ What it was is too well known to need descrip- the. &Nli. is is quite beyond all my powers. There in wh ed up by a lurid MaN of smoke, stood the the centre, ligsfa, fue of Mehemet All, behind it I could large equestriari :ce. Of the rest I can only say that I see the Palais de .tatva. On either side of me was one long distinguished nothing:- enenitadae hoof ?asset fTeluletshaaatym. made line of fire. At every' sound which recalled the calm. ''stinguish one house from walked on, I tried, but failed,. fo 01. 'en almost daily for 17 another. In a place which I bete ;ngs of the 'familiar years, I could not even find out the ern% nly guess where streets leading to the markets. I cotTlei its' to the , certain familiar houses had been from the Fe!.... I walked statue, which stood alone in the centre. bounding from side to side to avoid the falls of re_r‘.en v,t he offentive odour would cause me to look throtitaa, -ye smoke. At last we distinguished two moving flgares: went to them, and I acted as interpreter while they talt.'efe a history which reminded one of Dante's Inferno. / he'?"(4' no time to enter into the descriptions of all they recounte&, for lam writing this in a rolling ship, which is hurrying off. with my despatch; but the perfect calmness, the utter absence of excitement with which they told the tale of horrors, the business-like accuracy with which they showed us where we were to go to _find persons in distress, and the quiet manner in which, after giving us all the information we required, they left to return to their work of danger and charity, as quietly as if there were nothing extraordinary in their position, was a proof of a sort of heroism which won the admiration of all, and compels me to give their names They were Pere Guillaume, a Belgian Franciscan, and Frere Mivielli, a French Lazarist. At last we made our way to the other end of the square. Through the trees of the garden and the smoke we could see the English Church still standing, though I think slightly injured, and perhaps looted. The Italian College, the Sala Storari, and the Catholic Church seemed to be untouched, but appearances are very often deceptive. The postmaster tells me that he found his house locked and apparently intact, but on enter- ing he found it perfectly empty, though the door had not been forced. Lombard-street and all one side of St. Catherine's-square are a mass of rubbish. The Piazzia di Paglia and the low quarters round are toterably safe. The sister street was destroyed in the upper part, but not much injured in the part towards Gabari. In the street Meidan every shop is open and emptied of its contents, the roadway being strewn with the paper in which the goods were wrapped. At Minet-el-Bassal the stores are not burnt, but generally rifled. There is now little fear of further looting on a large scale, at all events in the town itself, for there is little left to loot. The smallness of the number of persons left to do it and the severity of the punishment render the game not worth the candle." The fires in the town were undoubtedly the work of the soldiers, at the direct instigation, if not of Ourabi himself, at least of Alahmoud Samy Toulba and his prominent sup- porters. The hoisting of the white flag and all the negotia- tions which followed were simply to gain time to enable the soldiers to leave Alexandria and to fire the town before doing so. Ourabi during the engagement was at Fort Napoleon, which neither fired nor received a shot. At about half-past eleven, when the ships had ceased firing, he rode through the town accompanied by Mahtnoud Samy and others of that Ministry. There was then looting on a small scale being carried on by the lower class of natives. It was in the after- noon that a party of soldiers came down to the Square and deliberately set fire to the French Consulate. Another party of soldiers took the opposite side of the Square and treated it the same way, while the party which had begun with the Consulate separated and burnt the remainder of that side. The English Church, standing a little way off the pathway, surrounded by the garden, was saved by its palings. I omitted to mention that in the Marina quarter the only place that was burning was an English shop. The Minet- el-Bassal quarter, where are situated the large cotton and grain stores was apparently safe. The Daily News correspondent says :—lt is difficult to form an opinion of the number of Christians massacred, and the truth will never be known, as it is believed many were murdered in shops and houses which were afterwards fired. The calcined bodies needed no burial, and the deaths will never be registered. It is certain that there were more Christians ashore on Tuesday, the 11th, than the Consuls thought. Many escaped aboard ship, but it is prooable that hundreds perished. No picture can give the slightest idea of the complete and wholesale ruin of the but yesterday flourishing city of Alexandria. One must live and move here to realise a tenth of the truth. But as I foresaw it would be, I could never have conceived anything so ghastly._ Unless prompt measures are taken, we are only at the begin- ning of the troubles. This is not the moment to reflect on the conduct and consequence of the week's operations, but it is universally regretted that the Government did not so arrange that the bombardment and landing of the troops should be effected the same day, and thus have saved hundreds of lives and the destruction of millions worth of property and the main of Egypt for twenty years. Lieu- tenant A plin, of the Hecla, accidentally shot dead by his own pistol, was buried this afternoon. A Standard correspondent says :—During our march through the streets several Greeks and Italians with their families greeted us with cheers. Many of them had become insane in consequence of the three days' terror to which they had been subjected. Our column was accompanied by several of these poor people. As we passed through the streets, windows which had been closed for the last four days would open, disclosing the faces of Christians who had been waiting their doom, but who were now happily rescued. We had the greateet difficulty in making progress owing to the several streets being blocked with the debris of ruined houses. It is not easy to drag our Gatling gun over the rubbish in the Grand-sqnare, which was also dim with smoke. We saw about a dozen bodies of Europeans, of whom two were Frenchmen.

IN THE CITY DURING THE BOMBARDMENT. M. Gouissio, manager of the Anglo-Egyptian Lank, who with his wife remained in Alexandria during the bombard- ment by the British fleet, relates the following incidents : "The whole night long the native population had peured, screaming with terror, into the interior. At five minutes past seven on the 11th came the first shot from the frigates. The excitement of the population aud the volume of the emigra- tion instantaneously increased. At nine the soldiers began parading the town, assuring themselves by search whether the Europeans were in communication with the Admiral by telephone or telegraph, or not. An officer, accompanied by several soldiers, mounted on the terraces of the houses and cut the wires of the telephones. One of the soldiers we saw carried a hatchet, covered with blood. My berbery told me that the man had just assassinated an Englishman whom he found in communication with the Admiral. This was pro- bably the young French telegraph clerk, who sought refuge in the Eastern Telegraph Company's• offices. The bombardment continued all day. All day the popu- lation were fleeing with frightened faces. On the 12th the flight of the inhabitants continued in even greater numbers. In the afternoon the exodus from the town had become general. At three o'clock the soldiers gave the signal for pillaging. As on the 11th of June, they began by opening the doms of the stores and dividing the merchandise which they found. Soldiers under the direc- tions of the officers and superior officers, divided the booty in a fashion disgraceful, but at the same time having its comical side. Pieces of calico were cut into pieces and handed round; while albums, watches, and fancy goods were carried off and frequently puled to pieces, after having been in the hands of men who did not understand their use. The officers frequently carried two or more guns, so as to leave free hands to the soldiers who were carrying off the booty. A colonel mounted on a horse had a pair-of new shoes under his arm; another threw down and broke into a thousand pieces a clock which he found too heavy to carry. In fact, the property destroyed was of greater value than that which was actually carried away. As soon as a shop was empty- the paper and all the debris that could- be hastily collected were thrown into it; then small explosive pellets were added and in a moment the whole was in a blaue. At five o'clock the Egyptian heroes, loaded with booty instead of laurels, retreated in the greatest disorder. Since two in the after- noon the Bowabs, or house porters, had received the ;?t,ot d'ordre to desert the houses which they guarded. By six all the European quarter was in flames, and the town,pre- seated the appearance of one huge furnace."

div.head: TALES- 01? SUVFERING.
div.p: TALES- 01? SUVFERING.

Telegraphing, on Tuesday, the Daily News correspondent at Alexandria says:—The history of the bombardment of the forts and the burning of the town of Alexandria will be the most thrilling and exciting narrative of modern times. Every day harrowing scenes and facts are brought to light. In going my rounds I came aarossa family whose axperience and sufferings exceed those of any other case II have yet heard of. it is a highly respectable family, wealtnown to me, consisting of father, mother, and eight children, mostly of tender age. They were left in charge of- a valuable house of a wealthy relatiou. After the bombardment the house was attacked and, robbed, and many of the houses near being on fire, the family removed to another house at Cumetdik, in the outskirts of the town, where they thought , to be safe from the mob and the fire. In. this they were right, as everyone had fled from there, and there was nothing worth, molesting. Expecting X. remain only a few hours, the family' half-clad, took refuge on the top, floor of their house. Although they had plenty of money with then), they ha& no food. These ten creatures tasted: neither food-nor drink from Tuesday,the 11th, to Friday, the 14th, with the exception of an infant at the breast, Below and round them they saw the fire raging and themob pillaging, and they huddled together with fear. They gradually became incapable of thinking about their own safety,and without hope were resigning themselves to,adinger- ing death. On Friday, the 14th,a gentleman was passing the house and saw the father signal to him with a baby at the window. He immediately rendered assistance and rescued the whole family from their terrible position, bat with great difficulty, owing to their extreme weakness. The gentle- man succeeded in marching the family to the landing place and getting them on board the steamet Molded, where they are at this moment gradually recovering, thanks to the kindness of all concerned. At Ramleh, an English barrister and his wife, the only English family who elected to remain there, had a severe time, and escaped only with their lives. They veln frequently attacked. They resisted as long as possible, and then obtained a gaud and peemeetlei to the oersoelVlsoldLls

1 guaidhouse prison. Here they were protected from Wednes- day, the 12th, to Sunday, the IGth. Their only clothes they wore, and th-2v had a small dole of Arab food. On Sunday they walked, from Ramleh to the Matins, seven miles under a burnine; sun, and embarked with scanty clothing aboard the Tanjore, where tley were gladly received, as it was

feared titey 'were murdered. The number of such cases, the details of which will never be published, is legion. The dead, as usual, will be soon forgotten, but the living must be compensated. Nothing can repay them for the mental anguish and bodily sufferings of the past short week, but England must find the ways and means to alleviate to some extent the fearful ruin of innocent people. It is impossible to exaggerate the extent of the destruction. If the official reports do not convey full accounts, members of Parlia•nent and others have only to visit A.lexandria in the autalna instead of going to Pompeii or Rome, and they will sea iflOta ruin and desolation in one day than in Italy in a week. visit' TO THE RAS-EL-TIN PALACE AFTER

THE BOMBARDMEN r. On entering the palace, says the Dail,y Telegmph's c, r.es. pondent, I found Stone Pasha, who forinerly ratheradini.red Arabi, now with the Khedive. He confirmed the report about A rabys order to kill his Highness, and he added that i' on quitting Alexandria Arabi gave orders to sack the toivn. I was the only correspondent who witnessed the return of the Khedive. About four a party arrived, including Ismail Kama Pasha, Frederics Pasha, and General Stone. Half an hour afterwards Sir Beauchamp Seymour walked up, and a ' • minutes later Tewfik arrived In a victoria with Dervish few ,Pasha. Re was received with a geneval salute fro ,i; a guard henouy eonsisting of about 400 marines, drawn up ulidz th:c'tornmant: of Major Phillips. He shook bands cordially with 04 admirai, and went upstairs. He c.".peared to be . pale, bat very comp`osed. He had driven in from Rarnleh, where he Itlel been staying the last day or two. Immediately afterwards the palace pryented a most animated, and' at the same time a most pitiable t.'Cepe. About a dozen broughamc drove up, containing the femate portion of his household, and there came in on foot about 100 refugees, whom the lile-' dive had taken under his charge at Ramleh. All of them. speak in the highest terms of his kindness. Our first inti- mation that the Khedive was still alive was given by three officers who came in from Ranleh to ask that assistance might be sent to the Khedive, whose palace was surrounded by Arab troops, who nominally came as his guards. The Khedive would probably have been murdered on their arriva bad not Dervish Pasha interfered on his behalf. The admiral promised to keep the streets clear :or him, and the officers said that he would drive straight in if not hindered from leaving the palace by the troops. Early in the afternoon the Condor was sent to cruise close to iiitmleh to overawe the troops surrounding the palace. At half-past three she signalled that a considerable movement was visible there, and an hour later the Khedive with Dervish Pasha, drove through the town, and reached Ras-el-Tin Palace, where a strong body of marines was posted. In the evening pro- clamations in Arabic were issued in the name of the Khedive, ordering all soldiers to leave their regiments and go back to their native villages.
ORDERED TO KILL THE KHEDIVE: THE STORY
OF HIS ESCAPE.

Continuing, says the Daily Telegraph's Alexandria correspondent, my trip of investigation, we perceived sailors and marines on a despatch steamer getting ready to receive the Khedive, who had been in retirement at Rarnleh. Here the officer in com- mand warned us not to go on alone, but ventured to push on. to the landing place near the Post Office, where there also arrived a party of marines and sailors from the Invincible. These formed up a column at the bottom of the street lead- ing into the city, and on going along with them we saw Arabs firing one private house and plundering others. We bad here a small street fight, killing a couple of rascally Arab robbers. But the mob thickened, and the officer fell back for reinforcement, which came presently in the welcome shape of a Gaging gun from the Monarch. With this gun a second advance was made into the middle of the street, and after a short, sharp flight, the party killed five more Arabs and partly cleared the vicinity ; but beyond this was a howling mass of cut-throats, and the officer find- ing his force still very small, he judged it better not to push to the centre of the quarter. Meantime a number of Euro- peans, chiefly Greeks and Levantines, who had hidden all day and night from the time of the bombardment, came running down. Some French ladies were among them, whose condition was pitiable. From them we learned that the Arabs had killed all the Christians they could. These fugitives had hidden in cellars. I learned that just before the bombardment the Khedive and Dervish Pasha quitted Ras-el-Tin for the Palace at Ramleh. There they stayed all day, the Khedive being terribly anxious and despondent. Next morning Arabi suddenly ordered a detach- ment of soldiers to surround the palace where the hheclave and Dervish were, as Martin, the Khedive's secretary, be- lieves, with full intention to kill them both. Thereppon Ragbeb went to Arabi and demauded sternly what thia manceavrerneant. Arabi replied no particular harm; the troops wished to keep the Khedive. He promised to order the soldiery away, but did not keep his word, and at the last moment he actually told his men to kill the Kheaive. The soldiers, however, by that time heard the English were com- ing, ar.d deserted their posts everywhere, refusing to kill the Khedive. who at that moment was left almost unguarded. Hearing the English were coming, his Highness sent word to tell them where he was, asking how he could come off safely, whereupon the admiral quickly arranged everything, and sent a party to the Khedive's yacht, the Mahroussa. It was found that she could net be got in working order; ac- cordingly another Egyptian steamship was utilised, which was employed to get him off. The Khedive being safely under English protection at the palace, and confident in the support of England, now ap- pears, says the Daily .11rors' correspondent, in better health and spirits, and it is only rendering justice to his Highness to say that his coolness and courage never left him at any moment during the bitter crisis. Ha is naturally deeply afflicted at the fearful destruction of life and property caused by the burning town. In the harem portion of the palace the flames burst out afresh during the night. Pumps and men were landed from the ships and arrested their further progress.

THE SITUATION. The Conference decided on Saturday to call upon the Porte to intervene in Egypt, and a significant hint wasgiven that an early reply was looked tor. A reply has not yet, however, been received. The Khedive, who has called his Ministers round him has issued & decree formally deposing Arabi Pasha. from the office of Minister of War' and it Is rumoured that a price has been set on the head of the ex.; Dictator. The centre of anxiety is shifting to Cairo. Order has been ,tolerably well established in Alexandria now, and the panic that existed as to the safety of the Suez Canal has in a large measure subsided, but uneasiness is increasing with regard to Cairo, where some of the spoil from Alexan- dria has been exhibited in the market place, as tempting the • natives of Cairo to loot deserted European residences there. Arabi's position, too, is being strengthened, and there is a feeling that if he be left undisturbed much longer, the Arabs will conclude that he is still master of the situation, and a kood deal of mischief will be experienced before he is finally disposed of. A curious and inexplicable feature in the situation is the marked friendship the Khedive has begun to show to several persons who are well known to have been intimately connected. with Arabi. Dervish Pasha has been summoned to Constantinople to give the Porte the benefit of his views upon the situation in Egypt, and on Wednesday hastily took his departure for the Turkish capital. Fortunately, the time is drawing new when, if Turkey does not agree to the proposals of the Conference, another policy will be adopted; and a Convention which has been agreed to between England and France as to the Suez Canal gives good prom,se of an effective and prompt manner of disposing ef the Egyptian question, speedily, if only the Porte is once left out of consideration. THE PORTE'S REPLY TO THE IDENTIC NOTE. The text of the Note addressed on Wednesday by Said Pasha on behalf of the Porte to the representatives of the six great Powers, in reply to the Identic Note of the 15th inst., is as follows :—The undersigned has received, the Identic Note presented on the 15th, requesting the despatch of Turkish troops to Egypt, as necessitated by the present, state of things in that couutry. If the Porte has not hitherto decided on its own initiative to send troops it is because it was convinced that vigoreus measures could be avoided. Feeling confidence in the solicitude of the Powers for the re-establishment of order, and observing with satisfaction that on this occasion also the Powers have formally and repeatedly reedned their deference for the in- contestable and unriuestlaned rights of tovereignty of the Sultan in Egypt, the undersigned, by order of the Sultan, informs the representatives of the great Powers that the Porte consents to take part in the Conference now assembled at Constantineple with sole reference to Egyptian affairs, in order to discuss.and determine the measures to ensure the restoration of a regular and normal Stato of things in Egypt. (Signed) SAID. PREPAIIIN4 TO RESIST ARABI'S ADYANCE. THE EXECUTIONS. A seccuel edition of the Daily Telerraph of Wednesday contains the following :—Alexandria, July 20, 7.30 a.m. Last night our garrison here lay down under the impres- sion that an attack by Arabi's forces was imminent. The chief ground for this anticipation was that the rebel leader had moved his outposts still nearer te the town. Prepara- tions were accordingly made to prevent any surprise. At the first streak of dawn this morning everybody was on the alert, but n3trace of any further movement of the enemy was to be seen. Signals which had been arrangtd th direct • the combined action of the scattered regiments were anxiously looked for by the men, I but none were made. The morning broke qu.et.y, and as, I telegraph a further recon- naissance is being mada to discover whether' there is any* prospect of Arabi Atterapting to attack us. With regard to' the public execution& that are to be carried out here to-day or to morrow, I sal asked tO point out that the victiros.of this very necessa:y misery are all , prisoners who have been convicted of murdering Eu.ropeans under circumstances of exceptional barbarity during the bombardment. n each case been tried with great care and cenTdeb sneYnedEatvoedeiath ca sufficient evidence. In all probabih ty these murderers will be shot by the Egyptian troops. Lord Charles Beresford, acting as com- mandant of police, besides disliking the employment of for such a purpose, is further of opinion that English troops tegyptians the lesson to the . if the work is done by the natives will be all the mere effective. It is quite. possible that these executions may continue some time. Every day ringa to light fresh assassins, who availed themselves of, e confusion following the bombardment to.coramit ' murder.

Belling certain blasphemous libels in their journal. Mr. ' Bradlaugh, the :junior member for Northampton, who is rated as the occupier of the premises in which the Free- thinker is produced, has been summoned for a similar , offence. Very few people will believe that Sir Henry Tyler's religious convictions have been so much outraged that he felt compelled to bring the action, and nobody is foolish enough to suppose for one moment that the cause of Christianity can be advanced by such a prosecution. The fact is, it can only serve one purpose, and that is to increase the popularity of the Freethinker, and cause it to be more extensively read. Such, we know, was the case with "The Fruits of Philosophy "—another abominable production— when its printer and publisher was prosecuted. There are no less than eleven distinct libels charged against the de- fendants, and if two of these be proved against Mr. Brad- laugh, it is said they will be fatal to him taking his seat in Parliament. Sir Henry Tyler has done much to keep Mr. Bradlaugh out of his seat in Parliament, he declares that this prosecutioß has been brought by Sir Henry as a dernier ressort, and if that be the case—l have no doubt it is—he deserves to fail, as I trust he will. At the same time it must not be supposed I approve of blasphemous libels. I dare say I abhor them as much as Sir Henry Tyler, but I object to their authors being made notorious by a prosecu- tion. FREE METHODIST SUNDAY SCHOOL, WIDNES.—The scholars attending this school had their annual treat on Saturday. Meeting in the school about 2 o'clock, they walked in procession, led by the Sons of Temperance Brass Band, to the Central Station, whence they proceeded by train to Hough Green. The scholars, including teachers and a few friends, numbered about 250. The rain and clouds of the morning had given way to a sunshine and a clear sky, and a thoroughly enjoyable afternoon was spent in roaming the fields and participating in games of various kinds, to the enlivening music of the band. Tea was putaken of in the open air. The party returned to Widnes about nine o'clock. THE CRIMINAL ASSAULT AT WIDNES BATHS.-At the County Sessions, held in Liverpool last week, William Woolstencroft was charged with committing a criminal as- sault upon Annie M'Gurl, at Widnes, on the 24th of June. Dr. O'Feeley prosecuted, and Dr. Commins, M.P., defended. The prisoner and another man, named Chinaworth, who were employed at the baths at Widnes, saw the prosecutrix and another girl passing. They pulled them in, and under the pretence of showing them the baths took them over a part of the building. The prisoner took the prosecutrix into a room, and it was there that he was said to have com- mitted the offence with which he was charged. The prisoner was fouud guilty of attempted rape, and was sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment.

About 600 scholars assembled in the school at two o'clock, and were formed in processiosal order. Headed by Mill Brow Brass Band, Runcorn, they marched down Oakland-street, Waterloo-road, and by way of Moor- lane to Simm's Cross, returning along Mersey-road to the school. Here tea was provided, but as the school did not afford sufficient accommodation, a good number adjourned to the adjacent Board School. Varlet a amusements were afterwards indulged in, and as the weather was fine, the afternoon's proceedings passed off successfully. PROPOSED RESTORATION OF FARNWORTH CHURCH TOWER.—For some time it has been well known that the tower of Farnworth church was in a somewhat unsafe con- dition—in fact, that it was somewhat dangerous to properly ring the bells. The vicar, the Rev. G. Bond, and his church- wardens have determined, however, to commence the work of restoring the tower, and putting the peal of bells in a state of efficiency. It is cstimated that this can be accomplished for £l5O, and with characteristic vigour the vicar and his

will be held in Bethesda Church. The floral decorations are to be on an elaborate scale, and remembering the success which attended the service last year, there will no doubt be large congregations. The Rev. J. D. Thomas will condnct the service. Appropriate music will be rendered. WIDNES WINDOW PLANT ASSOCIATION.—The annual exhibition connected with this association will be held in Widnes Market Hall, on Tuesday next. Although the plants are grown under very adverse circumstances the show is a good ene, and is well worth a visit. Upwards of 50 valuable prizes are to be competed for, and they will be distributed in the evening. by Mrs. Cross, of Moss Bank, Farnworth. Further particulars will be found on reference to our adver- tising columns. PAVILION THEATRE, WIDNES. —Mr. Russell still Bustaine the popularity of tills establishment. Nightly during the past week the performances have been patronised by large audiences, who have testified their appreciation of the histrionic talent displayed by the various actors by repeated plaudits. Mr. Fuller, who has been very successful, will c-mclude his engagement to-night. Another attractive pro- gramme is provided for next week, the popular drama, "The Ticket-of-leave Man," to occupy the boards on Mon- day and Tuesday evenings; while on Wednesday will be parformed Shalcespere's comedy, " The Taming of the Shrew," and the drama "Bound to the Stake," in which Miss L'zzie Stanley will appear and take her benefit.

Her face was injured with the blow. He pleaded guilty to the charge, and said he had been trying to get a few coppers to obtain a night's lodging with, but could not do so. ty, Elizabeth McKecanie was charged with having been found in a state of drunkenness on the premises of Henry Matthews for an unlawful purpose.—Mr. Superintendent Williamson said the facts of the case were simply these. Some two or three months ago the prisoner was the occupier of the house in which she was found, but through her habits of drunken- ness the home had to be broken up. 'Receiving £3 from her husband, who is a ship's steward, on Friday week, she got on the "spree?" and entered the house under the impression, he (the superintendent) believed, that it was her own home. He did not pretend to say she was there for an unlawful puipose. When apprehenned she was in a curious state of mind in consequence of drink, and he thought a little quiet- ness in the police quarters would do her good. The prisoner was respectably connected, and be was sorry to say that her brother, who was in business in the Isle of Man, refused to have anything to do with her. As she had somewhat recovered, the Superintendent asked that she might be dis- charged with a caution.—ln reply to the Chairman, the Superintendent said the doctor had seen the prisoner, and informed him that the treatment she had undergone was the best that could have been adopted. It was total abstinence. —The Bench then discharged the prisoner, advising her not to get in such a bad state again.

Sir James Bacon, the chief Judge in Bankruptcy, who had reversed the decision of the judge of the Liverpool County Court, and declared the trustees of the West Derby and Everton Perpetual Building Society entitled to the proceeds of certain distresses by virtue of their mortgage over the debtor's property, of which the debtor was attorned tenant. The debtor carried on business as the Lancashire Manure Company at Farnworth, near Widnes, and under his failure Messrs. Voisey and Sheen were appointed trustees. Mr. Winslow, Q.C., Mr. Montagu Cotton, Q.C., and Mr. Mul- holland, appeared for the appellants, the trustees of the estate; Mr. Horton Smith, Q.C., and Mr. J. Linklater for the respondents. At the conclusion of the arguments of the appellant's counsel, without calling on the other side, the Master of the Bells gave judgment, dismissing the appeal with costs.
