Among those who passed the recent Matriculation Examination of the London University was John Arthur Tonge, of Silcoates School, Wakefield—in the First Division —son of the Rev. J. Yonge, minister of Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church, Warrington.

By an order in Council, the Archeleaconry of War- rington will comprise the rural deaneries of Childwall, with 17 pariNies; of South Liverpool, with 19 parishes; of Pres- cot, with 21 parishes; of Toxteth, with 17 parishes; and of Winwick, with 21 parishes. PAUIEEISII IN THE PRESCOT UNION. —A return re.- cently presented to the Guardians of this Union shows that there are in the Union workhouse 448 paupers, and in school, training ships, and other institutions 179 children charge- able to the Union; making a total of indoor p :tapers of 627. On the outdoor relief lists there are 2,370 persons, of whom 225 are adult males, 982 adult females, and 1,163 children. Adding to these 175 for lunatics in asylums, and children placed out with foster-parents, the grand total of persons in receipt of relief is 3,172.

WIDNES PRISONERS AT THE COUNTY SESSIONS —At th- County Sessions held at Liverpool last week, John Fitz- harris was sentenced to 14 days' imprisonment for wounding William Myres, at Widnes. Thomas Sumner, twelve months' imprisonment, for indecently assaulting a child named Elizabeth Bennett at Widnes.—James Heath was acquitted on the charge of injuring a plate-glass door at the house of Alice Lightfoot, at Widnes.—Paul Kerby was found guilty of doing grevious bodily harm to Lul=e Kelly, at Widnes. The prisoner war.; ordered to come up for sen- tence next sessions, in the meantime it being understood that he would give the peosecutor compensation.

FATAL ACCIDENT TO A. PENILE:TR FARM LABOURER.— On Saturday night an accident, which resulted fatally, ocf curred to a farm labourer, named John Brannon, 55 years o- age, employed by Mt. John Wright, farmer, Penketh. De- ceased was in the habit of sleeping in a hayloft at the farm to which he obtained access by means of a ladder. On Sun- day evening he went to his sleeping place under the influence of drink, and fell down the ladder as he was ascending. He afterwards succeeded in getting into the loft, where he was subsequently seen by his master, to whom be complained of being ill, remarking, "I am done for." Brannon was con- voyed on Monday to the hospital at the Warrington Union, wilere he died early on Tuesday morning.—Mr. C. E. Drif- field, county coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Workhouse, on Thursday morning, and a verdict of Acci- dental death "was returned.

A StisI'ICIOUS Ca.-0a Weanefiaay, at the County Petty S.?ssions—before Messrs. IL Bleckly (chairman), S. Rigby, and P. Stubs—Thore.as Moores, shopkeeper, Orford' was summoned for he-ving opened his licensed premises during prohibited hours, on Sunday, the 2nd July; and Mary Baxter, an elderly woman, was summoned for having been found on the prereises• durir,g prohibited hours.—Mr. G. T. Moore appeared for the defendants.—The evidence showed ri.dat in consequence of numerous complaints of S drinking, P.S. Pattineon and P.C. W m hittinghaw.unatctesd the premises early on the morning of the 2nd inst. ' They saw Mr. and Mrs. Baxter walking about, and after- wards saw a man leave the premises, and on going there they found Mrs. Baxter in the house with the servant girl, who had several jugs of fresh drawn beer.—Mr. Moore, for the defence, explained that Mr. and Mrs. B ixter had been sitting up nearly the whole of the night with a sick chile?, and early on Sunday morning Mrs. Baxter went to the shop to obtain for the child a mixture which Mrs. Marsh, who resided at the shop, was in the habit of supplying. The servant had been instructed to bottle some beer on the Satur- day evening, but she forgot to do so, and rose early next morning for the purpose of carrying out her instructions before her mistress came down. She was so engaged when the police entered.—After hearing several witnesses, Mr. Bleckly announced that the Bench had decided to give the defendants the benefit of the doubt. The circumstances were suspicous, and justified the officers in the action they had taken; but the Bench thought as the case stood against the defendants it was not one in which they could convict. SUDDEN DEATH OF CHILDREN IT WARRINGTON. A child named Ernest Cann, aged five weeks, son of James Cann, a factory operative, residing at /6, Gaudy's-terrace, died very suddenly at an early hour on Sunday morning, under the following circumstances :—Deceased and mother went to bed about half-past 11 o'clock on Saturday night ; and when the mother woke about five o'clock on Sunday morning deceased was looking very black i# the face, and on taking he child up in her arms she found it was dead. She then called her next door neighbour, who immediately c %me and rendered her assistance. Deceased had been a healthy child since his birth ; and the evidence showed he had not been overlaid. Mr. C. E. Driffield, county coroner, held an inquest at the Old Crow, Fennel-street, on Tuesday, and a verdict to the effect that deceased died from natural causes, in all probability from convulsions, eras returned.-- About one a.m. on Sunday morning William McCormick, aged one year, son of Henry McCormick, railway porter, living at 16, New-road, Latchford, died suddenly. About eleven o'clock en Saturday night Mrs. McCormick put the child to bed, and then came downstairs to finish her work. On going to bed about twelve 'o'clock she saw deceased with its eyes turned up, and apparently in a fit. The mother then shouted downstairs to Sarah Cartledge, who was in the house at the time, to come and hold deceased whilst she went to her 'mother's to get someone to fetes a doctor. Her brother went for Dr. Joseph, but he could not attend, and before the services of any other doctor could be obtained the child died. Deceased had had fits several times since its birth, an 4 had also had an attack of measles about three months age. On Tuesday, Mr. H. C. Yates, the Cheshire coroner, held an inquest on the body at the Golden Lion, Latchford, and the jury returned a verdict of "Died from natural cau.ses."

SHENIUSDS7 ANNITERSARY AT LATCHFORD. —On Saturday Ist, the members of the 'Pride of Latchford Lodge," of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds (Warring- ton District), celebrated their anniversary, when about 40 members sat down to a capital dinner provided by the host, Mr. Thomaz Ireland, of the Cheshire Cheese Inn, Latch- ford. Amongst the company present P.P.C.S James , Delooze, Br. James Cantrell (lodge surgeon), P.M. John Murphy, P.M. W. Millington (secretary), and P.M. Isaac Jones, and Mr. Thomas Barber. After dinner, the chair was taken by P.P.C.S. James Delooze, and the vice-chair by Bro. William Jackson. The toast of the Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds having been given, P.P.C.S. James Delooze stated he was pleased to say that the Order was progressing throuehout the country. It comprised 88.24(3 members, with a balance of £146,024 24. 4d. In replying to the toast of the Warriagton District, P.P.C.S. James Delooze read & letter to the members apologising for the. non-attendan3e of the Chief and Corresponding Secretary, who were detained opening a new •lodge in town, and wish- ing the .meeting success. He gave a brief account of the working of the district, and conclded by stating there were 11 lodges and 896 members connected with it. The worth of the ledges combined was £2,060 7s. 7d. There was paid for funerals £l2O, and for sickness £4BO ss. The worth of the lodge sick and funeral fund was £2,242 15s. Bd., being a gain upon the year of 193 lie. 2,1. P.M. Win. Millington, in responding to the the toast of ' the Pride of Latchford Lodge, showed the lodge as going along in the right direction—number of members 35. P.P. ' C.S. James Delooze, in responding to the toast of the Widow and Orphans' Fund and Juvenile Burial Society, said it was established for the purpose of providing for the widow and orphans at the death of a member, and that it was a society all members should join, the contributious being only 7d. per quarter with an entrance fee. It was composed of 65 members, with a balance of £9O. The .Juvenile Burial Society contained 1,100 members. It had a balance of £285, and there had heen paid £ll4 ss. for deaths during the year, as against £75 during the previous year. The toast of the Lodge Sur-on was responded to by Dr. James Cannel). The company then formed themselves into a quadrille party, and dancing: was kept up until 10.30, when the comp.mf allinaving thoroughly enjoyed themselves.

THE EGYPTIAN QUESI lON

• ANOTHER MASSACRE OF EUROPEANS. THE KEIEDIVE DENOUNCED BY ARA.BI. A second edition of the Daily Telegraph yesterday con- tained the following message :—Alexandria, July 21st, 9-30 a.m. It will not be surprising if the critical measures which Arabi is taking in threatening and actually intercepting the water supply of this city leads to an immediate advance of the British forces. I understand that General Sir Archibad Alison has telegraphed home for instructions. The emer- gency is obviously culminating, and some action must be taken soon. Admiral Seymour has sent to Port Said for a ship tilted with condensers capable of producing 120 tons of condensed water daily, and attempts are being made to obtain others here. *lt appears certain, however, that all these efforts will be insufficient when once the natural supply to the town is cut off. Already it seems the flow of water in the canal is perceptibly less than it was before the cutting, and the utmost that condensing could do would be to supply the ships and the troops. It will be no light matter if Arabi floods the country. The difficulties of an artillery advance, already serious enough, will in that case be enormously in- creased. The Arab who brought the information of Arabi's action in regard to the cutting of the canal stated that at present the ivator was only up to the knees, in the most flooded district, but that will have the effect of rendering the earth too soft for guns to pass. No movement of troops of any importance has yet been made, and so far as I can learn this morning all is quiet. l'esterda7;- our patrols were pushing forward for seven - miLs abo• • the Mahmoudich Canal. They saw no Arab soldiers, though they heard a good deal about them. It is a distressing thing to pass through the country, and see the ruin and havoc wrought by Arabi's marawlers, the Bedouins and liberated scoundrels of Alexandria. All alonc, the route you come upon handsome houses completely wrecked. In some places the canal is full of debris of costly furniture, car- riages, and other effects, which the looters, unable to carry with them, have thrown into the water. Admiral Seymour's proclamation, backed by the salutary examples that have been made of some of the captured miscreants, is having a wholesome effect. The looters who had concealed .their booty in various parts of the city, are beginning to disgorge under the promise of the offered amnesty. Whole cart loads of stolen goods arc being tra mferred to Lord Charles Beresford, and there will be no small difficulty in restoring this extraor- dinary collection of property to its real owners. An Arab has been shot just now by Major French's sentry, who caught him in the act of attempting to fire a house in the very centre of the city. Orders have have been issued to take the greatest possible care of the water everywhere. It must be used with the utmost economy, and carefully stored. Arabi's dam to intercept the supply seems to be working imperfectly, for the stream is still flowing though reduced in volume.

The following telegram appeared in a second edition of the Daily News :—Alexandria, Friday Morning.—The following information has been received from your Port Said correspondent by letter, telegraphic communication being uncertain :—Port Said is full of people. Enormous charges are being made for board and lodgings at the hotels. Yesterday a large number of people were brought from Ismailia by a German man-of-war. They were chiefly Ger- man refugees from Cairo, Tantab, and other towns in the interior. They bring alarming reports as to the doings of the natives at Tantab. Many Europeans have been brutally murdered in cold blood by the natives. One respectable man describes seeing a Tofta sitting on the ground cutting the throat of a European while holding his victim's head between his knees. The European population hear is badly armed and unaccustomed to the use of firearms, and the town is swarming with women and children. In the eyent of an attack by Arab or Bedouin soldiers, the loss of life would be fearful; for although the guns of the English fleet command the peninsula, the European population ashore numbers ten or twelve thousand, including refugees, and hundreds would be killed by the guns or massacred by Arabs. Many people are leaving by every steamer but others arrive from the interior and thus there is no sensible decrease in their number. The town and defenceless population are considered at the mercy of the soldiers and fanatical Arabs. After the bombardment of Alexandria on the 11th, Arabi sent information to Cairo and Port Said alleging that seven English ships had been sunk, that Admiral Seymour was a prisoner, that two English trans- ports with Indian troops had been seized at Suez, and that the Sultan had retaken Cyprus from the English. With such information it is not surprising that the Arabs think the English beaten, and are anxiou s to do something to complete the defeat. Their conduct is insolent and angry, and our position is very critical. Another cause for great anxiety here is the insecurity of the Suez Clint. There are fin-of-war at either end, but none along idly portion of the ninety-nine miles of the Canal. The Peninsular and Oriental steamers arm the Officers, crew, and passengers, as well as possible, and hitherto no vessels have been stopped, but at any moment the canal could he blocked and steamers in transit unarmed, might be pillaged by I edonins from either side of the canal and the crews murdered. M. De Lesseps is expected here daily, and possibly seeing a fleet at the entrance and the exit of the canal, will report all well, but by others the canal is con- sidered unsafe, and many owners will not allow their steamers to pass. Arabi Pasha has issued a proclamation maligning the Khedive, and stating that his Highness is wollting with the Christians in order to effect the ruin of the country ; and that be (Arabi), the only patriot, declares that all Ministers are kept prisoners in Alexandria by the Khedive; and as he is the only Minister free, he calls on the people to rally round him and arive the foreigners out ef the country. LIMASSOI„ FIZIDAY.—The Turkish gunboat Akin, mount- ing three guns, arrived this morning from Tripoli. Her , destination is unknown.

At the London Mansion House, yesterday, Mr. Bradlaugh and other defendants, charged with blasphemy in the Free- thinkv, were committed for trial. Yesterday, the Irish Lord Chancellor grantal orders on the Attorney-General's certificates, removing to Dublin under the Gth section of the new Prevention of Crime Act the trials of nine prisoners now in custody for agrarian murders and outrages in Westmeath, Kerry, and Clare. The Heywood Town Council have obtained a remission of the extraordinary surcharges which were made upon the members of the Hey wood Local Board arising out of the Board's transactions. The total amount remitted by the Board is over £12,000. Twelve members of the late Local Board were includealin the surcharges. The receipts from the various mills and workshops at Oldham up to Thursday night, in connection with" Hospital Saturday," for the benefit of the Oldham Infirmary, amounted to £Bl2. The list is not yet closed, and further receipts will be forthcoming. lip to the present the receipts are slightly in advance of last year. A meeting of Conservetive peers was held yesterday, at the town residence of the Marquis of Salisbury, in Arling- ton-street, to take into consideration the course to be pursued in regard to the Arrears Bill. About one hundred peers attended, among whom were the Duke of Richmond and Gordon, Earl Carnarvon, and Marquis of Waterford. The meeting lasted an hour. It was announced yesterday, at Rowley, that the majority of the employers in the South Staffordshire and East Wor- cestershire chain trade had consented not to reduce 44,fte ' wages and that the strike which has lasted about one ',nonth has now practically ended and work resumed. It is thought that if the employers will abolish the truck aystern and underselling there will be no further disputes. Yesterday evening, Mr. Henry Churton, coroner for Che- shire, held an inquest at Tarvin, near Chester, on the body of John Crawford. Deceased, who was engaged in harve;t operations on the farm of Mr. Lightfoot, was driving the horses through a gateway when the Animals bolted. Craw- ford jumped off, but slipped, and he was jammed between the wheels and the gatepost, receiving such dreadful injuries to his breast that he died almost immediately. A verdict of accidental death was returned.

DEPUTATION TO THE PRESIDENT OF THE BOARD OF TRADE. A deputation of delegates from the fishing ports of Hull, Grimsby, Great Yarmoutbr Lowestoft, Ramsgate, and Brix- ham waited upon the President of the Board of Trade, yesterday, for the purpose of calling attention to the hard- ships and loss sustained by the fishing interest owing to the large number of desertions which had taken place since the passing of the Merchant &amen Payment of Wages Act, 18S0, more efpecially directing attention to section 10, which abolished imprisenruent. Mr. Chamberlain engaged in a very long discussion on the question, but assured the depu- tation that the House of Commons would never go back to the old system of imprisonment.

div.head: DESERTING HIS FAMILY.
div.p: DESERTING HIS FAMILY.

At the Blackburn l'olic2 Court, yesterday, William Henry Mayor, a "steeple Jack," of Newcastle-on-Tyne, was charged under a warrant with neglecting his wife and three children. The prisoner, who had been arrested five times previously on similar cbar4es, deserted his family in October last. During five years his family had received over £lOO in relief. The prisoner was sentenced to three months' hard labour, and ordered to pay the costs or undergo another month's imprisonment.

THE NEXT OF KINT FRAUDS. THE SENTENCES. . At the Manchester Assizes, yesterday, sentences were passed on the three persons convicted of complicity in the next of kin frauds. Rogers, the principal, was sentenced to two years' imprisonment with hard labour, and Makenzie and Shakespeare each to twenty-one months' imprisonment with hard labour. Beeton was discharged, the prosecuting counsel having decided not to prcc.aeci with any further case. Evans was liberated on Thursday night.

div.head: FATAL FALL.
div.p: A FATAL FALL.

About half-past six o'clock yesterday morning, a married man named John Allison, residing at Hollinwood, and -employed as a labourer at the Oldham Twist Company's new mill, was killed whilst assisting to hoist some scaffold- ing on a temporary platform. They had just wound the scaffolding to the landing when the weight of the planks overbalanced him, and he fell to the ground, a distance of 24 feet, and his body coming in contact with some large iron beams, he was dead'whm picked up. . . ! BISHOP FRASER ON CHURCH MUSIC. Preaching at'St. Lukt's Church, Blackburn, at the open- ing of a new organ, on Thni slay evening, the Bishop of ! Manchester spoke the place that music ought to occupy ! in church strvices, and warned his hearers against an abuse

of it. He urged that everything should be designed for tai edification of the congregation and declared that the congre. gational was the best type of singing, lie objected to florid acompartiments of the Creeds asd the Lord's Prayer, arut deprecated the introduction of tunes from low music halls.

div.head: FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS.
div.p: FATAL FALL DOWNSTAIRS.

Yesterday morning a man named William H. Goodwin, a sawyer, residing in Waterloo-street, Bolton, died in the in. firmary in that town from injuries received through falling downstairs. His family went marketing on Saturday night, leaving him alone in the houss. On their return they found him lying at the foot of the staircase with his skull frac* tured. lie was rernovei to the infirmary, where he died MI above stated.

TYPHUS FEVER AT BOLTON. Dr.ergeant, medical officer of health for Bolton, reports a serious outbreak of typhus fever in that borough. It wal introduced from a vfliage near Tuam, a-nd is of such a ma. lignant character that of eleven persons attacked in twO streets, in Great Bolton, to which the disease was confined, eight died. 1)r. Semcant says in the majority of cases death occurred with remarkable quickness. Every effort has been made to isolate the cases.

Mr. CHILDERS reply- ing to a question said, pending Her Majesty's approval he could not state the composition of the force going to the Mediterranean.—Sir W. SHOCKING AND FATAL A.CCIDENT AT FRODSHAM STATION. —A sad and fatal accident occurred at Frodsharn station on Thursday evening, to Thomas Jackson, who it appears was on duty shunting the produce train which calls during the season for goods for the Manchester market, and about 10-30 o'clock he was found on the main line opposite the station- master's residence, with his right leg crushed to above the knee, and badly bruised about the he tel and other parts of the body. Mr. Potts, the stationtnaster, at once arranged to take him to Chester Infirmary by the 11-10 Ulan, and the Injured man was accompanied by Mr. Potts, Thomas Fletcher, Joseph Lockett, and Dr. Robinson. On arriving at the Infirmary the leg was amputattd, but the patient gradually sank and expired at 2-20 on Friday morning. It is supposed that the deceased was riding on a waggon, and by some means slipped under the train, but as no one appears to have seen the accident this is simply conjecture. The sad affair has thrown quite a gloom over all connected with railway work at the Frodshana station, as the deceased had been in the service for upwards of 26 Years, and was highly respected by all who knew him, for his willing and oblig- ing manner.

div.head: ST., ITELENS COTTAGE HOSPITAL.
div.p: ST., ITELENS COTTAGE HOSPITAL.

The ninth annual report (1881) of the work carried on by this useful institution is just about to be issued by the committee. In presenting it, the committee in the first place regret the resignation of their esteemed secretaly, Mr. Allen, by whose " enthusiasm and exertions," it states," the. the hospital was originated ; and, during the nine years. of its existence, be has performed the duties of secretary often at much personal sacrifice and inconvenience." Though there had not been so many patients treated as during the previous year, the efficiency and popular appre— ciation of the hospital continued to be maintaieed ; but the committee regret to find a serious falling off in some of their sources of revenue this last year, chiefly in the penny-a- week subscriwions at the various works in the town, which , have yielded only £483 in comparison with £BOB the pre- vious year. This unfortunate circumstance has prevented a contemplated extension of the building, so as to provide a ward for women and children, which has been much wanted. The penny-a-week systeen, the committee add, has worked admirably, and while in operation has been the main stay of , the finances of the hospital. It was the result of a move- - ment originating with the workingmen themselves, and the committee would gladly see them take as great an interest as before in this branch of the revenue, which alone is necessary to ensure its being maintained. It is also pointed out that there are still many werkff in the town and neighbourheod at which neither weekly nor annual collections are made. If all would co-operate, it is added, to ensure an increased revenue, the size and useful- ness of the institutien could be immediately extended. The number of patients received during the twelve months was 109, of whom 102 were males and 7 females. The summary of results shows that 79 were discharged convalescent, 11 relieved, 7 left, and 9 died. Of the number treated 58 were subscribers of id. per week, and 51 paid Is. per week whilst in the hospital. The average stay of each patient was 441 days. The occupations of those received is a noticeable feature, and the report shows that 51 were engaged at the chemical works; 23 at the glass works ; 12 at the collieries ; and only 3. at the copper and iron works, which, together with 13 miscellaneous, and the 7 women 'make the teal of 109, of whom, it may be added, 43 were married .ancl 66 unmarried. The total income for the year was £1,420 19s. 1-lel., of which £BB 2s. 7d. was subscribed by the Orloos churches and schools, and the opposite side of the balance sheet shows that there is, after the payment of all expenses, the satisfactory balance of £514 19s. 10d. duo f7om the Itreasurer.

Sir,—l have been informed by a large ratepayer of Newton that the telephone erected between Mr. Brierley's office and MISCIELLANEOITS.—WiIIiam Baines was summoned for the gas manager's office i for the accommodation of corn- having, on the 7th inst., at Sankey, ridden on his wagon s mercial gentlemen, who may chose to call to solicit orders, asleep, and was fined 55. and costs, 9s.—Robert Dainteth, Peter Green, Jos. Stringer, Geo. Welsby, and John Stringer SO that Mr. Brierlev can ask the gas manager if anything is wanted. Now as Mr. Brierley passes daily, why not call were each fined ss. and costs, for being drunk at Croft, on say once a week, and ascertain what goods are required? I the 11th inst. think most of the ratepayers will agree with me in thinking A BARE-FACED ROBBERY.—Charles Proudlove, boatman, that the rates are uite high enough without the Commis- was charged with having stolen a hen, value 35., from the q hencote of John Worthington, at ltixton, on the 17th inst.— goners spending money to benefit no one but their servants. —I remain, yours respectfully, On the day named the prisoner went to the prosecutor, Newton, July 19, 1831. 'ANOTHER RATEPAYER. Adam Robertson, farm bailiff to Mr. Worthington, at Rixton, in reference to a boat-load of manure. After transacting his business with the bailiff, prisoner turned to leave, and the bailiff noticed him going towards the hencote. Robertson, who had missed a number of fowls, went to the prisoner and found him on a wall with a hen under his arm. When he saw the bailiff coming towards him prisoner jumped off the wall and let the hen fall.—The Bench committed the prisoner for six weeks' hard labour. LICENSING PROSECCTION —Michael Scally was sum- moned for having, on the 2nd inst., opened his licensed house during prohibited hours, and further for allowing drink to be consumed on his premises on the same day. Richard Baxter, John Norman, John Soulsbv, Jas. Higham, Wm. Sankey, James Feilding, and John Stokes were charged with having been found on the premises during prohibited hours.—P.S. Pattinson said that shortly after six o'clock on the morning of the 2nd inst., he and P.C. Whittingham pro- ceeded to Scally's house in Winwick-road. They immediately saw two men leave by the back door, and after remaining there a short time they saw 3 men enter by the same door. Ina few minutes one of the men came out and joined the other two who had previously left the house. They (the officers) then proceeded to the house and found the back door open, and on entering the house saw all the defendants sitting round the table. There was a jag full of beer and also a glass. On speaking to Scally, he replied that the other defendants had been assisting him to get a horse out of a ditch, and he was just treating them to half a gallon for it. They how- ever, searched for the horse, but failed to ind it or any trace of a horse having been in the ditch.—Mr. Moore, who ap- peared for the defendants, said the men went to Scally's house and told him they had got his horse out of the ditch, and, believing their statement, he gave them some beer.— Scally having been previously convicted, was fined 40s. and costs for each offence, the license to J)e endorsed for the first. The other defendants were each fined ss. and costs.
THIEVING AT THE CEMETERY.

Sir,—Perhaps you will permit me to call the attention of our Town Council to the fact that for many months past - there has been considerable annoyance caused to persons (; who visit our Cemetery in order to show their respect to et departed friends in tia, shape of decorating their graves, by certain persons who, it would appear, frequent the grounds for no other purpose than to carry away the most valuable plants and flowers that they can find. It was only the other day some friends of mine who visit certain graves each week found that one bearing the most valuable plants had been robbed of everything that was worth carrying away. This is only one instance out of many which have occurred suite recently. I think, therefore, if a little more protection *- were afforded to our Cemetery it would I,)s the means of encouraging those who feel disposed to spend an boor or two a week in their charitable work, besides tending to t' stamp out such outrageous practices.—Hoping that some influential person will take the matter up, I am, Sir, yours, drc., A. B. Warrington, 20th July, 1882.

div.head: NOXIOUS VAPOURS.
div.p: NOXIOUS VAPOURS.

Dear Sir,—For some time past the inhabitants of Runcorn have suffered from a most intolerable nuisance in the shape of a dreadfully disagreeable odour, from one of the numerous works by which the neighbourhood is infested. As soon as the wind gets in the east, and the condition of the atmosphere slightly depressed, the olfactory nerve is tortured by this overpowering and sickening stench. People of weakly constitutions are prostrated at once, and others, whose digestive organs are usually healthy, seem as if -suddenly smitten with sea-sickness. If it is absolutely necessary that glycerine should be manufactured on the Sprinch, it is as necessary that the air we breathe should be preserved from such disgraceful and wanton pollution, in consequence of those fearful fumes getting mixed therewith. The stoppage of the fountain, from a cause not very remotely removed from the nuisance of which I complain, Is but a small evil compared with this ever-recurring abomination. It seems almost unfair to single out this particular stench in a district where so many works are emitting noxious vapours, but it is like Aaron's rod, it svva,loves up all the rest and takes possession of the whole neighbourhood; and though it may not be so disastrous to health and vegetation as the chemicals it is more obtrusive, and ought to be immedi- ately prevented. Ido not wish to be thought an apologist o( chemicals. My detestation of the whole bunch of them, on both sides of the river, is unbounded. What have chemicals done for Widnes? Destroyed the fair face of nature and turned a pretty village into a smoking Sodom; and Runcorn is hurrying hard upon its heels. Where are the successors of those men who in the early days of black ash resisted the alkali invasion, and for so many years Vept our good old town from sinking under the dominion of dirt? They are, unfortunately, nct to be found ; and before very long the whole district, from Norton Priory to Weston Point, will be stripped of every bit of verdure. Very soon the withered and whitened trees like gaunt and grim ghosts will be seen stretching out their bare arms in piteous appeal to heaven for redress. It is sheer nonsense to say this kind of thing pays, and only among a "nation of shopkeepers" would such twaddle be tolerated.—Yours, , Runcorn, July 15, 1882. ARCADIAN.
"ANGLO-SCOTUS" ON NEWTON MATTERS: AN INTERESTING COMMUNICATION.

Sir,—l feel highly flattered to think that one of your Newton correspondents considers my letter anent the corrup- tion of Mrs. Glasse's cookery instruction a " learned " one; but as I do not assume a knowledge of philology, I sincerely hope he will excuse me from entering into a discussion con- cerning the effects of transposing the letters of a word, or subtracting or adding to it. And ever since I involuntarily became acquainted with the taste of a bug through being in- duced to indulge in a London sausage, entomology suggests to me unpleasant reflections. It is indeed a fair cry, from a Lon- don sausage to a Newton black pudding! Besides, although I bail from the " knuckle-end " of England," I confess to holding in utter contempt the whole category of "droves," from bogy fellows down to the sounds that come from the largest tube of the bagpipe—an instrument of torture, the crime or folly of inventing, which I am ashamed to see Scotchmen claiming for their ancestors, instead of leaving it to stick or attach to Nero and the ancient Greeks and Romans. So I also hope he will pardon my touching on bees, or their connection with bonnets. The assertion as to the growth of the stables, stands, kennels, the thousand a year, and the ten , per cent., I accept as another illustration of the adage about the ease with which a certain class of people can be induced to part with their money. If in their musical tastes, certain Scotchmen take their tone from the man who fiddled (and possibly fuddled) while Rome burned, I am not surprised that certain Newtonians should seek to combine for the pur- pose of perpetuating and being able to indulge in the sport Xenophen at times followed. And in this connection I would remark that although the hare was used in divination by the ancient Britons, it was never killed for the table; that it was formerly esteemed a melancholy animal, whose flesh was also supposed to produce melancholy in those who ate it. An old medical writer informs us how " bare-flesh engendreth melancholy blonde." The hare, too, was sup- posed to be so timid that it never—not even in sleep—closed its eyes. Chapman has drawn from this belief a fine epithet on the death of Prince Henry "Relentless vigor, and confusion faint, Frantic distemper, and hare-eyed unrest."

Again, the appearance of a hare in one's path is looked upon as ominous. "The Cornish miner turns away in horror when he meets an old woman, a hare, or a rabbit on his way to the pit's mouth." If the Newton hare gets loose and scour the roads in the neighbourhood, what excuses they may give miners and others who are ready to seize any pre- tence or excuse for a holiday or mike! Puss may indeed turn not an " unlucky " or " ominious " animal with a venge- ance. But lam digressing. lam anx:oue to learn more about the cow that was kept for the use of the greyhound. It must be an extraordinary animal if it really gives "butter and sweetlard for making cakes !" And what a maw that greyhound must have to contain eight or nine cakes at a time, from twelve to twenty eggs a day, and require over fifty beasts a year to be slaughtered so that it may weekly indulge in the luxury of a boiled cow's head! No wonder it does not win prizes! Is the correspondent in question trying to "pull my leg ;" or haa the editorial cat in a play- ful mood been joined by a frisky bull-pup, a mischievous printer's devil, a voracious Icarus communis, and the quar- tette had a glorious lark with his "copy ?" Talking of the devil and his desire to catch people, I see that certain New- tonians are fond of poultry keeping. (By the way, does any ' one remember the blue-pencilled bantams of the late Mr. Shaw, or how the colouring was produced?) Now, why not I take a rise out of Auld Cootie by means of feathers, to I counteract the ascendancy your correspondent asserts the ' owner of the cloven foot eeeks to secure through the agency ' of fur? I should net like to hear of staid Newtonians taking to the Yorkshire Shrove-tide practice of destroying their spare roosters by throwing sticks at them, but they might try, on the principle allowed by your correspondent, the efficacy of the French recipe, which says "that if you at midnight go to where four cross roads meet, with a fowl un- der your arm, and. cry "Robert" nine times, his satanic majesty will appear, take the rooster, and give you in ex- change a handful of silver." If the devil tries to get hold of you through hares, thump him with a cock-bird, especially if it be a paving transaction. I have so great a respect for my Newton -friends—(do they not, Mr. Editor, send me at times copies of the capital Examiner series? I wish they would do it oftener, accompanied by some black pud- dings)—your correspondent included (although I have not the remotest idea who he is), that I would not have either them or hits imagine I was straining metaphor or becoming irreverent. So I will remind them that it is a black cock that sings in the Scandinavian "Nifleheim." or "land of gloom ' and that the signal of the dawn of Ragnarok, "the great day of arousing," is "the crowing of a gold-coloured cock." I leave the application of the metaphor to readers; to whom I hope your modesty will not prevent ens temark- ing in concluding this epistle, that in your new venture they have got a capital newspaper.—l am, sir, dee., ANGLO-SCOTUS.
BURTONIVOOD.
ALLEGED ATTEMPT TO COMMIT SUICIDE,7OI7I Thursday

evening, a strong rumour gained currency to the effect that some person had made a determined attempt to take his own life by throwing himself into a pit of water near Bradley Hall, Burtonwood. Certainly, there was some foundation for the report, for on the facts of the case becoming known it was evident that such had been the case, or that a most singular and extraordinary accident had occurred. About twenty minutes past seven o'clock three young men, named John Hessian, Thomas Burke, and Thomas Donnelly, were walking along a footpath leading from Lumley-lane to Mill- lane, BErrtonwood, and when near Bradley Hall they observed an aged man some distance in front of them. A short time afterwards they missed him, but on reacting a small pit of water they observed his hat floating therein. They subsequently noticed that his body was floating in the water, and they get it out. P.C. Grundy, of Burtonvrood, was at once sent for, and the man was conveyed to the Earlestewn Police Station, where his tvet clothes were stripped from him. Dr. Patterson was sent for and attended to the man, who fortunately was not much the worse for his immersion. He stated that his name was Edward Risley, 63 years of age, a glassworker by trade. Up to about five weeks ago he had been employed at the works of Messrs. Pilkington, of St. Helens, at which town he resided. His story was a somewhat remarkable one. He said be had been out of work for the last five months, and had been suffering from bronchitis, his medical attendant being Dr. Gaskell, of St. Helens. On Thursday evening he was having a walk along the footpath mentioned, when he had a "mazy fit," and accidentally fell into the water. After being attended to at the Earlestown police station by P.B. Cummins and Dr. Patterson, he was removed home in scab.

div.head: LATE MR. CHARLES SOULBY,
div.p: THE LATE MR. CHARLES SOULBY,
OF RUNCORN.

The late Mr. Soulby was one of the superintendents of Brunswick Sunday School, and on Sunday afternoon Mr. Simister, a colleague of the deceased, paid a fitting tribute to his memory in an address to the scholars. He said he should have been glad if Mr. Simpson, the senior superin- tendent, had been present that afternoon, but as he was away on the continent for a few weeks, the duty of saying a few words about their late friend and superintendent devolved upon him. He had known Mr. Soulby ever since he came to Runcorn, 14 years ago, and found him a very pleasant companion, and one deeply interested in all that was good. His father died when Mr. Soulby was quite young ; but he had a most excellent mother—one of the most devoted Christian women he (Mr. Simister) had ever known—and her influence on his early training was invaluable. He was very early in life the subject of religious impressions, and when quite a boy became a member of the Methodist society, and continued to meet in class to the end of his life. He was apprenticed as a pupil teacher at the Wesleyan school in his native village—Bingley, in Yorkshire—and was alway suc- cessful in his lessons. After fulfilling his term of five years as a pupil teacher, he went to the Training College, West- minster, and the same close attention to study which he dis- played as a pupil teacher made his career at college most brilliant. At the termination of his college course of train- ing, the Runcorn Day School Committee, being in want of a master, applied to Westminster; and Mr. Soulby, with the best of credentials, was sent. Ever since the appointment the managers of the school had felt themselves fortunate in securing a teacher so gifted and suitable in every way. He joined that Sunday school. Not feeling equal to the mental strain which the preparation of lessons would entail, in addition to his work in the day school, the lighter duties of librarian were assigned him, and three years ago he was appointed one of the superin- tendents, and his value in that capacity they all knew and appreciated. His addresses in the school surpassed all he had ever heard. Mr. Simister remembered his last address, delivered from the place where he was then standing, in which he went beyond himself, and as he sat listening to his words and looking at his shattered frame, the cons iction forced itself on his mind that they were listening to Mr. Soulby's last address. They would remember that the sub- ject was "The Lord's jewels." He had now become one of those jewels himself. In the beginning of May the doctor told him his only chance of recovery was to go to the south for change of air. He asked the doctor if he thought there was any likelihood of his getting better if he went; if not, he would rather stay and spend what little health and strength he had in the work he had so much at heart. The doctor gave him hope; and he accordingly with his wife ani daughter went, first to Hastings and then to the Isle of Wight. In tbe hope of returning soon to his work, his mind while away had been full of plans for future usefulness, conferring often with Mrs. Soulby respecting what he could do to make the boys love him more, and the addresses he should pre- pare for Brunswick Sunday Sthool. His plans were doomed never to be carried out. His sufferings during the past fortnight had been very great, and only ended with his death, which took place at ten o'clock on Tuesday night; and on Friday last, three lonely widows—his mother, his wife, and his sister-in-law—committed his body to the grave in the Cemetery at Shanklin, in the Isle of Wight. In conclusion, Mr. Simister affectionately urged his young hearers to copy the example of their deceased superin- tendent. It is proposed to erect a memorial stone over the grave at Shanklin, as a tribute of affection on the part of the teachers and scholars of the Sunday and day schools. Old pupils of the late Mr. Soulby's can send their subscriptions to Mr. F. J. Norman, treasurer, Greenway-road, Runcorn. .

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

SAD DeOWNING CAM—A little boy named Thomas Dodd, aged seven years was drowned in the Weaver canal, near Cameron's bone works, on Monday morning. The parents of the boy live in a cottage on the bank of the canal, and he was last seen by his sister about ten o'clock on the morn- ing of the occurrence, play ing in the water, and was then taken away from it. The little fellow did not, however, put in an appearance at dirner time, and his cap having been found, search was at once made by grappling in the canal, and was continued night and day by the father and a large number of willing and anxious helpers until Thursday afternoon, when the body was found by the father, near the spot where it is supposed the poor little fellow slipped into the canal.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL FRODSHAM..—Anniver- sary sermons on behalf of the Frodsham Primitive Metho- dist Sunday school were preached on Sunday afternoon and evening last by the Rev. T. Swallow, of Liverpool. The collections amounted to the sum of £ll 10s. Mr. James Hough presided at the organ throughout the service, and under his management the choir, with the assistance of a few friends from Runcorn, rendered the hymns in a very efficient manner. The annual treat to the scholars took place on Monday, at Mr. Darlington's farm, Haley, and was a decided success.

CHURCH CHOIR TRIP.—The annual trip of the Iron Church choir took place on Tuesday to Llandudno, the party leaving Froisham by an early train, and arrived at Llandudno in good time in the morning. Complete arrange- ments had been made for dinner, and this having been done full justice to, the various places of interest were visited, one persevering party of pleasure seekers even paying a flying visit to Conway and Bettws-y-coed. A few sharp showers fell during the day, but with this exception the weather was everything that could be desired, and all re- turned well pleased with their outing. FRODS HAM CHURCH.

Some considerable alterations and restorations are now going on in the structure of the ancient church of St. Law- rence, Frodsham. The church is an object of considerable interest to the traveller between Warrington and Chester, standing as it does on an eminence just under the craggy precipices of Overton Hills. Of the exact date of the original foundation little is known, though according to Mr. Helsby, in the last edition of "Ormerod, certain passages in the" Doomesday Survey" clearly indicate that a church stood here in Saxon times' of which there are probably some remains in the present edifice. A list of the vicars of Frod- sham, from the time of Radulpho de Ffrodesham, A.D. 1209-11, down to the present vicar, has been preserved. It is stated, however, by Canon RAines, in a note in Gastrell's " Notitia Cestriensis," that Hugh Lupus and Ermentuede gave the tithes of Frodsham before 1093, to St. Weiburgh's Abbey, but the advowson of the vicarage continued united with the manor until the building of the Abbey of Vale Royal, when the rectory and vicarage were both conferred by the Royal founder, Edward 1., who gave the (Wester monks £4 a year as a compensation fOr releasing their share of the tithes. In the "Bishop's Registry at Lichfield," according to the same authority, is the ft Rowing entry: "Frodesham Ordinatio Vicarise. flat. apud Heywood, 6 Cal. Sept., AD. 1358." From 1312 until 1547 the patronage was vested in the Abbots of Vale Royal, when Henry VIII., at the Dissolution, conferred be rectory and advowson upon the present patrons, the Dean and Chapter of Christ Church, Oxford. The general style of the present structure, according to Ormerod, is that of the fifteenth century, but the porch and a considerable part of the south side was rebuilt in 1715. The fabric is built of red stone, and consists of a nave, the chancel, side aisles, and tower containing six bells. The arches in the nave, and the pillars supporting the arches; the chancel, with the Kingsley or mother chapel; and a piscina, on the south side of the altar, under a gothic arch; with a trefoil and canopy, between two pillars terminating in crockets, are among the most inter- esting features in the old structure. Among the monuments are several of interest, notably those of , Francis Gastrell (a son of the bishop's), George Villiers. and Prebendary Sawkins, former vicars of the church; Robert Hyde, of Catten ; Henry Ardern, of Harden; Randal ph Helaby de Kingsley • and William Allen, , formerly of Davyhuline Hall, fatlier of Bishop Allen, of Ely, who, with Edward Byrom, Roger Sedgwick, and Edward Place, founded the first bank in Manchester. Among the brass.a affixed to the walla is one with the

following inscription :—" Near this place lies the body of Peter Banner, carpenter, of Frodsham, who died of a dropsy, October 21, 1749, aged 50. In 33 weeks he was tapp'd 58 times, and bad 1,032 quarts of water taken from him." The surprising longevity of the inhabitants of the district is plainly written on the monuments and grave- stones. Canon Raines furnishes one extraordinary entry from the parish register :—" Thomas Hough was buried here March 13, 1592, aged 141 years, and on the following day Randle Wall, aged 103." Ormerod says about 30 years ago there was an old tombstone (which has since disappeared) inscribed to the memory of "Dame Margery Knowles de Hellesby, aged 107." Her burial is thus entered in the registers :—" 1694. March 13, Margaret Knowles de liellesby, aged 107."

TIIE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 22, 1882 • WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell jun. and John Brock. THIEVING NATURALISTS.—Uatherine Larkin (18) and Michael Kelly (13) were brought up on remand from Friday, charged with stealing a tame tortoise and 51b. of scrap-iron, from a back yard in Kent-street, the property of Michael Lancaster; and also with stealing a rabbit and birdcage, of the value of 2s. 6d., the property of a labourer named Abbot, living at 2, Milton-road, Widnes. The circumstances of the robbery were reported in the last issue of The Examiner, and P.C. Almond having given evidence in the case, the bey was ordered to receive 12 strokes with the birch rod. Larkin was committed to gaol for 14 days on the first charge; the other was dismissed. ,INEBRIATES. Francis O'Hara, Wm. Bowers, John Clarke, Wm. Dwyer, Michael Burns, Mary Ellen Hickey, and Michael Flood, were each fined for drunkenness and disorderly conduct. BEGGING.—John Jackson, who stated he came from Liverpool, was charged with begging from door to door in Charles-street, Simms Cross, on the previous day, and on the evidence of P.S. Strickland, he was sent to prison for seven days' with hard labour. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Micbael McKean was charged by P.C. Barker with committing a breach of the peace in Wellington-street on Saturday night, and he was bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO and one surety in WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. J. Brock (chairman), and Holbrook Gaskell, jun. MISCELLANEOUS.—MichaeI McDonald, for being drunk in I Mersey-road, on the 13th inst., was fined ss. and costs.-- Martin Quinn was fined 7s. 6d. and costs, with the alterna- tive of 10 days' imprisonment, for creating a disturbance in Victoria-road, on the 30th ult.--A woman named Mary Mannion, who was helplessly drunk on the Old Marsh, on the 26th ult., was ordered to pay ss. and costs.---Joseph Wright, for being drunk on Saturday night, in James-street, was mulcted in the sum of ss. and costs, or, in default, seven days' imprisonment.—John Conner, for committing a like offence, on Sunday morning, in Midwood-street, was fined ss. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment.--A man named Patrick Kennedy, who made his 10th appearance, was ordered to pay 103. and costs, the alternative being 14 days' imprisonment, with hard labour, for being drunk and creating a disturbance in Ann-street West.----Patrick Power was charged with being drunk and guilty of disor- derly behaviour in Penn-street, on the Bth inst.—A fine of ss. and costs was inflic'ed.--James Campbell, for com- mitting a similar offence, on the 3rd inst., in the same street, was fined ss. and costs.---Two men named Frederick Whalley and John Jones were charged with drunkenness and disorderly conduct in Warrington-road, on the Ist inst.—P.C. Anderson (No. 455) gave evidence which went to show that the defendants were in the act of fighting whilst in a bestial state of drunkenness. He separated them and despatched them to their homes.—They were each fined ss. and costs, or, in default of payment, seven days' imprisonment, with hard labour.—Michael Donoghue, for being drunk and disorderly, in Waterloo- road, on the previous morning, had to nay ss. and costs. —Patrick'Noilan was brought up uuder a warrant charged with committing a breach of the peace, in Anne-street West, on the 19th of February last. The prisoner was shouting, swearing, and making a great noise, and refused to desist when requested by a constable.—He was bound over, him- self in £lO and two sureties of £5 each, to keep the peace. —Wier Jones, who did not appear, for being druak and incapable, in Windermere-street, on the 2nd inst., was fined ss. and costs.—Arehibald McDonald, who was found drunk and asleep against some rails in Church-street, on the Ist inst., was ordered to pay ss. and costs, or go to prison, for 7 days..---Christopher McGuire, who did not appear, was mulcted in the sum of ss. and costs for drunkenness. in Lugsdale-road, on the 10th inst.—Catherine Matthews (who did not appear) and Peter Hughes were charged with cnmniitting a breach of the peace, on the Bth inst., in Queen-street. The defendants were causing a great dis- turbance in the street, and were throwing bricks at each other.—The latter was bound over, himself in £lO, and two sureties in £5, to keep the peace for three months; and a warrant was ordered te be issued for the apprehension of the female defendant. Dnuene ON LICENSED PnEerrsus.—John Smith, a rough, destitute-looking fellow, was charged with being drunk, nal with refusing to quit the licensed premises of Mr. John Anderson, of the Railway Hotel, Victoria-road, on the pre- vious afternoorr—The evidence of P.C. Skinner (No. 111) was to the effect that he went into the parlour of the Railway Hotel and found the prisoner helplessly drunk. Witness called the landlady's attention to prisoner, but she said she did not know that prisoner was in the house, and he had not been served with any beer. Witness asked prisoner to leave the house; but he refused, and was taken into custody. The constable stated that previous to finding the prisoner in the Railway Hotel, he had removed him out of Waterloo-road, where he was lying on the footpath drunk.—Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs, or, in default, 14 days' imprisonment with hard labour. AN ADJOURNED CASE.—A young and respectably dressed man, named Aubin Young, was charged with being drunk on the licensed premises of Mr. John Smith, Griffin Inn. Church- street, Farnworth, on Sunday night, the Ist inst.—P.C. Ross (801) deposed that he visited the premises on the day in question, when he saw the defendant standing in a drunken posture near the door. He had been refused drink by the landlady, and he (witness) had to request him to leave the house several times before he would do so.—Defendant stated that he had been teetotal for three weeks, and was not drunk on the day in question. He also stated that the constable had served the summons on him, when it ought to have been served on some other man named Young; but the constable contended that defendant was the right man, and he had seen him drunk previous to finding him in the public- house.—The Bench adjourned the case to next Wednesday to enable the defendant to bring witnesses. ALLOWING A HORSE TO STRAY.—A man named John Fazakerly for allowing his horse to stray on Ditton-road, on the 30th June, was fined Is. and costs. INSULT AND lerecely.—Ellen Costello was charged with using abusive language and assaulting a woman named Mary Butler, on the 11th inst.—lt appeared that defendant asked complainant whether her name was Mary Butler, and if she had been interfering with her little boy. Comphainant on replying in the negative, was subjected to language of a most vile and filthy nature, and was struck on the face six or seven times by the defendant. Complainant then went into her house and had only just shut the door, when de- fendant threw a stone at her window, which smashed three panes of glass.—The Bench fined the defendant ss. and costs for the assault, and is. and the damage to the window 2s. THREATENING WITNESSES. Mary McDermott, the mother of the prisoner McDermott, who was committed a fortnight ago on a charge of wounding John Norton on the Widnes Old Marsh, was brought up under a warrant charged with threatening Hannah Keogh and James Smith, who appeared to give evidence against her son and the other prisoners.—James Smith said that he was standing near the iron bridge on the Old Marsh, on Wednesday, the 12th inst., when the prisoner came up to him and threatened him with death before the assizes took place. Prisoner similarly threatened Hannah Keogh on the 11th inst.—The Chairman said they looked upon this as a serious case, and bound the prisoner over to keep the peace, herself in £2O and two sureties in £2O each, or in default 21 days' imprisonment ASSAULT. Abel Plumpton summoned James Ridyard for assaulting him en Saturday night in Warrington-road ; and the latter summoned Plimpton for a similar offence at the same place.—Mr. Husband appeared on behalf of Ridyard. Abel Plumpton stated that he was going down Warrington-road about nine o'clock last Saturday night when he met the defendant, who asked him what he had been saying about him at Lightfoot's. Complainant said he had said nothing about him, whereupon defendant "cams out with" an oath, and struck complainant between the eyes. The blow was of such a violent nature that it caused him to fall into the gutter. Defendant then got on the top of complainant, and held him down with his left hand whilst he beat him with his right. Two men then passed and defendant subsequently desisted from illusing him.—Josh. Liptrott gave corrobora- tive evidence. James Ridyard deposed that he met Mr. Plumpton along with two other men whom he did not know. They were all drunk, and Mr. Plumpton said to the other men, "this is the —we have been wailing for." He asked him what he wanted him for, and Plumpton then struck him and knocked him against the rails on the side of the road, and a man named Richard Clarke came and parted them.—A little girl named Mary Ellen Lightfoot and Kichard Clarke gave confirmatory evidence.—The Chairman said they were satisfied that Plumpton was the aggressor, and they would fine him 103 and costs. They would dis- miss the summons against Ridyard. ASSAULT AT DrrroN.—William Jones was summoned for assaulting a boy named Michael Ford,at Ditton, on the 10th inst., and Ann Jones, wife of defendant, was charged with using defamatory language towa de Mary Ford, complain- ant's mother. There was also a cross-summons charging Michael Ford with assaulting William Jones at the same place.—Mr. Swift represented Michael Ford and his Mother. —lt appeared from the evidence of complainant that he went on to a piece of waste ground which belongs to the railway company, but which is •used as a recreation ground, to see some young men play cricket. He had gone a few yards on the field, and was talking to a little boy, when the mete defendant came up to him with an open pocket knife threatening what he would do if he did not get out of the field. The lad Fort,. was about to leave the field when defendant seized him and knocked him over a piece of wood. On getting up, defendant seized him by his coat collar, threw him to the ground, and vielently kicked him. Ford's mother then came up and told Jones she should summons 'him for assaulting her boy, but defendant said be would serve her likewise.—Defendant said the lad had stolen a chain which belonged to the railway company.—Mrs. Ford said that when she got home Mrs. Jones came to her house, threatened what she would do for her, and called her vile names.—William Janes stated that he went into the railway company's yard, and there saw Michael Ford uncoupling a chain which he secreted under his jacket. He followed Ford, but when he got near him Ford cut his face with a stone and knocked one of his teeth oat- He did not bit defendant at all, but scuffled with him in trsting to take the stones out of his hand. Mrs. Ford told her son to throw stones at him--For the assault on the boy Ford, William Jones was fined se. and costs, and the other two cases were dismissed. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun. DRITNICENNESS.—EIizabeth Jolley, of Runcorn, and John Spolian, were each glued ss. and coats,

• FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE. The American Senate, on Wednesday, decideJ to fix the tobacco tax at 12c. per lb. from the let of January next. The American House of Representatives has confirmed the election of Mr. Smalls, a negro, to the seat for Sourh Carolina, vacated by Mr. Tillman, Democrat. A detachment of the United States troops have had an engagement with a number of renegade Indians at Cherlon Fort, Arizona, resulting in the defeat of the latter with heavy loss. The troops lost one man killed and seven wounded, including two officers.

The death of the widow of the late Abraham Lincoln, pre- sident of the United States of America, is announced from New York. A fire at Smyrna has destroyed 1,400 houses and rendered 6,000 persons homeless. The destruction of property is said to be very great. A ministerial crisis has been produced in France in con- sequence of a vote adverse to the Government regarding a proposition to establish a central mairie in Paris.

- A despatch by the Royal mail steamer Sherbro brings from the West Coast of Africa news of desperate fighting on the banks of tke Niger. After a long delay it is announced from the Hague that Baron von Lynden has finally relinquished the mission which he had received from the King to reconstruct the Cabinet.

A panic continues among Maltese, who are leaving Tripoli in large number. One hundred left on Wednesday and 500 on Thursday. The alarm is extending to Italians and Jews. Perfect order is, however, maintained by the local authorities.

Prince Alexandra, of Bulgaria, ha 4 graciously offered M. ZAnkoff his liberty, on condition that he will voluntarily exile himself to Russia. The Liberal leader, however, rejects the proffer, and demands to bd liberated uncondition- ally, and the people of Rustchuk and Sofia are petitioning in his favour.

The Servians are carrying out the reorganization of their army at an expense which will bear heavily on the people. The Ministry of War demands a vote of £BOO,OOO, and the Government expect to raise that amount from the salt monopoly. The army is to be raised to 120,000 men, and new cannon and rifles are to be provided for the whole force.

The National Fete has b2en celebrated everywhere throughout France and her colonies with great rejoicing. Paris offered a series of magnificent spectacles. One, of a rather thrilling kind, was not on the programme, bat never- theless will live in the memory of those who witnessed it when the fireworks are forgotten. Several balloons were sent up to compete in a race, and one of them burst at a height of 300 feet. By a remarkable chance, the covering formed a kind of parachute, and the inmates of the car were let down slowly to the ground and in perfect safety . A SAD ACCIDENT AT PETERHOPF.—The Times correspon- dent at St. Petersburg telegraphs :—The following account of a sad accident, which is said to have occurred last Satur- day, at Peterhoff, is circulating here, though I cannot vouch for its absolute truth: The Emperor was out walking in the Park, and for some reason or other became interested in the operations of several workmen, or gardeners, who were at work some distance of. His Majesty appears to have beckoned to one of the workmen to come up to him, intend- ing to speak to the man, and perhaps ask some questions. The workman noticed the sign, threw down his tools' atcl ran towards the Emperor. When only a step or two from His Majesty's person he fell dead at the Czar's feet, shot by a sentinel close at hand who had not seen the Emperor call the man, and who had imperative orders to fire on any strangers approaching the Emperor. His Majesty, it is said, helped to lift up the body, and showed the bitterest grief. The wife and family of the unfortunate man are to be thoroughly cared for. THE PRINCE AND THE PUBLICAN'S DAUGHTER: A CHAPTER OF ROMANCE.—The old Princess of Hanau, who has just died at Prague, in Bohemia, was a remarkable woman, who made a considerable stir in her earlier life. She was the widow of the last Karfurst or Prince-Elector of Nesse. It was through her grasping ambition, and her equally resolute grasping after wealth, that the ruler became involved in quarrels with his Ministers and people. The Princess was a sort of Griselda or Cinderella, without the romantic tenderness of those heroines of legend. She was the daughter of a wine dealer at Bonn, on the Rhine. Lieutenant Lehmann, a young Prussian officer, fell in love with her ; they were married, and had several children. The future Elector, then the Crown Prince of Hesse, was fasci- nated by her, and is said to have bought her from her husband for the sum of 40,000 thalers. After a legal divorce had been effected, she married the Prince. Evil tongues said at the time that the Prince was not moved solely by lave to Frau Lehmann, but by a desire to spite the reigning Elector, and vex the Countess Reichenbach, to whom he was betrothed. The wine dealer's daughter ruled her princely husband to his hurt. She attained the second object of her ambition as well as the first, and became enor- mously rich. She is said to have left property amounting to nearly fourteen million marks, which, however, has to be divided amongst half-a-dozen children. Her late husband, after all his subj,cts had deposed him, magnificently absolved them from their oath of allegiance, and the old German Sovereign State of Electoral Hesse was incorporated with the Prussian Monarchy. The Elector, by his pacific accept- ance of the situation, secnred the immense property. which he carried into Bohemia from his fateful palace at Wil- hel pshiihe, where, four years later, in the same month of September, Napaleon 111. was lodged as a prisoner of the Prussian King.
ZULULAND. VISIT OF CFTEvVAYO TO ENGLAND.

A correspondent in Natal, whose letter is dated June 18, says :—We know nothing of what is actually passing in Zululand except through mere untrustworthy rumours. It is clear to us, however, that Sir Henry Bulwer has been able to restrain the intentions of John Dunn to punish his people who took put in the last deputation. A friend, writing from Cape Town, says that he went out to see Cetewayo lately with Mr. Saul Solomon. He says:—" It is a long time since I have seen such genuine pleasure depicted on any man's face, white or black, as that which Cetewayo exhibited when speaking of Mr. John Robinson's defeat in the recent election at Durbin. "Whew !" (with a long whistle), "the news is too good to be true. What have I done to him that he should hate me so?" were some of Cetewavo's expressions. Sir Hercules Robinson, I observe, gave him a place of honour at the review on the Queen's birthday.

We believe that Cetewayo on his arrival in this country will be attended only by Mr. Shepstone and Mr. Fynney, both of whom accompany him from South Africa. Mr. Fynney has had much experience of Zululand as a border agent, and he, as well as Mr. Shepstone, has a thorougk knowledge of the Zulu language. MINISTERIAL CRISIS IN FR INCE. RESICiNATION OF M. DE FREYCINET.

A Standard telegram from Paris dated midnight Wednesday, says :—lt is really the case that M. de Freycinet has thought fit to resign, after having carried a vote approv- ing his foreign policy, because he was defeated on a mere municipal question. Everybody will regard it as a mere excuse to get out of the Ezyptian difficulty. The Ministry resigned at six o'clock. President Grevy refused to accept the resignation, but M. Freycinet persisted. The " crisis " which was so suddenly provoked in Paris on Wednesday is at an end. M. de Freycinet was warmly advised by the President to remain in office. He accepted that advice, and the incident has terminated. It is not quite certain, however, that M. Goblet, the Minister of the Interior, will remain. It is now said that the order of the day which was adopted on Wednesday was intended rather to strengthen the Cabinet against the Communists than to censure it.

div.head: OVER.
div.p: OVER.

The anniversary services of the Over Congregational Church were held on Thursday, when the Rev. J. W. Woods, 8.A., of Cavendish Chapel, Manchester, preached in the afternoon. In the evening he delivered a lecture on "Screws," after several other of the neighbouring ministers had addressed the meeting, foremost of whom may be named the Rev. G. H. Walker (Nliddlewich), Rev. W. J. Hopper (Prea Methodist), Rev. T. Turner (Primitive Methodist), the Rev. F. Carter (Northwich), and the Pastor. A collec- tion was taken, and it amounted altogether to a good round sum.

PRESENTATION AT WHITEGATE, NEAR OVER.-011 Thurs- day last, after the week-night service at the Free Methodist Chapel, when the Rev. T. Naylor preached his last sermon there prior to leaving the circuit for Crewe—the church officials (Messrs. Moses Wood, Joseph Edwards, Robert Lightfoot, and Thomas McFall) and the congregation wor- shipping there presented him, through Mr. Bird, with an illuminated address setting forth their attachment to him as their minister during the three years he has laboured in the circuit, and the best wishes on the course he is about to enter, and hoping and praying his married and ministerial life might be happy and succesful. The address was accom- panied by a marble timepiece. The' anniversary sermons of the Primitive Methodist Sunday School, High-street, Over, were preached on Sunday last by the Rev. 3. Fergeaon, in the afternoon and evening. There were excellent congregations to hear this popular and talented preacher, who give two much appreciated addresses—during the morning's march of the scholars and teachers, and those interested in such, one at Over Cross and the other at Winsford. The singing and instrumental music in both Weaver-street, and Delamere-street, were a great attraction; as was the performance by the choir aipthe chapel under the leadership of Mr. J. Kitchen. The collec- tions amounted to .£l2.

div.head: LYME
div.p: LYME
Scarlet fever continues in this neighbourhood and Mel- wall.
Holloway's Star Theatre of Varieties has had a good week's patronage, and the company seem to give general satisfaction.

The Altrincham Brass Rand are having their annual Liverpool excursion on Saturday, when their train will stop at Dunham, Heatley, and Lymm to pick up passengers. The arrangements are now complete by which the com- bined Sunday schools of Lymm will have the advantage of a special train to Llandudno on Rush-bearing Monday, August the 14th. There is no doubt this trip will be largely patronised, as Lvmm, during the second week in August, takes its annual holidays.

A children's flower show, in connection with the parish schools and Temperance Society, will be held in the parochial schools to-day (Saturday). It is to be hoped that the welther will be favourable, so that it may be a success The Rev. Mr. Guest is chairman of the committee.

The Lymm Parish Church Schools are haying their excursion to Rhyl, on Monday, in which they are joined by several of the neighbouring church choirs. It is expected that a good number of outsiders will accompany them, as the new rector is decidedly popular. _

THE ELOPEMENT.—The woman who left her fourth hus- band and eloped with a youth of 17 years of age from Lymm som four weeks ago returned to her home the other night. She was met at the station by her husband, whose welcome was very different from that of a crowd of neighbours, who serenaded her with tin cans, frying-pans, penny whistles, fog horns, Sr.c. The youth has also returned to his mother.

. THE SEWERA.GE SCHEME.—An adjourned meeting of the committee of the Lymm Ratepayers' Association, was held on Tuesday evening, at the Church Hotel, to consider what further steps should be taken in regard to the sewerage question. The Secretary reported that in accordance with the resolution of the previous meeting he bad written to the law clerk of the Local Board, asking permission for the rate- payers to examine the plans of the schema, before the Local Government Board inspector came down to hold further inquiry, to which the clerk replied that he would lay the request before the Board at its next meeting.—Mr. Taylor read extracts from the inspector's late report which showed that there is no probability of the Board getting their pre- sent scheme passed.—lt was resolved that the secretary write to the Local Government Board asking that a copy of the report furnished to the Local Board in November last, be sent down for the benefit of the ratepayers, as that document has never been made public, and it is believed that it con- demns the Board's schemes. It was further resolved that the secretary get up a requisition to the chairman of the Local Board, asking him to convene a public meeting to elucidate the aims and plans of the Board; and to explain certain questions on which the public are at present in ignorance.

div.head: LYM3I PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: LYM3I PETTY SESSIONS.
FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. G. C. Dewhurst (chairman), Peter Stubbs, Henry Stanton, and A. W. Mills.

- DISORDERLIES.—John Flinn, a labourer, was mulcted in a penalty of ss. and costs for drunkenness, on Church Green, on the 16th June.—John Hume, a painter, who failed to answer to a charge of being drunk and disorderly, in Broom Edge, on the 18th ult., was ordered to pay a fine of ss. and costs, or, in default, 14 days. A SLEEPY DRIVER.—Samuel Oakes was cbarged with being asleep in his cart and allowing his horse to stay on the highway at High Legh, on the 28th ult.—The evidence showed that defendant was fast asleep in his cart, and when wakened by a costable, who requested his name, replied "I have none," at the same time spurring his horse forward and running away.—Defendant, when before the magistrates, stated that he had had the toothache and could not keep awake.—He was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. A RATE DEFAULTER.—Joseph Parker, landlord of the Green Dragon Hotel, Heatley, who did not appear, was sum- moned, at the instance of Mr. Ridgway, clerk to the Lymm Local Board, for the nonpayment of the district rate, £5 Os. 11d. An order for immediate payment was made. BRELCH OF CovrßacT.—John Leigh, who did not appear, was charged with neglecting to finish a piece of work for which he received 225. 91 Matthew Woodhead, the prose- cutor, said that he advanced the defendant the money to complete a piece of work for him, but defendant went away and left it incomplete. An order for payment at the rate of 33. per week was made upon defendant.

CRUELTY TO A GOOSE.—A youth named Arthur Cope- land, aged 12 years, of Bollington, was charged with wilfully ill-treating, abusing, and • torturing a goose belonging to Edward Forster, on the 7th inst. • Mr. Ridgway represented the defendant. The evidence of the wife of prosecutor and his servant, was to the effect that, whilst driving the goose along with four others out of Mr. Starkey's field, defendant struck it with a stick several times, breaking its wing and leg. Mr. Ridgway, for the defence, contended that the geese were trespassing, that the boy had orders to drive them out of the field, and did not wilfully abuse, torture, or ill-treat the fowl. The Bench, after hearing the evidence, dismissed the case. Another and similar charge was laid against the defendant, but was withdrawn.

div.head: m....,...r0w•1i.pW1..0...•
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Ed. Thomas and Hy. Reynolds. MiscELLANEops.—Martin Radigan, an Irish labourer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly, at Weston, on the 9th inst., and be was fined 10s. and costs 9s. 61, or in de- fault 14 days' imprisonment.—Mary Hodgett, a young married woman was charged with having, on the 14th inst., used obscene language in St. John-street, Runcorn. She was fined 10s. and costs 9s. 6d., or in default go to gaol for 14 days.—For having committed a breach of the peace in High-street, on the 11th July, John Shilton was bound over to keep the peace for six months, in his own recognisances of £lO. ASSAULT ON A WOMAN: AN UNPLEASANT BATH.— Richard Talbot was charged with having unlawfully assaulted and beaten Sarah Clarkson.---Mr. Hitchen defended. —The complainant said the defendant was her lodger, and on the Bth July he went home. She asked him why he did not give ber his wages, when he seized the fire shovel, and then an axe, and she ran into the road. He followed, and struck her on the head with the axe. He then knocked her in the gutter and held her in the water with his foot.—Mrs. Trevor, a neighbour, said she saw the defendant kick and beat the complainant. There was a heavy stream running in the gutter at the time, and the defendant laid her on her back in the stream, put his foot upon Irer, and held her there. Afterwards complainant ran into the house where the witness was. Defendant followed her, and seized her with the intention of dragging her from the house, but wit- ness interfered, and defendant then threatened he would "serve her the same" if she interfered.— Mr. Hitchen called a young man, named Mann who lived in the house, to show that the defendant was the master of the house, and that complainant lived with him as his wife. On the day in question he went home at noon and found the 1 complainant in a state of intoxication. She was ordered out of the house and refused to go. He denied that the com- plainant was kicked or an axe used, but admitted the defend- ant put the complainant into the gutter.—The Bench fined the defendant £1 and 16a. costs, and bound him over to ha I of good behaviour for six months. A Carratic AND HIS SEAMAN.—Charles King was charged with neglecting to pay John Dalton the earn of £5 165., the amount of 'wages justly due to him for his services as seaman on board the brigantine Danube, of which the defendant is captain.—Mr. Burton appeared for the complain- ant.—Defendant said the money was due to the complain- ' ant, but he had not the means to pay him.—The Bench made an order tos the payment of the money claimed and. the casts, and intimated that, in default, a distress warrant' would be issued.
