div.head: POLITICAL ITEMS,
div.p: POLITICAL ITEMS,

Messrs. Woodall and Broadhurst, members for Stoke, addressed a Liberal meeting in that bown on Saturday. Resolutions were passed expressing confidence in the Irish and Egyptian policy of the Government. A Lewes correspondent states that Mr. Jenne, Q.C., has been invited to contest Lewes in the Conservative interest at the next election, in place of Mr. Christie, M.P., who has declined, on the ground of failing health, to came forward again._

-Mr. H. M. Richardson, solicitor, of Bolton' announipes that at the next election he shall contest the borough on the platform of "true devotion to the principles of the late Lord Beaconsfield." The midi:late, of the Conservative Association have not yet been announced. The present members will be the Liberal oandidates.

Lord Salisbury, writing to a newly-formed Conservative association at Littlehampton, Sassex, says it is difficult to overrate the importance of these aasociations. Though the number of those who wish to preserve greatly exceeds those who wish to destroy, it is difficult to awaken the Conserva- tive classes to a sense of danger in time to repel the active asslilants of their Institutions,

It is understood that negotiations are passing between the Liberal and Conservative leaders in the House of Commons, with the view of arriving at such an understanding as to the new rules of procedure as will enable them to be disposed of befdre the close of the present session, and thus obviate the necessity of the House meeting in the autumn. Should the negotiations be sueeessful, it is expected that Parliament will be prorogued on August 18th. A meeting of the Council of the Birmingham Reform League was held on Saturday evening, at which& resolutien was passed thanking Sir Wilfrid Lawson and other members of Parliament for their denunciations in the House of Com- mons of the bombardment of Alexandria, and heartily rejoicing to hear that Mr. Bright has left a Government which has bean scandalously false to nearly every principle that they aivocated, or pretended to advocate when out of office. . TEA 1111PRESINTATION OF SMITE-EAST LINCISKINE.—A private meeting of the chairmen and secretariei of &he various Conservative Associations in the Parliamentary Division of South-East Lancashire was held on Friday evening, at the Central Association Rooms, Spring-gardens, Manchester, under the presidency of the Honourable Alger- non Egerton. The subject of discussion was the state of the register in the county. Addreises were delivered by the chairman and Mr. W. W. B. Hulton. A further meeting will be held to choose a second candidate, who, with Mr. Egerton, will contest the division. __

A deputation of three Maori chiefs, with the Rev. T. Grass as interpreter, waited on Lord Kimberley at the Colonial Office, on Monday, to ask his lordship to cause in- quiry to be made chiefly with regard to the Treaty of Waitangi, which they complained was being broken by the English and certain tribee. The treaty had reference to the distribution of land.—Lord Kimberley, in reply, said that as the ehiefs had not placed the matter before the Colonial Government, he could express no opinion on the question, but he promised to communicate with the Colonial GOMM. r ment on the qubject, and see what steps could be taken.

The Standard understands that the leaders of the Opposi... tion have decided to submit to the House of Commons a motion condemning on certain points the Egyptian policy of the Government. °The motion will probably be entrusted to Mr. Bourke, but this is not definitely settled. It is expected that any resolution aimed at the existence of the Govern- ment will be supported by the Parnellite members, and that on a division involving their Egyptian policy a good many of the usual supporters of the Ministry will decline to vote. A resolution will be moved below the gangway on the Ministerial side unreservedly condemning the bombardment. AcTrox AGAINST MR. BRADLAUGE.—Proceedings have been begun by Sir Henry Tyler, M.P., against Mr. Brad- laugh, for blasphemy. There are eleven charges, all founded on the Freethinker. If two convictions are obtained against Mr. Bradlaugh, the legal effect would be to deprive him, under the statute 9 and 10 William 111., of all civil rights, and in addition to fine and imprisonment, to disqualify him from sitting in Parliament. Speaking at the Hall of Science, on Sunday evening, Mr. Bradlaugh made allusion to his Parliamentary position in refererce to proceedings com- menced against him by Sir Henry Tyler. The prosecution, he said, was not founded upon anything he had ever written or published himself, and it was an endeavour to make him technically liable for something for which he certainly had no moral or legal liability. It was only an endeavour to prevent the real question he was Rghting from being de- cided, inasmuch as such proceedings if successful debarred him.

div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

The employers of Edinburgh, at a meeting held on Mon- day night, resolved to maintain the present average rate of wages, namely, 6i-ci per hour, with fd per hour additional to hewers whore shed accommodation is not provided. The workmen had made a demand for an advance, and some employers had been paying 7d per hour to builders and hewers working in the suburbs. Preparations aro being made at the Ruabon Ironworks belonging to the New British Iron Company, the most extensive ironworks in North Wales, to relight the blast furnaces, which have been standing idle for nine years. This will be welcomed, inasmuch as the Welsh coal trade since the recent strike has been in a very depressed condition, some collieries working little more than half-time. Many of the miners and their families are suffering great priva- tion.

On Tuesday afternoon 17 delegates of signalmen along the Midland Railway from London to Carlisle had an inter- view with the f, Board of Directors at Derby, in order to support a memorial recently presented for the removal of grievances. Various speakers referred to the injustice and hardships of the present system, and pointed out, among other things, the necessity of reducing the working hours from 12 and 13 to eight; of increasing the pay in different classes by 3s: and of improving the working uniform. Tux STAFTozestartE STEEL EXPERIMENTS.—The syndi- cate formed to conduct the experimental making of soft steel from Staffordshire cinder pigs by the basic process met again the other day, when Mr. Percy C. Gilchrist was him- self present. It was announced that the proposal to form a company to manufacture steel upon a commercial scale in Staffordshire from common pigs had met with considerable favour. Application for admission to the company was received from another influential iron concern. It is under- stood that this addition will swell to very considerable pro- portions the £25,000 previously subscribed. TYE WEATHER AND THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark Lane Earrees says :—" Very heavy rains occurred at the com- mencement of the past week. The middle of the week appears to have been fine generally, but since that time there has been considerable rainfall, and the weather is unsettled throughout the country. As July has advanced such reasonable hopes and anticipations as farmers may have entertained with regard to the wheat harvest have been gradually Iwindling away and something verylike disaster is now apparent. With the crop fairly in sight, and its con- dition but too well understood, it is difficult to imagine any possible set of exceptionally favourable circumstances which could bring anything beyond an indifferent wheat harvest, whilst in the prolonged absence of dry heat and brilliant sunshine it must be entirely bad; the cereal crops have been laid in many places by heavy storms of rain and hail, and want of bright sunshine hindering their develop- ment and making late hearvest a certaiaty. Supplies of native wheat are now very small, and if the harvest is very late they may become altogether nominal; consequently an advance of 2s. per quarter, which has occurred on marketable samples, may be considered perfectly legitimate. Country flour has gained from is. to is. 6d., and all other articles against buyers."

THE LLEOITE MIRIEET.—The labour market bas entered on few important changes during the past week, and as there is a perceptible diminution in the recent returns of registered pauperism, it may be assumed that the industrial condition of the country is on the whole fairly satisfactory. In the metropolis the miscellaneous industries are well occupied, but there is no significant demand for any class of labour from the outside. The new docks at Tilbury are, however, likely to attract a large number of navvies, and several im- portant metropolitan improvements are in contemplation. In the North collieries are faikly busy, but in Lancashire many pits are on short time. At Birmingham the hardware branches are somewhat quiet, but gun makers are generally busy. At Sheffield the heavy branches remain well em- ployed, and throughout the North iron shipbuilders and marine engineers remain specially busy. In Cleveland a considerable development of ironetone mining is taking place, and prospects are good. Building in the same diatrict continues active, but throughout the country large contracts are somewhat scarce. Advices from the United States show that the strike of colliers in Pennsylvania has come to an end, but several important braiches of trade remain very unsettled. In Canada a commencement has been made with steel making, and every opportunity is being taken to make known the resourees of the Dominion. Meanwhile the stream of emigration to America continues for the present to slacken. Good servants are in active demand in all parts. ---.l.abentr News.

THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADE : MANCHESTER, WEDNESDAY.—Lannshire makers of pig iron have Wen doing rather better during the week, and tolerably fair sales have been effected on the basis of about 455. to 465., less 21, delivered equal to Manchester, and there is now a tendency to stiffen to the extent of about 61. per ton upon the minimum quotation. District brands of pig iron are very firm at from 475. &I. as the minimum up to 48s. 61. and 495., less 21i, for Lincolnshire and Derbyshire irons delivered here. In the finished iron trade a moderate business con- tinues to be done at about late rates, bars averaging about Ld 7s. 6d. to £6 103., hoops £6 10s. to £6 155., and sheets £8 se. to LS 10s. per ton delivered into the Manchester dis- trict. Inquiries for various descriptions of engineering work s em to have q nietened d ,wn considerably during the last few weeks. Tn the coal trade business continues very quiet, with pits, as a rule not working more than four to four and a half days a week, and although there are now about 4,000 men on strike in tke St. Helens district the supplies coming into the market bays not been appreciably affected. All classes of round coal, both for house-fire and manufacturing pur- poses, continue plentiful. There is still a good deal of sell- ing in the market, but the average run of prices is without change, and colliery proprietors ia some oases are showing a disinclination to contract forward at present rates. At the pit mouth quotations average about 81. to Bd. 6d. for best coal, Os. up to 7s. for seconds, 4s. 9d. to ss. 6d. for common coal, 3s. 9d. to 4s. &I. for burgy, and 3s. to 35. 9d. per ton for slack. The shipping trade continues unsatisfactory, and Lanceshire steam coal can still be bought at either Liver- pool or Garston at from 61. 6d. to 7s. per ton. Coke is in good demand, at prices ranging from 9s. up to 11s. and 121. for the best sorts at the oTens. , THE LANCASHIRE ENGINEERING TRADES. Although a slackening off in the number of inquiries oorning in for new work has been complained of recently by employers, and this complaint is borne out by the fact that pattern makers are now in less pressing demand than they were a short time back, the general condition of the engin- eering trade throughout Lancashire, so far as present employment is concerned, continues satisfactory. Most of the works are kept fully going, to a fair extent on home, bat largely on foreign orders, and in some branches a good deal of overtime is being worked. The last returns sent in by the various branches of the Amalgamated Society of Engi- neers report trade as good in all the important Lancashire centres, with a continued scarcity of men required for loco- motive building and tool making. In the Manchester and Salford districts especially the men are kept well employed. and at the present time there are less than two per cent. of the total number of members on the books of the society as actually out of work.

div.head: BAMFURLONG.
div.p: BAMFURLONG.

THE FATAL ACCIDENT AT BAMFIIRLONG COLLIERIES.— On Saturday morning, Mr. Driffield, the county coroner, held an inquest at the Bamfurlong Station Hotel, on the body of Ellen Taylor, aged 15, who was fatally scalded the previous Tuesday at the Bamfarlong Collieries of Messrs. Cross, Tetley, and Company. Mr. Smith, one of the mana- gers, was present on behalf of the company. From the evidence it appeared that Taylor, who was formerly employed about the collieries, was warming her breakfast can in a cistern filled with hot water, when she lost her balance and fell forward into the scalding water. The acci- dent was soon perceived, and the girl was promptly taken out of the water and conveyed to her home near the collieries, where it was seen that the injuries she had sus- tained required medical treatment. Dr. Brayton, of Hindley, was accordingly called in, but in spite of his treatment the unfortunate girl died at half-past twelve the following day. —A verdict of "Accidental death "was returned. "1 ant astonishe& at your Honour's decision," said a young lawyer to a judge who had decreed against hl. "This re- mark cannot be permitted," said the judge, "and an apology will be necessary on your part." "Permit me," said the senior counsel, "to offer an excuse for my young friend; he is new in these matters, and when he has practised as long before year Honour as I hays, he will be astonished at nothing."
