_ IRISH NATIONAL FORESTERS.

DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. Runcorn had an unusual animation imparted to it on Monday morning last, when the members of the Irish Eetional Foresters commenced their annual proceedings by' an out-door demonstration of a somewhat unique description. For only five years has the order, which partakes of the nature of a friendly association, been in existence; and Run- corn and Widnes enjoy the distinction of being the first English towns in which the High Court meeting has been held. A foolish rumour has been circulating for a few weeks that the society was a Fenian organisation, but their pro- ceedings on Monday, and what we report below, will show that that rumour was without foundation. The delegates and the members of the Pride of Erin Branch, Widnes, arrived in Runcorn about ten o'clock and proceeded to the Public Hell, where they were met by the mem- bers of the Branch "Wolfe Tone," Runcorn. The proceed- ings in the Hall were of short duration, but marked by great enthusiasm, the audience repeatedly rising from their chairs and waved their hats and cheered. The following delegates ware present :—Messrs. Smith, Williamson. Coleman (Run- corn), G. Quiety (Limerick), C. Sawin, Petrick McGark, Henry Kelly (Isle of the Sea, Dublin), John McCabe, Fegan, Joseph H. Price, Daniel Boyle (Manchester District), Thos. Cassidy, Jas. Power, Parnell (Manchester), Patrick Doran (Shamrock, Skelinersdale), Edward O'Dea, Peter Mc- Grange, L. O'Toole (Dublin), J 39. Clements, Thomas Brady (Star of Erin, Govan), P. Whelan, Horan' Connor (Pride of Erin, Widnes), Brady, Kean (Shamrock, Glasgow), Matins, Doyle, O'Byrne (Dublin), Thos. Foley, Jas. A. Bashell (Robt. E I.:met, Manchester), Patrick Power (Wm. Orr, Pen- dleton), M. Dougherty, McLoughlan (St. Columkille, Port Glasgow). Mr. J. Groves, Rd. Hugh O'Neill (Dublin), J. Rogerson, Thomas Finegan (St. Alb n's, Warring- ton), Collins, Devlin (Dublin District), Connally, Dunne, Bernie (O'Connell, Liverpool), J. Higgins (Hibernia, Edgworthstown), P. Boland, J. Redmond, J. O'Shaugnesey (Cape Town, South Africa). Mr. WILLIAIII9ON read the following " address of welcome " : Worthy High Chief, Sub-Chief Officers, and Fellow Country men,—Oa behalf of the officers and members of Branch "Wolfe Tone" I beg to offer you a hearty " Cead mille faulthe" and to return sincere thanks for the honour that our important and influential society has conferred upon this small town of Run- corn by allowing the 11 C. meeting to come here on this occa- sion. The whirling of time has brought round the filth annual meeting of our Irish society. We have been ambitious to meet you, and it was with thoughts full of anxiety. and longing hearts that the members of the Committee of 'Sfanagement, os whom rests the responsibility of helping to carry through the success of the Irish cause, awaited your arrival, to either censure us for not being cheerful in doing our duty to our country or to praise our efforts. (Cheers.) We have been full of enthusiasm at the thought of meeting our kindred, who are working with Us in one grand united bond of lcve and brotherhood, who are using their utmost endeavours to unite their fellow-countrymen In one powerful association for their own benefit and thus to fulfil the grand object for which our immortal patron Emmet died. (Cheers.) We are proud to see you even in exile, though some of us have not seen for years the land of our fathers or breathed the pure air of our native country. But t.-day re- minds us of the fertile hills awl green valleys of the Island of Saints which we were forced to leave through wicked, cruel. and unjust laws; we were driven here to waste our lives in thinking of Erin with our spirits crushed by the disappointment of all our hopes of fatherland. (Cheers ) Bravo, our executive council! It shall be remembered for you in the hereafter when Iceland's cause is in the crisis. You will, we know, do your duty to her, and net forgetting our noble founder. You were the first to establish our Irish society, ani long may you live to continue true to its cause. To you all we tender you a hearty welcome. Centuries have passed away. yet national suffering continues to be an abiding sore. The centennial of the one bright spot in poor ould Ireland's history is completed at this time: it is 100 years since the church of Dungannon was full to the door, when Protestantism forgot the animosity of sect and the intolerance of c-eed, and recognised Irishism as the only qualification for national liberty, when Catholicism threw aside the bitter memories of penal laws, and long days of persecution, in frater- nization for Ireland's sake, when in a word all classes com- mingled together in the aspiration and the effort to make their country a nation once again. (Cheers.) The men of that day taught us how to dolt; be it ours now, profiting by the lesson of 1782. not only to do but to keep on doing, not only to obtain but to retain. Fellow countrymen. we are glad to see you. We know you have all come to do great things in our Irish Parliament of 1883 under the united banner of orange and green, and we are thankful that Providence has betowed upon you all health and strength to enable you to carry out the many duties devolving upon you during the past year. and we pray that success may attend sour deliberations, and that every blessing and prosperity may beam on the future of our native land and her sons. (Cheers.) Mr. JIM'S O'K. RYAN then rose to read the following address on behalf of the Widnes Branch, and of St. Mary's (Widnes) Total Abstinence League. He was repeatedly cheered. The address read as follows -- Brothers in the cause (3, Irish National Forestry. To yen one and all we bid you welcome. We welcome yoo to Run- corn, because we feel that by selecting that place as the point at which you intend holding your annual con'erence, you clearly demonstrate that you aopreciate the humble labours of the Irishmen of Runcorn and Widnes. who were the first in this part of the country to bring into notice the benefits which such a society holds forth to the exiled son of Ireland. (Cheers.) We are proud of you as Irishmen, and we ho sour you as patriots, bemuse we know that in the past you have one and all striven with a wilt peculiar to only self-sacrificing men t 3 promote the interests of this society by every leeitimate means in your power, and we know that by as doing you have sue- ceeded in establishing a bond of union, harmony, and brother- hood among the children of the scattered Gael in this and other lands. (Cheers.) To you—especially the members of the High Court-the exiled son of Erin should be great ful f tr establishi .g branch-s of the Irish National Forestry Bociety In Irish popu- lated districts where the demoa of temptation very often exists, and where often, too, the imnrovident nature of cur country- men reduces them and their families to such a state of penury that the only means of existence offered them in times of de. pression of trade are to be found inside the portals of the foreigners' workhouse In establishing branches of our society in such districts, we vsert that you place yourselves in the light of benefactors to the whole Irish race and stems> your- selves as lovers of Ireland and Irishmen. (Cheers.) With you lies the credit, be it said, of rescuing many a hardy son of toil from that which is worse than death—a pauper's grave.—and many is the one who has been comforted in his dying agonies by the glowing thought that though it is Gods will for him to I die far away from the green hills of Ireland, he will be borne to his last resting place on the shoulders of brother Irishmen. (Cheers.) Apart from that, you have worked strenuously and, let us hope, successfully in premoting that which our country stood sorely in need of. You have been untir ng in your exertions towards bringing about that fellow-'eeling of toleration and unity amongst all classes and creeds of Irishmen, irrespec- tive of political opinion or religious belief, and by so (Ling you have helped on the cause of Irish Forestry, the cause of Irish nationality, and the cause of union and brotherhood amongst our countrymen the world over. (Cheers ) We know from past experience how our motherland has been cheated of her Godgiven rights to freedom by the petty jealousies of her chief, and the consequent dominion of her people, and we feel that the work which you have begun and carried into sateh brilliant effect in the past, shall, with Heaven's help, in the future be nroduetive of still greater results in unitine Irishmen. and therefore help on the cause for which Emmet and Lord Edward died, and for which Allen, Larkin, and O'Brien suffered the indignities of the rope and scaffold. (Cheers.) In the chequered history of our country there never was or has been a moment in which union was so much needed as the present one—for in spite of the vast armies now infecting our fair cities and verdant fields—in spite of the many indignities whom brothers are subjected to, in spite of the spy and traitor and ball and buck-hot, the grand "precept stands out in bold relief emblazoned in letters of gold on that history, that Ireland united is Ireland free, Ireland disunited is Ireland in chains. (Cheers ) Therefore, brothers in the cause, we hope you will cling to work with a will in the cause of unity, and we promise yru that it shall alwass be our endeavour to help you on by every means in our power, and by hoping to see our expoc'atiOns realised—by hoping to see all classes and creeds o Irishmen united in our own day, we are expressing the seetinsents of • many who have loved Ireland in times even when it was "treason to love her and death to defend her." In conclusion, we once more bid you welcome, and remain brothers in the cause God save Ireland. (Loud cheers.) The members, numbering about 509, now formed into processional order, headed by Sarsfield Bend, Liverpool. Then came the handsome new two-poled banner of the Widnes Branch, borne aloft by two sturdy pole bearers. On the front side were minted the Forester's arms, and those of the four counties of Ulster, Munster, Leinster, and Con- naught. Encircling the painting were the words, "Let Erin remember the days of old," in orange coloured letters on a green background, while on a scroll on the bottom was the motto " Dnion is strength." On the obverse was represented "the Maid of Erin," who held the shamrock in her outstretched hand, and crouching by her side was a wolf dog. A landscape stretched behind in which the cross shadowed boldly forth. The banner had an orange-coloured border, and, in the bright sun, its appearance was very pretty, and drew forth much favourable comment. Follow- ing the banner were the members of the Executive Council, who wore the "Robert Emmet" dress, which consists of a green coat plentifully but tastefully decorated with gilt ornaments and buttons, white waistcoat and trousers, high boots, and a tall soft hat with a white feather. Next came the delegates, the members of the Wolfe Tone and Pride of Erin Branches of the Order, wearing a bright green scarf, bordered wall orange, the.procession in its entirety forming an attractive scene, for people turned out in hundreds to view it as it pissed along the streets. Excellent order was maintained throughout the whole route, and reflected not a little credit upon the marshals. Brother Coleman was the chief marshal], Bro. P. Smyth, sub-chief. assisted by Bros. P. Horne, Whelam, Thomas Royan, P. Lavelle, W. Burke, James Ryan, and the Executive Corn- . . reittee. The route taken was to Delph Bridge, returning up High-street, Waterloo-road, and across the bridge to Widnes, where they proceeded to the residence of Dr. O'Keeffe, who e d livered a short address. After parading the principal streets of Widnes, watched by a host of admiring soectators, they returned to Runcorn. an amongst those tiplorsoevipdreedsenfot were de s- legates at Wilson Hotel, n pr. O'Keefre (who contested Tralee the last general elec- tion), Dr. McDougall (the society's physician), and Mr. Byrne (the founder of the order). The cloth having been drawn, Dr. O'Keeffe was unitimously elected chairman. In addressing those present, The Clearneeene expressed his thaniKa for the honour that had been conferred upon him, and said he felt exceedingly proud to be even for a few short minutes, or half hour, chairman of an aeeenehly like that, which represented a very great portion of the talent of the scattered Irish nation. (Hear, hear, and cheers). Indeed .they had proved that that day, as they had done on. many other occasions before a hostile pnblic—(" No, no," and hear, hear)—a public very much inclined to judge them conscientiously, and which keenly watched their procession that day. (Hear, bear.) was prod to sly that there never was a better conducted procession in Encel end, in Ireland, in Scotland, or any other part of her Majesty's dominions or in any other country. (Cheers.) They hid shown that Irishmen were not such feels and idiots as the British public believed them to be. (Hear, hear.) They had shown a di 'cretion and a judgment, which was a natural consequence of being members of the Foresters, which wad an honourable society approved of her law, and a

society that afforded benefit to many a helpless family in times of sickness. (Hear, hear.) Therefore he was proud to take part in the procession that day—(applause)—and he should be proud to attend the annuli meeting wherever it was held. -( Applause.) Their conduct that day would in- spire the British public with a feeling of respect for them— (hear, hear,)—such, perhaps, as they had not felt hitherto. (Loud applause.) He then called upon Dr. MCDOUGALL, who was received with cheers, and pro- posed success to the Irish National Foresters. He believed he was right when he said the Irish National Foresters existed solely for a charitable purpose, and.so far as his ac- quaintance with the Runcorn portion of the Order went, he could speak with warmth and with a good deal of feeling, of the good which it had accomplished since its establishment in the town, between three and four years ago. There were other orders in the town previous to that time but somehow or other, the Irish members of the community did not find their way into them; they did not seem to find an appro- priate institution with which they could identify themselves; and they established there the National Foresters, the foun- der of which he believed was that day in their midst. (Loud cheers.) He must say he thought it extremely creditable to his head and his heart to have found out a method by which Irishmen in exile could associate together in a society con- ducted according to the law of the land, and ' which aimed at assisting its members in time of sickness and distress. (Hear, hear.) From his personal knowledge of the Irish in Runcorn, for the last 14 years—and no person had been more identified with them than himself, except their clergyman—he could speak of that institution with authority. There were occa- sions when sickness would come to all of them, and if they had to seek aid it was far better that they should seek it , from those with whom they were familiarly acquainted,l than to be compelled to apply to the poor-law officers. So far as he knew, and he 'should have heard if there had been anything to the contrary,the Foresters' Order was conducted in a right and proper manner, and a more orderly number of young men in their station of life he did not know. (Ap- plause.) " The speaker expressed the gratification it afforded him to be present that day to identify himself with the Order, which he had every reason to believe existed for a purely charitable purpose. (Hear, hear.) The Runcorn Branch had a membership of about 40 or 50. The weekly allowance in times of sickness was 10s., and how infinitely better it was to receive that sum from the secretary and have the benefit of the attendance of the medical man, than to make an appeal to the Poor-law Guardians to maintain , their children. A glass of ale was a good thing for a man, but to drink a good many was a bad thing, and instead of spending their money in ale on Saturday night, he advised them to invest it in a society like the Foresters, by which they would provide for the day of sickness and make them- selves independent of everybody. (Applause.) He re- marked on the excellent order which had been maintained by the procession, and concluded by asking them to drink "Success to the Irish National Foresters," coupling with the toast the name of the founder. (Applause.) Mr. BYRNE (Dublin, the founder of the Order) responded. He remarked that the establishment of the Order in 1877 was an endeavour to unite his countrymen on a common platform irrespective of political views and religious creeds, and to form a mainstay in sickness and in death, and said it had extended its ramifications to all quarters of the globe , where Irishmen existed. He contended that Irishmen had as much right to found that society as the Englishman, the Scotchman, and the Welshman had to establish similar orders, observing that ere time had passed away there would not be a spot on the face of the civilised globe where the green and orange banner of the Irish National Foresters would not float to the skies. (Loud cheers.) Mr. BOYLE (Manchester) proposed the toast of "The Reception Committee," which was responded to by Mr. WILLIAMSON and Mr. RYAN, and the company separated. In the evening, a ball was held in the Public Hall; and was very successfully carried out. The floor had been laid with holland, and the room decorated. The duties of M.C. were admirably performed by Mr. James Match. The refresh- ments were supplied by Mr. Henry Jackson, of Wilson's Hotel. The company separated about three o'clock. HIGH COURT MEETING.

The delegates met at the Public Hall about ten o'clock on Tuesday morning, for the transaction of business. Mr. Thos. Wm. Bourleigh, High Chief Ranger (Dublin) pre- sided, and opened the meeting in the usual formal manner. He then addressed the meeting. He said during the twelve months the Executive Council had had many obstacles to encounter and overcome in their endeavours to advance the cause of the society, but yet he thought from the report to be submitted to the meeting they would at least agree that if there were some drawbacks and failures there were many successes, and of such a good substantial nature that the failures sunk into insignificance. He believed the Order was now so firmly established that nothing could defeat its onward victorious march. He appealed to them on that occa- sion to take energetic steps to enable branches to be estab- lished over the world wherever Irishmen resided. Their decisions would be watched by their anxious countrymen; their language, when committed to print, would be eagerly perused and studied, and therefore let their language be calm and their actions decisive but ; and thus show to the world the capabilities of Irishmen to manage a parlia- ment of their own in the old land. During his term of office he had endeavoured fearlessly and impartially to uphold with credit the dignity of that position which with their sincooe he held ; if he failed, then blame not his will,butincapability. He once more bade them welcome, and hoped that this par- liament would be a forerunner of the day when they would witness the opening of the old House at College Green. He now declared the fifth rarliameut of the Order duly opened. The minutes of the last High Court meeting, held at Dundalk, were read by Bro. OTYRNE, the general secretary, and on the proposition of Bro. P. DOYLFI, seconded by Bro. MCGRANE, they were confirmed. Bro. OTYRNE, read the report for the twelve months end- ing the 17th inst. It stated that during that period the following branches had been established :-0 wen Rae O'Neil, Michael Davett, and Charles Dawson, Dublin; Young Ireland, Longford ; Thomas F. Meagher, Water- ford; Violated Treaty, Limerick; as well as the Dublie District. In England branches had been formed under the following names :—St. Alban., Warrington ; John Mitchell, Ashton-Under-Lyne'; Michael Davitt-, Stockton-on-Tees; Ireland Liberator, Rotherham, Yorkshire; Manchester Dis- trict; O'Connell and Exiles of Erin, Liverpool; Treaty Stone, Birkenhead ; a clear gain of eight branches, proving that the exiles were mindful of Fatherland, and where determined to uphold the flag of the Society. (Cheers.) From Scotland were reported the opening of branches Star Of Erin, Govan ; St. Laurence O'Toole, and Pride of Erin, Pennicuich ; T. F. Meagher, Greenock; and Glasgow Di - trict. The branches were in a flourishing condition, and re- flected great credit on the officers who presided over them. In Africa, 7,000 miles from Erin in a foreign clime, toiling under a burning sun, their brethren worked for them, and with glorious success, as was instanced by the fact that Branch Sarsfield now numbered 110 members with a capital at £l5O, whilst as a proof of their love for Erin, and their endeavours to resuscitate the failing manufacturers of that country they had procured from Dublin Irish manufactured goods at a cost of £l2O. Another branch had been estab- lished in the colony at Grahamston under the title of Branch Grattan. The members in Dublin were gratified by a visit from Bro. J. T. O'Reilly of Branch Sarsfisld, a pro- minent Irishman, influential merchant, and leading Imemb.r of the Town Council at Capetown who promised to every member who was compelled to emigrate to South Africa, a good position with every opportunity to advance himself, and a warm reception from the brethren and a coed mille failthe at his private mansion, Erin Lodge. (Cheers.) The report went on to state that districts had been established at Glasgow, Manchester, and Dublin, which was a very wise step, and it was the duty o' every branch to join such districts, as no one knew when a heavy rate of mortality might occur, and thus the entire funds of a branch be swamped. Branch St. Columkille, Port Glasgow, had established afleurishine, juvenile branch under the title of St. Bridget, No. 1 ; and the report advocated the establishment of similar branches in all parts. The numerical strength of the society was—lreland 650, England 740, Scotland 500, Africa 200, 'America 280, making a total of 2,370. The financial position was as follows :—lreland I £320, England £430, Scotland £420, Africa £l5O total, £1,470. During the past year many prominent Irishmen bad proved their attachment to their cause by enrolling themselves under the banner, amongst the rest being Michael Davitt—(cheers)—father of the Land League; J. G. Biggar, M.P., T. Sexton, M.P. Having remarked on the satisfactory balance sheets received from the branches, the report stated men whose age exceeded the limit allowed by the rules had been admitted into branches, and said this matter should be settled, and the society not left open to the charge of being glad to snatch at all persons. Reference was then made to certain propositions which would be proposed, and concluded : Worthy Brethren,—l have finished my duty', and this little record I place before you with the feeling that a great, gloeious, and prosperous career is before your Order, and that if you persevere in unity, brotherly love, and patriotism, ere long your eyes will brighten as you read the annals of a body which five years past sprang from a mustard seed, end has grown into a mighty tree. Your heart will beat with impulsive emotion when you know that the green and orange lia7, of your Society floats over every spot where your exiled kindred have found a resting place. We must succeed be- cause success attends us. You have read the records of other societies, of the troubles, anxieties endured, super- human endeavours undertaken to make them successful after years, but where can you find a society not yet five years established boasting of such success as your own ? founded by humble persons, boasting of neither riches or position, yet from a tiny barque. has sprang a powerful vessel, which has sailed to all places where Irishmen are ; located, and has left behind memories which are dearly cherished, and fresh recruits when needed to steer it safely, and floating under the canopy of heaven, the ereen and orange flag of Erin emblazoned with the letters I.N.F. Five years have elapsed since the foundation. Let us hope that when five more years have elapsed the society shall be recognised S 5 the most powerful Irish Association, crowned with laurels of well earned victory. We at home can hasten such success by unity and persevering labour; the exiles when travelling by propagating its principles, and inviting their kindred to enlist in our body; all working for that principle SO often sighed for by our poets, prayed for by our saints, and fought for by our forefathers, a united, untrammelled Ireland, faction and disunion at an end, and orange and green united in one bond ef brotherhood. (Loud cheers.) Brother O'DEA (Dublin) proposed the adoption of the report, speaking in very eulogistic terms of the labours of Brother O'Byrne, whose name would be handed down to posterity, and occupy a prominent Iplace in the history of his country. Brother McGee/es seconded the motion, which was carried.

,Bro. O'BYRNE read the balance sheet, and Bro. J. GROVES having made a few observations thereon, Bro. BOLAND moved its adoption. A long discussion ensued apon a finan- cial dispute between the Executive Committee and the branch at Dundalk, and eventually a small committse was appointed to inquire into the matter. The adoption of the balance sheet was then deferred. _

A list of propositions occupying a book of 16 pages now came up for consideration. Branch O'Byrne, Dublin, sub- mitted the following :—"That a token or password be adopted, whereby members may recognise one another," which was proposed by Bro. DOYLE, and supported by Bro. MALINS, neither of whom, however, personally agreed with the proposal. The Dublin delegates were of opinion that the adoption of such a motion would bring upon them the censure of the Roman Catholic clergy; while others argued that the adoption of passwords would be injurious to the society, which would then partake of the nature of a secret order, and have the effect of reducing the ranks in Ireland though it might, perhaps, act beneficially in England.—A DELEGATE observed that the possesion of a card by each member would ensure his recognition wherever he might be.—Bro. BOYLE (Manchester), with reference to the opinion of the priests, said he should like to know what support the society received from the clergy. He understood that the ball held on the previous night was in opposition to the wishes of the priest in that town; and if they did not accept the resolution the society would not, he thought, receive any more support from the priests in the future than they had in the past. (Cries of " Yes " and "No.") In his opinion a password would undoubtedly be a boon to the members when they were travelling, and he heartily sup- ported the resolution. Bro. DOUGHERTY narrated an instance where an Irish priest had refused to allow any of his parishioners to join the society because he was opinion it was ef a secret nature.—Bro. McLoucattaia (Port Glasgow) opposed the resolution. They did not fear publicity as was instanced by the presence of the reporters that day.—Bro. WILLIAMSON (Runcorn) re- marked the Father Fennelly upheld and respected the Society of Irish National Foresters ; he only condemned the ball which was held on the previous evening; and he always would condemn balls.—Bro. BOYLE : Not when they are for the church.—Bro. WlLLremsoN : Whether it is far the church or not, I can assure you we have the support of our priest.—After some further discussion, there voted for the amendment, 21, and for the resolution, to which there had been added a rider that the password should be renewed quarterly, there voted 17. The amendment was declared carried amid cheers. The delegates then adjourned for luncheon, and on re- suming about half past two discussed a resolution from Branch Olyrne, Dublin, that all the annual meetings should in future be held in Ireland. It was however decided that the meetings should, as at present, be removable. The Branch O'Byrne, Dublin; and Wolfe Tone, Runcorn, had two propositions of somewhat similar terms upon the list, with reference to the constitution of the Executive Council. The Dublin delegates withdrew their resolution in favour of that from Runcorn, which was adopted. It stated that there shall be appointed officers at each Annual High Court Meeting, viz., High Chief Ranger, Sub-Chief Ranger, treasurer, general secretary, assistant secretary, three trustees, and beadle. Any branch of the society within ten miles of the registered office, should be at liberty to nomi- nate candidates for the above offices, and a town in which to hold the next High Court Meeting. The next business engaging the attention of the meeting was the remuneration of the secretary, who was at present paid no fixed salary. Brother CONNOLLY moved, and Brother FOLEY seconded a resolution "That the general secretary be paid a regular salary in fitting with his position, to enable him to devote his time to the welfare of the society." It was carried unanimously.—ln. answer to a number of in-

guides, Brother DOYLE state,' the com:nittee had decided last year that the general secretary should receive 45 per cent. of the receipts, but when the salary should have been paid him, several bills came in, and Brother O'Byrne generously paid them.—Brother OTYRNE said he had only received 18s. for his services for the past year, but he did not want to make any gain out of the society, and he should be content with the terms of 45 per cent.—lt was ultimately decided, amid loud cheering, that the general secretary be paid at the rate of £2O per annum, quarterly. On the proposition of the delegates from Branch Parnell, Manchester, the following new rule was adopted :—That no branch, being aware of the circumstances, be allowed to initiate a person who may have been refused acceptance in another branch, until they have received the consent of the district committee in which the party was originally pro- posed, or, where no district committee is in existence, the committee of management of the society, under a penalty of 205., without mitigation, the same to be paid into the district fund; or where there is no district, into the funds of the society. The meeting adjourned at half-past five. The deliberations of the High Court were resumed at ten o'clock on Wednesday morning. The High Chief Ranger (Bro Bourleigh) presided; and the majority of the delegates were present. The consideration of a series of propositions from the Manchester district was the first busi- ness, and without discussion it was decided to make an addi- tion to rule 63, on the motion of Bro. DOYLE, seconded by Bro. FEGAN, which provided that five months' notice of the annual meetir.g be given to the branches, and that the printed copies of the proposition be issued a month previous to the meeting. From the same district was a proposal to strike out rule 43, and insert the following:—" A branch contain- ing 30 members, or under, shall be allowed to send one delegate; from 30 to 60, two delegates; and one delegate for every 30 additional financial members, to the annual meet- ing, whose wages and travelling expenses shall be paid by the branch sending them. A district of 100 members shall be allowed to send one de'egate; two hundred, two delegates; and one for every additional 100 members; whose wages, elm, shall be paid by the district by which _
they are .ment."—lro. FEO-1N moved, and Bro. _PRICE

seconded the resolution.—Bro. GROVES and Bro. BRADY spoke against the proposal, and Bro. CONNOLLY made an amendment that each branch should be allowed to send only one delegate, with a number of votes proportionate to the numerical strength of the branch ; distric's not to be repre- sented.—The amendment was ieconded by Bro. BERNIE.— Bro. WILLIAMSON (Runcorn), spoke against.the proposition, and Bro. McCABE pointed out that if, as desired by Bro. Connolly, the meeting decided that districts should not be represented, the whole constitution of the society would have to be changed.—Bro. FOLEY spoke effectively in favour of the resolution.. When put to the vote. the resolution was negatived by 24 votes to 11.—On the motion of the Man- chester district, it was resolved to add to rule 46 that a branch more than one quarter in arrears with its levies, should not be allowed to send delegates to annual meeting, and be suspended from all benefits until it complied.—Branch Robert Emmett, Manchester, submitted a resolution " that no branch be allowed to send representatives to annual meet- ing which has not been established six months previously." It was carried unanimously. Bro. WILLIAMSON on behalf of Branch Wolfe Tone, Run- corn, propesed a resolution that the High Court meeting appoint three auditors to audit the accounts, examine and prove the stock, and report thereon to the society. The auditors to meet about the first day in July, one of whom to attend the next annual High Court meeting, to give an explanation of the society's position. A method for the working of the rule was given.—Bro. SMIT/I (Runcorn) seconded the proposal; which was adopted.—Other resolu- tions of no public interest were -dealt with, and Bro. COLE- MAN (Runcorn) moved, and Bro. DOUGHERTY (Glasgow) seconded, a proposal to amend rule 55 of the general laws, that a member be not deprived of benefits until 12 weeks in arrear instead of 8. After some discussion, the motion was carried, and the delegates adjourned for lunch. Os reassernblinT, the delegates proceeded to the discussion of the rest of the propositions on the paper, and these having been disposed of, the annual balance sheet was adopted. The next business was the election of officers, and the following were appointed : High Chief Ranger, Bro. Boland ; Sub-Chief Ranger, Bro. McGrano ; ' treasurer, Bro. Hanlon; general secretary, Bro. El. J. O'Bourne ; assigtant secretary, Bro. Bourleigh ; trustees, Bros. Tyrell. O'Dea, and Doyle • beadle, Bro. Thornton; auditors, Bros. Groves and Connolly. All the officers reside in Dublin, where the chief officers are located. It was decided to hold the next meeting at Glaegow. The thanks of the meeting were accorded to the Runcorn Reception Committee, who had so kindly entertained the delegates during their stay in the town; Bro. Daugherton observing that he had never experienced such kindness before, as he had received at the hands of the Thincorn brethren. The thanks of the meeting were also tendered to the representa- tives of the local Press. Bro. Boyle proposed 'a vote of thanks to the retiring High Chief Ranger, the Council, and the General secretary, and the resolution was carried by acclamation. The newly-appointed 11.0 R. then took the chair, and having made a few observations on the general objects of the society, the proceedings terminated at seven o'clock. We feel constrained to state that the proceedings throughout were conducted in an orderly manner, each delegate evincing a desire to promote the wvlfare of the society.

THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JULY 229 1882 • HARTLAND WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES. LAYING OF MEMORIAL STONES. As in other towns, the early pioneers of Wesleyanism in Widnes commenced their labours in a humble way, the first religious services in connection with tbat denomination being conducted in two cottages situated on Widnes Marsh. About the year 1850 a chapel was erected in Satton-lane, which, however, was recently sold by auction. Twelve years later the handsome edifice in Victoria-road was built by the late Mr. Thos. Hazlehurst, of Runcorn; but the extra accommodation thus provided proved inadequate for the requirements of the denomination, when 10 more years had elapsed. West Bank was the district in which it was imperative another religious organisation should be established, and a legal obstacle to the acquirement of a site in that locality having been removed, the present school chapel in Oakland-street was erected. But the rapid growth of the town, not unnaturally caused an augmentation of the followers of Wesley in a corresponding degree, and this building soon became full to overflowing. For a con- siderable period it has. been too small, not only for the purposes of a chapel, but also for the school. Each Sunday about 200 scholars have to be taught in the adjacent Board School; a fact which indicated but one remedy. The Oakland-street chapel does not occupy the whole-of the land held by the trustees, about 2,000 square feet being unbeilt upon; and the trustees decided to build a chapel on this plot at a cost of about £2,000. The project was sanctioned by the quarterly meeting, and the trustees (whose names are Messrs. W. Hartland, T. Whitby, B. Brown, S. B. Stringer, H. Hartley, John Hartley, Joseph Clarke, Charles Jones, T. Baiter, John Riddell, and William Price) invited plans. Those submitted by Mr. Herbert Isbitt, architect, of Bradford and Wigan, were approved of. The new chapel will face Irwell-street, and its dimensions will be 50 by 58 feet. In its construction the stele known as mixed Italian will be adopted. It will be built of patent bricks, while stone from the Appleton quarry will be used in string courses. Buttermere sea green slates are to form the roof, and each of the windows will have a marginal of tinted glass. On each side of the front will be an entrance so arranged as to form a transcept, into which the galleries, which are to run round three sides of the building, will open. The appointments of the interior are to be of first- class workmanship, and when completed will be in thorough harmony with each other. The pews will be of stained deal, and constructed in the ordinary manner. An arti3tic design has been prepared for the woodwork of tee gallery, which will form a decorative feature in the interior; and the rostrum will be a commodious and shapely structure. Be- hind the rostrum a space is to be left vacant with a view to the introduction of an organ at some future time. The ceil- ing of the chapel will be divided into panels, a circular device with a sunlight pendant forming the centre. Two commo- dious vestries will form a portion of the building. Light will be obtained by the ordinary gas brackets; and the chapel will be heated by hot water. While well screened from draughts, an effective sysi.em of ventilation will ensure the escape of the vitiated air. Mr. J. A. Chapman, of Bradford, is the builder. It is thought the original estimate will be exceeded, and the cost of the edifice reach the sum of £2,500. Over £l,OOO of this has already been obtained, Mr. F. H. Gossage and Mr. T. S. Timmis having given generous aid by a dona- tion of 500 each. In making these donatiens Messrs. Gossage and Timmis requested that the edifice should re- ceive the name of Hartland Chapel, in recognition of the life long labours of Mr. William Hartland in the cause of Wesleyanism in Whines. It is ,only reasonable to suppose that such a desire was in unison with the wishes of the trustees, who at once acceded to the request; and the name of Hartland will consequently for ever remain linked with the spread of Wesleyanism in the town. The ceremony of laying two memorial stones of the chapel took place on Thursday afternoon, under most auspicious circumstances. The wet and gloomy weather of the morning had given place to a bright sky and a clear atmosphere, and the flags which flattered across the street rendered the scene not a little gay. There was a large assembly of people, and amongst those present we noticed the Revs. T. Brighouse (Manchester), J. Nowell, G. Hack, T. Peters, J. Tessyman, T. Hughes, and Messrs. W. Hartland, Geo. Procter, T. Robinson, B. Brown, W. Jones, T. Whitby, W. Whitby, W. Hunt, S. Myers, Isaac Turton, S. B. Stringer; Mesdames Briggs, Pattison, Duxbury, Harper, Whitby, Procter, Clarke, Lawrinson, and Miss Downey. The Rev. J. Tessyinan conducted the proceedings. A hymn having been sung, the Rev. T. Peters offered up prayer, and the Rev. G. Hack read a portion of the 6th chapter of the second book of Chronicles. Miss J. Rogers (West Bank) was called upon to lay the first stone, in a cavity beneath which was placeda bottle con- taining the Methodist Recorder, a circuit plan, a list of the members in society, the number of Sunday school scholars and teachers, and other officers of the church, and a silver and bronze coin of the realm. Miss Rogers was pre- sented with a silver trowel and a mallet with which to perform the ceremony, by the Rev. J. Tessyman. The trowel bore the inscription," Presented by the trustees of the Hartland Wesleyan Chapel, Widnes, to Miss Jane Rogers on laying the memorial on the 20th July, 1882." She executed the duty in the customary manner, and Mr. HARTLAND said as he was the grandfather of Miss Rogers he might be permitted to say a few words. Mr. ' Rogers had already given £5O towards the building of that chapel. He had two daughters in whom he was equally interested, and that day he was giving an additional £3O; £l5 in the name of each daughter. It was a noble action indeed, and ha was sure they would all say so. (Applause). It was a large sum to be given by a workingman, and if he had not he.en interested in the cause of the Saviour, and in the welfare of the poor in the neighbourhood, he would not have done so. (Hear, hear). Mr. JOHN HOUGHTON, of Appleton, was then presented with a trowel and mallet similar to those presented to Miss Rogers, and after haying laid the stone in the customary way, he said standing before that large assembly that clay his mind went back 13 years, when they were opening Vic- toria-road Chapel, and when the Rev. Dr. Pun- shon was preaching, surrounded by other rev. gentlemen. It was a grand day for Widnes. That day they were laying the memorial stones for a new chapel in Oakland-street, and they trusted that that day would be remembered by them and their children as long as they lived, and he prayed that the blessing of God might rest upon the chapel and upon all of them. Liberty and truth had always been preached in the little sanctuary close at hand, and they believed that the Gospel in its purity would be preached in the house they were that day preparing for the service of the Lord. It was their humble prayer that that chapel might be the means of saving hundreds of thousands who entered, and might each of them be blessed not only with saving grace, but with sanctifying grace of God impressed upon them. Mr. HARTLAND here announced that Messrs. Gossage and Timmis, in addition to their handsome donation of £l,OOO, had that day sent a £5 note each for the collection that day. (Applause ) Success to the firm of Messrs. Gossages. (Applause.) Mr. Houghton, he also announced, had contri- buted that day £l5. (Applause.) The Rev. THOS BRIGHOUSE then delivered an address, in which he asked what was their object in erecting that build- ing. It was that they might form, fashion, and beautify characters; make eind model noble lives; make men more like God and earth more like Heaven. He believed the perfection of our nature consisted in our resemblance to Jesus, and just in proportion its our lives were noble and sublime, were they the reproduction of the life of Jesus. He pointed out the universality of the love of God, and touched upon the fact that the crucifixion of Christ had made regeneration possible, obeerving that they could net estimate the importance of genuine con- version to God. True conversion must be the starting point of all efforts after holiness. Our life would be just as we made it; we could make it into a divine and beautiful thing or it might be blighted and blurred. Divine manifesta- tions, spiritual awakenings, christian conversions, holy lives —these are the objects of building sanctuaries, and the ob- ject ef preaching the everlasting Gospel. Religion satisfied our reason tranquilised our consciences calmed our spirit, and enabled us.to live with comfort and with comfort to die. A religious man contemplated the great future with calmness and confidence, and as his frail body sank into the darkness of death, he felt he was entering upon an everlast- ing life. The rev, gentleman concluded by expreesing his gratification at the success which had attended the auspicious proceedings of the afternoon. The Rev. GEO. Hem then spoke a few words of congra- tulation to the assembly on the success which had attended Methodism in the neighbourhood ; so successful that they were kuilding a new and larger sanctuary. (Hear, hear.) It was far better building a sanctuary than a theatre—(hear, hear),—or a public-house---(hear, hear.)—and as long as the house they were building that day should stand, they might be perfectly c,-Ttain there would come no harm to a single individual as a result of the doctrines which would there be taught. (Hear, hear.) They were on the winning side thatday so far as Christianity was concerned. He was certain of that from the constant streaming forth. of Christian literature from the printing presses; from the evangelical agencies at work, and from the magnificient temperance movements, call them what they would—Blue Ribbon Armies or by any other name. What meant these but that Christianity was on the winning side. As Methodists they had great.reieon to be thankful for the work of the past year. The membership was now 60.000, an increase of something like 12,000 on the previous year, and he was anticipating a still greater suc- cess during the coming year. They had a grand minister as president, the Rev. Chas. Garrett. (Hear, hear.) • They were glad he was in the chair, and under his presidency they hoped to reach glorious results next year. He referred to the generous donation of Messrs. Goesage that day, after giving £l,OOO by way of expressing tkeir respect for the faithfulness of a servant, who, in a Christian way, had served them many years, and he thought such generosity merited their public recognition. (Heir. hear.) Se far as be was concerned long may the firm of Gossage prosper, and send another £l,OOO when the Wesleyans wished to build another chapel in this growing town of Widnes. (Hear. hear.) He wished the Oakland-street friends success in their enterprise, and might the sanctuary be indeed a house of God, by repeated manipulations of power in which conversions of scores and hundreds would occur. (Ap- plause.) A collection was then taken and the proceedings ter- minated. The amount received during the afternoon amounted to £65 12s. sd. A public tea was provided in the Oakland-street schoolroom, of which a large number of persons partook. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mesdames Cummings, Tessyman, Brown, Stringer, Duxburv, Proctor, W. Whitley, Ankers, Houghton, Watson, and Miss Downey. a public meeting was held in Lacey-street schoolroom, evening, rooemve, There was a good audießce, and Mr. B. Brown

presided, in the absence of the superintendent minister. Amongst those on the platform were the Revs. T. Brighouse, J. Tessyman, T. Peters, T. Hughes, Mews. Jones, Hunt, Rogers, John Hartland, Stringer, and George Proctor. Dur- ing the evenine. the Oakland-street chapel choir sang a number of anthems in good style under the conductorship of Mr. Wm. Whitby, who also presided at the harmonium. After devotional exercises had been engaged in, The CHAIRMAN addressed the meeting. He expreseed his sympathy with the superintendent minister, who was unable to be present that night. For several weeks he had suffered severely, but he was glad to say he was somewhat better, and was now on a visit to Buxton to try if a change of air would have a beneficial effect. He (the chairmen) was pleased at the success which had attended that day's ceremony, which he compared with several other "great occasions which had taken place in the circuit. In many instances the circnit had been put to expense which it could scarcely afford, in connection with certain work, and the success of that day had been of a somewhat similar character. But when the Lord worked the people must work ; when He led surely they could follow. If He blessed them with spiritual blessing they were bound to go in faith, and establish a church in the place which He blessed. This had been their position at Oakland-street. The school occu- pied as a preaching place was far too small for the regular congregation, and an extension of some kind had been wished and required for years, but the funds were not forthcoming. Now, through God's providence, and the liberality of Messrs.Gossage, they were enablel to build a new chapel, and he trusted God would honour them with a rich blessing, and bring the work which-would be carried on there to a great and glorious consummation. (Hear, hear.) He should not have liked Messrs. Gossage to entirely build the chapel for them. He was glad they had taken the course they had, and by making it possible for the congregation to build a chapel, left it to them to accomplish the object; for they could thus say that they had done their share in bringing about that grand result. He concluded by making an appeal for help, suggesting several methods for securing systematic contributions to the fund.

Mr. Pnocron read a financial statement, which showed that £l,OOO was still required to reach the estimated cost of the new chapel. Mr. CHARLES JONES, in the course of a few observations, remarked that he had seen every chapel in the circuit built and opened, with one exception; and during his Christian career in Widnes he had been connected with missions at Hale Bank, Ditton, and Moss Bank, and he never regretted the work he did for the Lord. He touched upon the necessity for increased spiritual activity in their chapels, and said the Salvation Army had entered the neighbourhood with a loud noise, apparently intending to turn Widnes upside down. They had not done so. He had no objection to the Salvation Army, and if they were doing good, they might if they wished do their work with bangos and violins. (Laughter.) Their method was of no consequence if they won souls to Christ. ( Hear, hear.) The Wesleyans were intending to form a mission, which would be divided into four branches, and were determined to go out in the streets and work as well AS the Salvation Army. West Bank was to be turned upside down. Mr. Orrnerod, the Rev. T. Brighouse' the Rev. T. Peters, Mr. Taylor (who produced his ctrd of membership, dated 1831), and Mr. S. Stringer also addressed the` meeting. On the proposition of Mr. W. NEWSOME, seconded by Mr. HUNT, a vote of thanks was tendered to the strangers who had assisted in the day's services; and a similar compli- ment was paid to the ladies who had presided at the tea tables, on the motion of Mr. PROCTOR, seconded by the Rey. T. HUGHES. The latter gentleman congratulated those present upon the success of the day's proceedings, and remarked that he was exceedingly glad to have been allowed to be present. The Rev. T. PETERS proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman. Mr. Duxamor seconded the motion, which was carried.

Mr. Was. WHITBY here desired to make a few remarks, and he stated that he had promised to place a harmonium in the new chapel, providing a recess was provided. He under- stood no recess was to be formed, and he should ccnsequently withdraw his promise. The choir were thanked for their services, on the motion of Mr. B. STRINGER, seconded by Mr. WILLIAMSON. Whilst the proceedings were in progress, forms had been handed to each p.rson in the audience on which Co state a sum they were willing to give towards the erection of. the chapel. These papers were collected, and Mr. Proctor announced that £155 had been promised. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

The Wigan Conservatives held their annual demonstra- tion on Saturday, when addresses were delivered by Mr. Knowles, M.P., and others. In the course of the proceed- it was definitely announced that Mr. Nathaniel Eckersley had consented to become the Conservative ctndi- date for Wigan on a writ being issued to fill the vacancy. Mr. Eckersley sat for Wigan in 188t3. NEW MAGISTRATES FOR WIGAN.—The names of the following gentlemen have been inserted in the Commission of the Peace for the Borough of Wigan :—Messrs. Matthew Bens?n, of 35, Dicconson-street, Wigan, gentleman; Charles Graham, of 9, Springfield-street, Wigan, gentleman; James Marsden, of The Limes, Standish, near Wigan, clothing manufacturer and cotton spinner; John Henry Peck, Of Wallgate, Wigan, sailcloth and tarpaulin manufacturer; and Thomas Stuart, of Gidlow, Wigan, house and land agent. THE WIGAN RECORDER AND THE STOLEN CORESE.—The Wigan Quarter Sessions opened on Wednesday, before Mr. J. T. Fitz idam, recorder. There are ten prisoners for trial, principally for felony. In charging the grand jury, the Recorder referred to the recovery of the body of the late Lord Crawford, and said the information had been received with great satisfaction by the whole of the inhabitants of the borough. MUNICIPAL CONTEST AT WIGAN.—On Wednesday, an election took place at Wigan, to fill the vacancy in the repre- sentation of All Saints' Ward in the Town Council, caused by the death of Mr. Councillor Charles Wood (L). The contest did not create much excitement, the ward being a small one. The result of the poll was declared as follows: —Mr. Alfred Barlow (C), 215; Mr. James Marsden (L),197 : majority 18. This is, therefore, a gain to the Conservatives; who bays already a large majority in the council.

div.head: LOYAL STONEHENGE LODGE, ORDER
div.p: LOYAL STONEHENGE LODGE, ORDER
OF DRUIDS. DINNER AT gTOCKTON

The biennial gathering of the Loyal 'Stonehenge Lodge of Druids of the Warrington District took place on Monday. The members, to the number of 160, formed themselves in procession and walked through the village of Stockton Heath to the church, where a short service, consisting of hymns and an address by the Rev. T. S. Toff, was gone through. They were headed by the Earl of Ellesmere's brass band from Worsley, and were led by Alfred Few, the secretary, Charles Beech, treasurer, Joseph Hargreaves, P.D.G.M., Daniel Dean, P.D.G.M., Wm. Besuick, and James Battersby, P.D.G.M. Several flags were hoisted on various houses in the village in honour of the event. After the service at the church was ended, the procession visited the houses of the principal gentlemen in the neigh- bourhood where several handsome subscriptions were handed to the secretary to defray the expenses of the clay's pro- ceedinge. The company then made their way to the Lon- don Bridge Inn, where a substantial dinner, catered by Mrs. Cook, was partaken of.—Dinner over, the Rey. T. S. ToFT, who was the chairman, said the first toast he had to propose was one which never came amiss to any Englishman, and he did not suppose that there was a more loyel company anywhere than they were there ; at all events for the honor of Stockton Heath he would not like to suppose that they were not.loyal people. All that he bad to do was just simply to mention the toast, and he was sure they would receive it with cheers at the present time. It was very ; necessary thet they should all show themselves to be loyal ; subjects of their Queen and Sovereign, for they could plainly see the blessings they receive from haying such a Sovereign. He then gave the toasts of "The Queen," and "The Prince and Princess of Wales, and the whole of the Royal family." The toasts were received with acclamation.— The rev. CHAIRMAN then proposed the "Army, Navy Volunteers," coupling with it the name of Mr. Cook, band master of Lord Ellesmere's band, and Mr. Cook suitably res- ponded.---Mr. C. BEECH, treasurer of the society, proposed "The bishops, clergy and ministers of all denomina- tions " to which the Rev. T. S. Tom responded.—Mr. Joseph HARGREAVES, Noble Grand Arch proposed "success to the Order of Druids of the Warrington district."—Mr. J. HARGREAVES, P.D.G.M. said it gave him great pleasure to respond to the toast which had been proposed by their Noble Grand Arch Brother Hargreaves. The duty fell upon him in consequence of the absence of their Past District Master. The district was in a very flourishing condition. They were gaining members, but he was very sorry to say that there were some of the lodges which were not in so satisfactory a condition as regarded the finances. In that matter he thought it was necessary that something ought to be done—something after the fashion of their funeral fund. They would have to form an equalized fund for the sick. They were aware, as he was aware, that their club had an equalized fund so that representatives of a man when be died always received his death money. It was certain out of that fund; but there were lodges in Warrington where if a man fell sick he was not sure of his sick money. Their own lodge was a wealthy and prosperous lodge, and they could afford to give their members their sick pay, but other lodges could not do the same, therefore if they couldrform an equalized fund, something after the fashion ot the feneral fund, whereby other lodges would pay a certain amount into that fund, the lodge would be helping the poor. A. great number could help a 'few, hut a few could not help many. A new rule would he proposed by their district secretary, at the next district meeting, as follows, which hehopeel they would agree with him would be to the advantage:—"The fund from which all sick benefits are paid shall be an equalized fund, and shall be raised and managed in the following m inner. Each lodge shall pay its own sick members during the current quarter, according to the rules of the society ; and the lodge .secretaries shall send in an account to the D.S's of the amount so expended, together with the names of the sick members and the natured their illnes.s at least 21 days before the next quarterly district meeting, and district secretaries shall then call for a levy upon all lodges according to the number of its members sufficient for the pnrpose; and the district officers shall out of that levy refund the amount so expended to each lodge after deducting the share of levy due from such lodge or lo lges." The speaker went on to 83V that their district secretary had informed him that if he could get the Stonehedge Lodge on his side he would have no fear of the motion not becoming law, for he would then be certain that the poorer lodges would take up the matter, and be agreeable for it to pees.—Mr. J. HOUGHTON observed that it would not be advisable without very great precau- tion to accept the resolution which had been proposed to be brought forward at their next district meeting,. He begged to give the toast of "The Order of Druide of the Stonehenge Ledge."—Mr. FEW, the secretary of the lodge, stated that he had received letters of apology for non-attendance from Lord Mulgrave, Mr. Robert Davies, Mr. James Marson, Mr. A. Mackie, and several others. It was something like two years since they had a gathering of ;that sort, and during that time they had lost seven members, and he thought they ought to feel very thankful that their lives were spared to meet once again. He might say that they had not paid any sick pay, since the 17th June. Their club Was 160 members strong in June 1880, and the society was worth £758 49, This year they had 162 members, and the society was worth £Bl3 lie. 61e1., showing again of £53 75 al. during the last two years. They could therefore see that they were in a very prosperous state.—Mr. GEO. PARR next pro- Posted "The health of the caterer, Mr. Cook," which was cordially received.—Mr. MARE CROSS proposed "The health of the chairman, the Rev. T. S. Taft," and the Vicar haying suitably reepooded, the meeting terminated.

SWING-BOAT ACCIDENT AT WARRINGTON.—A serious swing-boat accident occurred on the Fair tirounti, Queen- street, on Monday evening. About half-pAst seven o'clock two youths were enjoying the aerial flights of a swing- boat when one of them, named Wm. Tobin, residing in Portland-street, stood up as the boat was swaying with con- siderable velocity, and he was thrown to the ground. He sus- tained such injuries that he had to be removed to the In- firmary, where he now remains Suffering from, a compound fracture of the thigh.
TIIE WARRINGTON GOOD TEMPLARS.

An interesting gathering took place at the Co-operative Hall, Warrington, on Tuesday evening, when an aggregate 'meeting of the members and friends of the three local lodges of Good Templars was held. There was a good attendance, and many of those present wore the regalia of the Order, the officers, whose badges were resplendent with embroidery, occupying seats in the centre of the hall, which was set out in lodge form. Tl.e Rev. E. Moore occupied the chair, and he was supported by Bro. D. Y. Scott, G. W. Councillar, and acting G.W.C.T. of England, Bro. M.Bebbington, D.0.T., of South-west Lancashire, and Bro. J. W. Hall. There were also present, the three W.C.T's of the Temperance Mission, Walter Bonehill, and Wesley lodges, Bros. Tomlin, Goulden, and Roberts, and the following :—From Temperance Mission Lodge: Bros. Harrison, Taylor, Thornley, Lowe, Parks, Bibby, and Benson, Sisters Hall, Mitchell anti Massey, Bros. Corbett and Mason (W. Secs.) Walter Bonehill Lodge: Bro. Jones, Sisters Mitchell, West, and Bibby. Wesley Lodge: Bros. Bate and Beauman. Latchford Lodge: Bros. Ellison, Hugh, Harrison, and Riley; Bro. and Sister Lindon, St. Helens.

The CHAIRMAN said it was with very much pleasure that he acceded to the request to become chairman of that meet- ing. It was not often that it was his lot to be present at a meeting of so interesting, and, he might perhaps add, novel a character as that. He was quite sure that amidst the many organisations which had been set on foot, having for their object the diminishing of the great curse of drunken- ness in this country, Good Ternplary held a very con- spicuous position. They found its ramifications extending almost all over the entire civilised world, and he thought it was one of the benefits of that Order that wherever one of its members might go he was almost sure to meet with those who were, at any rate in this respect, at one with him. He was sure that even those who did not actually belong to the Order must fully sympathise with the objects for which it had been founded, and which it had kept constantly in view. Those objects were, he understood, total and personal absti- nence for the individual, and total prohibition of all in- toxicating drink as a legalised traffic in the nation. He was sure that if those objects were attained they should no longer have to deplore, as they did deplore, the terrible state of things that still exists in this country. It was a most deplorable thing to think that they could not walk down the streets without having to encounter those who had become intoxicated through their excessive drinking, and especially to his mind was it a painful thing, to say the least of it, that on the Lord's Day, the day that was conse- crated to His worship, when above all days they looked for sobriety, quietness, and peace, the streets should be hideous with the noise of drunkards, and its peace disturbed well nigh from morn to night. If the Good Templars and other temperance organisa- tions had no other object in view than the total suppression of this drink traffic on the Lord's Day it would be an unspeak- able blessing. But if the total suppression of public houses on Sunday tended to the sobriety and peace of the community, surely it was not an evil thing for other days toe. He hoped to see the day when the number of these temptations to drink, if not altogether aleolished, would at any rate be greatly diminished. He supposed the Good Templars would scarcely call themselves a political body, and yet he thought it was impossible for a society so strong and so completely organised to exist in a community without exercising a very important influence upon its politics; and whether they did or did not go in for all the Good Templar Order went in for, whether they did or did not approve of all the motives by which they went to work, of this he was sure, that they were working in the right direction, and the effect of their political action on the community would be at any rate upon the side of sobriety, temperance and virtue. They wished them all "God speed" in their work. (Applause.) Bro. BEBBINGTON expressed his pleasure to see such a. goodly gathering of bretheren, and proceeded to remark that he had been very much encouraged in going through the different districts of South-West Lancashire, to find some of the old brethren who had left the lodges had retnrned, and were now putting their shoulders to the wheel. The work which they had to do was a work which could not be ' done by any other society, and he suggested the desirability of continuing those meetings daring the winter so as to make the Order known. (Applause.) Bro. D. Y. SCOTT remarked that that night all eyes were turned towards Alexandria, and he was sure they, in com- mon with all their countrymen and countrywomen, heartily wished our country out of this Egyptian difficulty. (Hear, hear.) It was but the otber day since we were at war in India, in Zululand, in the 'Transvaal; but that night they were face to face with an enemy more powerful than either the Afghan, the Zulu, the Boer, or the Egyptian rebel. They were that night face to face with the greatest enemy our country had ever seen—an enemy which was wasting our country's resources, slaying men, women, and children by thousands—(hear, hear,)—and making thousands upon thousands of otherwise happy homes miserable. He chal- lenged contradiction when he said that the number of men slain, the amount of money expended, and the amount of misery produced by all the wars of the last 25 years—the last 50 years—in which this country had been engaged sank into insignificance compared with the number of persons slain, the amount of money wasted, and the amount of misery produced by the drink traffic. It was the mighty upas tree that flourished in our midst, sending its roots deeper and deeper, and twining them tighter and tighter round the institutions of our country, and spreading its poisonous branches on every hand, causing sin, misery, destruction, and death. That night the cry arose from ten thousand, thousand voices—and they were there that night to ask those present to let their voices go forth to swell the sound that was becoming louder and clearer than before,—"cut it down,why cumbereth it the ground." They were not there to commend the regulation or restriction of intoxi.cating drink. They went in for re- stricting and regulating it—regulating it off the face of the earth. (Hear, hear.) Parliament had been trying to regu- late and restrict the traffic for the last 400 years, but they p,,inted to the failure of these attempt as evidence of the i ',possibility to regulate it. They demanded Sund ty dos- ing as a right—(hear, he.tr)—and they demanded the total prohibition of the importation, manufacture, and sale of in- toxicating drink. (Hear, hear.) Some might say they were extreme, but they were extremely right. They 'tad had extreme men in every age, but he had yet to learn that a man or a measure was necessarily WI on..' because he or it was extreme. He asked those who had not yet enlisted under their banner to give up drink and join them. He asked them to give it up for their own sakes, and if they would not give it up for their own sakes to give it up for the sikes of their families; and he urged them to stir them- selves to do something towards blotting out that dark, dark spot on our country's escutcheon. He stated that when he joined the Order they had not a thousand members, but now they had over 00,000, and the number was increasing. Pub- lic opinion was coming round to their side and they !oust succeed when they had right and truth on their side. (Ap- plause.) Bro. J. W. HALL proposed a rote of thanks to the chair- man, who, he hoped, would be induced to join the Order,—. (applause)—as he was sorry to say, although in Warrington they had 300 members they had not a reverend gentleman amongst them. In conclusion he urged those present who had not already done so to join the Order and help to push on the work of temperance. Bro. SCOTT seconded the proposition, which was carried with acclamation, and The CHAIRMAN having briefly replied, the proceedings terminated.

FOTTL-110177114D WomEN.—Mary Honda-Fon and Martha Briars, resp-ctably dresse I elderly married women, realign.; le Wakefield-street. were summoned for having on the 13th :nst. made use of certa,n language towards Hetty Wade, also a married woman, calculated to provoke a breach of the pew,* Mr. P. Paves appeared for the complainant. and Mr. Wm siev for Vie defendants.—lt appeared the parties were before the Benc', in March last, when each had to pay her own e,s'a but since that time Vr. Davies said the defendants had made ase of Most " foul, indecent, and unnatural language for women like drAendants." MISCELLA..NEOUS.—Thomas Garritty and John Mather were summoned for committing a breach of the peace in Buttermarket-street, on the Sib instant, and w6re each bound over to keep the peace for six months.—Garrltt3r was also sum- mooed for obstructing the footpath in Ooc•khedge-lare. on the 13th instant, by wheeling a barrow thereon, and was tined 2s 6d. including costs.—Mary Maloney and Winifred Maloney were each blond over to keep the peace UT Ix months, On the evidence of P.O Corcoran, for committing a breach of the peace on the 10th instant by fighting in Horsemarket-street.—Owen Saxon was fined 21.6 d. Inc uding costs for obstructing Bridge-st. by allowing his horse and con- veyance to stand there an unremonable time.—Mary Gue.t was summoned for wheeling a perambulator laden with green- grocery on the font,ath in Bold-street, and fined ls —Joseph Lawrence was fined 2s 6d. for allowing two horses to stray In Knutsford-road, on the 10th instant ; and a similar fine was Imposed upon Lawrence Monk fcr allowing his horse to stray In Battersby-lane.

MO CONSUMERS OF GAS.—The Warrington Corpora- tion Gas Committee, being desirous of further en- couraging amongst their consumers the use of GAS FOR COOKING and other purposes, are now prepared to Ball, Let out on Hire, or Pen-chase, Lease, GAB COOKING STOVES at a small half-yearly rent charge. All the stoves will be selected from the best makers for economy in consumption of gas, perfection in cooking, and constructed on the best scien- tific principles. The Gas Committee, in order to make cook- ing by gas a success, will lay all extra services and connect the stoves, whether supplied by the Corporation or anyone else, ready for use free of all expense to the consumer.—By order, JAMES PATERSON, Manager.
